1: Introduction To Constitutional Law: Tutorial 1
Nicole Apsey (30514967)
BAccLLB
A. The Purpose of a Constitution
1. Purpose of a constitution
A constitution serves as the supreme legal framework of a state.[1] A constitution sets out government structures, defines the powers and activities of the state’s institutions, determines how public authority must be executed and it limits governmental power by subjecting all law and conduct to constitutional control. [2]
2. Types Of Constitutions
Flexible V Rigid

Constitutions may be classified according to the ease with which they can be amended.[3] A flexible constitution can be amended through ordinary legislative processes and does not require special procedures or enhanced majorities. By contrast, a rigid (or inflexible) constitution requires special amendment procedures, such as special majorities or referenda, before it may be changed.[4] The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa (1996) is a rigid constitution and sets out how amendments can be made in section 74.[5]

3. Constitutional Law V Other Branches Of Law In South Africa

Constitutional law differs from other branches of law, because it is the supreme law of the Republic and regulates the structure, powers and limits of the state itself.[6] Section 2 of the Constitution states that any law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid.[7] Unlike private law, which governs relationships between individuals, constitutional law governs public power and ensures that all other branches of law operate within constitutional limits. [8]

B. Constitutionalism
4. Define Constitutionalism
Constitutionalism is the principle that governmental power comes from and is limited by the constitution, meaning that the government is not above the law and is constrained by a higher legal framework.[9] Constitutionalism requires all public authority to comply and uphold the law and if do not act in accordance with the law they can be subject to sanctions, which thereby prevents the abuse of power.[10]

5. Explain what it means in the South African context.
In the South African context, constitutionalism reflects the shift from parliamentary supremacy under apartheid to constitutional supremacy under the 1996 Constitution.[11] The South African Constitution states that all public powers must now comply with the Constitution and its foundational values of dignity, equality and freedom.[12]
6. Explain the concept of constitutional supremacy.
Constitutional supremacy means that the Constitution is the highest law of the Republic.[13] Section 2 of the constitution states that any law or conduct that is inconsistent with the constitution is invalid.[14] Courts are empowered to review legislation and executive action to ensure compliance all is compliant with the Constitution.[15] This places the Constitution above Parliament and all other branches of government.
7. Briefly explain why South Africa is sometimes described as ‘quasi-federal’.
South Africa is sometimes described as quasi-federal because the South African governmental authority is divided into national, provincial and local spheres that are interdependent and interrelated.[16] Provinces in South Africa have been allocated constitutional powers, but sovereignty ultimately rests in the Constitution rather than in the provinces themselves.[17] The system therefore contains federal features without constituting a classic federation and that is why it can be called ‘quasi-federal’.

C. Separation of Powers and State Institutions
8. Three branches of government in South Africa.
The three branches of government in South Africa are the legislature, executive, and judiciary.[18]
9. The primary function of each branch of government.
The legislature branch makes legislation and overseas the executive branch.[19] The executive branch adopts and implements government policy and administers state affairs.[20] The judiciary branch interprets and applies the law, including enforcing the compliance to the constitution when law or conduct is unconstitutional.[21]
10. Principle of separation of powers.
The principle of the separation of powers is that government power is divided among three branches so that each performs different functions and remains institutionally independent, which prevents the misuse of power in one branch.[22] This division also supports accountability because each branch can act as a check on the others, reducing the risk of authoritarian control or abuse.[23]

D. The Preamble and the Injustices of the Past (6)
11. Purpose of a preamble (with reference to City of Tshwane Metropolitan Municipality v Afriforum.)
In City of Tshwane, the Court describes a preamble as a summarised statement that sets out a constitution’s purpose and underlying philosophy.[24] In the South African constitution, the Preamble is used to express the Constitution’s commitments, such as recognising past injustice and committing to healing divisions.[25]
12. What is meant by the “injustices of the past” (2)
“Injustices of the past” refers to the systemic harms created by colonialism and apartheid, including racial domination, exclusion, and the privileging of one group’s history and identity over others.[26]
13. How have these injustices influenced the structure, values and rights contained in the Constitution? (2)
The structure, values and rights contained in the Constitution have been influenced by the injustices of the past which can be seen in the Preamble which explicitly recognises past injustices and commits the state to healing divisions, social justice, and fundamental human rights.[27] Second, they influence the Constitution’s structure and legal design, including constitutional supremacy (so that abuses of public power can be challenged and struck down) and a rights framework aimed at transforming society rather than maintaining historical inequality.[28]

1 Journey to the 1996 Constitution
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, was the product of a
negotiated constitutional transition and was structured through a two-stage process to
balance democratic legitimacy and political compromise.
The historic transition began with the 1st stage of the constitutional process. During
the 1st stage, the Interim Constitution of 1993 was adopted through negotiations
between the apartheid government, the National Party, and the liberation movements
to facilitate the transition. The transition occurred due to South Africa’s history as a
deeply divided society characterised by conflict, injustice and racial domination, as
recognised in the Certification Judgement. 1 The Negotiations formally began in 1990
to avoid civil conflict and establish a democratic order. 2
During negotiations, a deadlock arose because the negotiating parties were not
democratically elected, and minority groups feared domination by majority rule. 3 As
explained in the Certification judgment, this impasse was resolved through a
compromise. The compromise provided that an interim government would govern the
country, while a democratically elected Constitutional Assembly would draft the final
Constitution. 4
The Interim Constitution also included binding Constitutional Principles, which
ensured that the final Constitution would reflect agreed fundamental values and
protect minority interests. 5 The Constitutional Assembly, elected through universal
suffrage, drafted and adopted the 1996 Constitution, which only came into force after
certification by the Constitutional Court. 6
The Constitution therefore resulted from a negotiated and legally structured
transition, balancing democratic legitimacy with political compromise.
1 Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 1996 (4) SA 744 (CC) para 5.
2 Ibid para 11.
3 Ibid para 12.
4 Ibid para 13.
5 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 200 of 1993 sch 4.
6 Certification judgment (note 1 above) paras 16–17.
2Student Number: 30514967 Module: Constitutional Law 178
2 Certification Of The Constitution
In Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 (4) SA 744
(CC), the Constitutional Court made it clear that its role in the certification process was
strictly legal rather than political because it possessed a judicial and not a political mandate,
which makes the certification task a strictly legal exercise.
The Court held that its opinion on the political process was irrelevant because its
task was limited to determining whether the new constitutional text complied with the
Constitutional Principles.7
The new constitutional text’s authority is derived from the Interim Constitution, which
required it to assess compliance with pre-agreed legal standards rather than the
fairness or desirability of the negotiations that produced the Constitution.8
The Court emphasised that certification required an objective legal evaluation that
was independent of the political compromises underlying the drafting process.9 It
further stressed that all provisions of the Constitution had to comply with the
Constitutional Principles, regardless of the level of political agreement or support.10 In
this sense, the Court’s role was to enforce what it described as the “solemn pact”
embodied in the Constitutional Principles.11
This approach reflects the principle of constitutional supremacy, ensuring that the
validity of the Constitution is determined by legal standards rather than political
considerations. The Court therefore excluded the political process from its reasoning
in order to act as an independent legal arbiter ensuring strict compliance with the
Constitutional Principles.
7 Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 1996 (4) SA 744 (CC) para 1.
8 Ibid para 17.
9 Ibid paras 1–2.
10 Ibid para 17.
11 Ibid para 15.
3Student Number: 30514967 Module: Constitutional Law 178
3 The constitution’s transformative nature
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, is widely regarded as a
transformative constitution because it seeks to fundamentally reshape South African
society rather than merely regulate it.
First, the Constitution represents a decisive break from apartheid, replacing a
system of racial domination with one based on human rights, democracy and dignity.
As emphasised by Langa, the Constitution provides a framework for transforming
society and addressing the inequalities of the past.12
Second, the Constitution embodies the idea of a “historic bridge” from a deeply
divided past to a democratic and inclusive future. Mureinik describes this transition as
a movement from a culture of authority to a culture of justification, in which all exercises
of public power must be justified.13
Third, the Constitution promotes substantive equality, requiring not only formal
equality before the law but also the redress of past disadvantage and the redistribution
of power and resources.14
Fourth, the Constitution mandates the transformation of state institutions and
society, requiring active efforts to restructure power relations and promote democratic
participation.15
Finally, transformation is understood as a long-term project that requires continuous
development to achieve dignity, equality and social justice.16
The Constitution is therefore transformative because it provides a framework for
deep structural change aimed at achieving equality, dignity and democratic
participation in South African society.
12 Langa ‘Transformative Constitutionalism’ (2006) 17 Stellenbosch Law Review 351.
13 Mureinik ‘A Bridge to Where?’ (1994) 10 South African Journal on Human Rights 31.
14 Langa (note 12).
15 Ibid.
16 Ibid.
4Student Number: 30514967 Module: Constitutional Law 178
4 The constitution’s transformative nature
In Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 1996 (4) SA
744 (CC), the Constitutional Court was required to determine whether the new
constitutional text complied with the Constitutional Principles set out in the Interim
Constitution.
The Court found that not all provisions of the new constitutional text complied with
the Constitutional Principles, which was a requirement for certification.17 It emphasised
that complete compliance was required, rather than mere substantial compliance.18
The Court identified several structural deficiencies, including concerns relating to
the separation of powers, the allocation of powers between national and provincial
government, and the adequacy of institutional safeguards.19 It also stressed that its
task required it to evaluate every provision both individually and collectively against
the Constitutional Principles.20
Because these requirements were not fully satisfied, the Court refused to certify the
Constitution. This decision demonstrates the Court’s role in strictly enforcing the
Constitutional Principles as binding legal standards.
17 Certification judgment (note 1 above) para 17.
18 Ibid.
19 Ibid chs IV–VII.
20 Ibid para 2.

1 Vertical v Horizontal Application of the Bill of Rights
Vertical application concerns the relationship between the state and persons. In this
setting, the Bill of Rights binds the legislature, the executive, the judiciary and all
organs of state, as stated in section 8(1) of the Constitution.
1 The question this poses
is, therefore, whether the law or state conduct unjustifiably infringes a protected right.
For example, if a public school, municipality, police official or government department
excludes a person from a benefit because of race, that conduct implicates the right to
equality. It may be attacked as unconstitutional state conduct.
2
Horizontal application concerns the relationship between private persons or private
entities. Section 8(2) of the Constitution recognises that a provision of the Bill of Rights
can bind a natural or juristic person if, and to the extent that, it is applicable, having
regard to the nature of the right and the nature of the duty imposed by that right.
3
Section 8(3) then instructs courts, when applying a right horizontally, to give effect to
that right by applying or, where necessary, developing the common law consistently
with constitutional values.4
The right to equality is a useful example. Vertically, a person may rely on section 9
where the state discriminates unfairly. Horizontally, a person may rely on equality
where a private actor or entity discriminates unfairly, because section 9(4) expressly
states that no person may unfairly discriminate directly or indirectly against anyone.5
1 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 ("Constitution") s 8(1).
2 Constitution ss 9(1)-(3); D Kleyn, F Viljoen, E Zitzke & P Madi Beginner's Guide for Law Students 5
ed (2018) 192.
3 Constitution s 8(2).
4 Constitution s 8(3); Constitution s 39(2).
5 Constitution ss 9(1)-(4).N Apsey (30514967) Introduction to Constitutional Law 178 – Tutorial 4
If a privately owned restaurant refuses to serve a customer because of their race, it is
not merely a private societal wrong; it is a constitutional equality problem given
legislative effect through the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair
Discrimination Act 4 of 2000.
6 This shows how horizontal application may operate
directly, where a constitutional right binds private actors, and indirectly, where
legislation such as PEPUDA or the development of the common law gives effect to
constitutional values in private relationships.
The distinct difference between vertical and horizontal application is that vertical
application controls public power, while horizontal application extends constitutional
duties into private legal relationships where the right and corresponding duty justify
constitutional control.
2 Representative and Participatory Democracy in South Africa
South Africa is primarily a representative constitutional democracy, but the
Constitution also contains participatory and limited direct democratic features.
Representative democracy is the dominant institutional form, meaning citizens do not
ordinarily make national laws themselves, but elect representatives who exercise
public power through constitutional institutions.
The representative character of the South African democracy is clear from section
1(d), which founds the Republic on universal adult suffrage, a national common voters’
roll, regular elections and a multi-party democratic government system.7 Section 19
gives every citizen political rights, including the right to vote in elections and stand for
public office.8 Parliament represents the people and provides a national forum for
6 Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000 (“PEPUDA”); Kleyn et al
Beginner's Guide 192-193.
7 Constitution s 1(d).
8 Constitution s 19(3).N Apsey (30514967) Introduction to Constitutional Law 178 – Tutorial 4
public consideration of issues, which are also addressed by elected legislative bodies
at provincial and local levels.9
However, the Constitution also contains direct and participatory democratic
mechanisms. The National Assembly, the National Council of Provinces and provincial
legislatures are required to facilitate public involvement in their legislative and other
processes.10 Local government must encourage the involvement of communities and
community organisations in local government matters.11 Citizens also enjoy rights to
assemble, demonstrate, picket and petition, and the President and Premiers have
constitutional powers to call national and provincial referenda respectively.
12
Accordingly, South Africa is primarily a representative constitutional democracy, but
its democratic design is enriched by participatory and direct democratic features. The
Constitution does not reduce democracy to voting every few years; it requires
continuing accountability, responsiveness, openness and public participation.
3 Value-Based Constitutionalism and the Culture of Justification
Value-based constitutionalism means that the Constitution is not merely a set of
institutional rules, but a normative legal order structured around constitutional values.
These values guide the creation, interpretation, application and limitation of law.
Section 1 entrenches founding values such as human dignity, the achievement of
equality, the advancement of human rights and freedoms, non-racialism, non-sexism,
constitutional supremacy, the rule of law, universal adult suffrage, accountability,
responsiveness and openness.13 The Bill of Rights further affirms the democratic
values of human dignity, equality and freedom.
14
9 Constitution ss 1(d), 19(3), 42(3), 46(1), 105(1) and 157(2).
10 Constitution ss 59(1)(a), 72(1)(a) and 118(1)(a).
11 Constitution s 152(1)(e).
12 Constitution ss 17, 84(2)(g), and 127(2)(f).
13 Constitution s 1.
14 Constitution s 7(1).N Apsey (30514967) Introduction to Constitutional Law 178 – Tutorial 4
This matters because South African constitutional adjudication is not mechanical.
Courts must ask whether law and conduct are consistent with the values of an open
and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom. Section 36
requires those values to guide the justification of rights limitations,15 and section 39
requires courts to promote those values when interpreting the Bill of Rights, legislation,
the common law and customary law.
16
Value-based constitutionalism also marks a break from apartheid legality. Under
apartheid, law often demanded obedience without moral or democratic justification.
Mureinik famously described the new constitutional order as a movement from a
culture of authority to a culture of justification, in which every exercise of public power
should be justified to those affected by it.17 Langa CJ similarly explained transformative
constitutionalism as a project of change from a deeply unequal past towards a society
based on substantive equality, human rights and democratic accountability.
18
Therefore, value-based constitutionalism means that legality is not enough in a thin,
formal sense that a rule merely exists. Law must be interpreted and exercised in a
manner faithful to the Constitution’s deeper commitments to dignity, equality, freedom,
openness, accountability, non-racialism, non-sexism and the rule of law.
4 S v Makwanyane and the Proportionality Test under Section 36
S v Makwanyane and Another 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC) concerned the constitutionality
of the death penalty under the interim Constitution. The applicants had been convicted
of serious offences, including murder, and sentenced to death.19 The Appellate
Division postponed the appeal against the death sentences so that the Constitutional
Court could decide whether section 277(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of
15 Constitution s 36(1).
16 Constitution s 39(1)-(2).
17 E Mureinik “A Bridge to Where? Introducing the Interim Bill of Rights” (1994) 10 South African
Journal on Human Rights 31 31-32.
18 Langa “Transformative Constitutionalism” (2006) 17 Stellenbosch Law Review 351 351-353.
19 S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC) paras 1-3.N Apsey (30514967) Introduction to Constitutional Law 178 – Tutorial 4
1977, which authorised capital punishment for murder, was consistent with the
Constitution.
20
Although the historic case was decided under section 33 of the Interim Constitution,
it remains central to section 36 of the 1996 Constitution because the First Certification
judgment explained that section 36(1) substantially repeats the limitation approach
formulated in S v Makwanyane.
21 The core question is whether a rights limitation is
reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society based on human dignity,
equality and freedom.
In S v Makwanyane, Chaskalson P held that the limitation of constitutional rights
involves the weighing up of competing values and ultimately an assessment based on
proportionality. There is no absolute standard for reasonableness and necessity. The
inquiry must be conducted case by case, balancing the nature and importance of the
right, the purpose of the limitation, the extent of the limitation, the relation between the
limitation and its purpose, and whether less restrictive means are available.22
Applying that approach, the Court recognised that the state had important aims,
including: deterrence of violent crime, prevention of further murders, retribution and
public safety.23 However, those aims had to be balanced against the rights and values
at stake. The death penalty destroys life, it assaults dignity, involves the risk of
arbitrariness and error and operates in a criminal justice system where social and
racial inequality have historically shaped who is most likely to receive the hardest
punishment.24
20 Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977 s 277(1)(a).
21 Interim Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 200 of 1993 s 33 (“Interim Constitution”);
Constitution s 36(1); Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 1996 (4) SA
744 (CC) para 90.
22 S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC) para 104.
23 S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC) paras 111-112 and 116-129.
24 S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC) paras 26-27, 135 and 145.N Apsey (30514967) Introduction to Constitutional Law 178 – Tutorial 4
The Court was not fully persuaded that capital punishment was materially more
effective than life imprisonment as a deterrent. Prevention could also be achieved
through long-term or life imprisonment. Retribution was accepted as a legitimate
purpose of punishment, but it could not carry the same constitutional weight as life and
dignity. Although public opinion favoured capital punishment, the Court held that even
public opinion could not replace the Court’s duty to uphold the Constitution.
25
The Court concluded that the state had not made the clear and convincing case
required to justify the death penalty. Section 277(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act
was held to be inconsistent with the Constitution to the extent that it authorised the
death penalty for murder. The practical result was that the death penalty could no
longer be imposed or carried out, and persons under sentence of death had to be dealt
with according to constitutionally valid sentencing law.
26
The significance of S v Makwanyane for section 36 is that it established South
African limitation analysis as a proportionality inquiry. In the South African context,
rights are no longer absolute; in every case, the state must justify any limitation by
showing that the limitation serves a sufficiently important purpose, is properly
connected to that purpose, impairs the right no more than is constitutionally
acceptable, and is proportionate in light of the values of human dignity, equality and
freedom.
25 S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC) paras 87-89 and 116-129.
26 S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC) para 146; Kleyn et al Beginner's Guide 282-283.N Apsey (30514967) Introduction to Constitutional Law 178 – Tutorial 4

Characteristics of Constitutionalism

and structures in terms of a written constitution
3. Describes nature and basis of relationship between the
institutions and structuresConstitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Characteristics of Constitutionalism
4. Provides the creation of binding rules/ laws for institutions
5. 6. and those who they govern
Places limits on exercise of public (state power)
Structure state and award and constrain powerConstitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Descriptive understanding of Constitutionalism
• Factual description of structures and institutions
• Focus on EXPLAINING how these institutions work,
inter4act with each other, share and distribute power etc
• Without reference to norms or normative values on
which constitutional system is evaluated by
• Focused on form rather than substance
• Colonial / Apartheid South Africa ConstitutionalismConstitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Prescriptive understanding of Constitutionalism
• With reference to norms / normative values on which
the constitutional system is based
• Constitutional system should adhere to some basic
doctrines, principles etc
• This is the approach the new Democratic South Africa
takesConstitutionalism (de Vos 2.2) Key Aspects of Prescriptive Constitutionalism
• Constitutional Supremacy
• Limited Government
• Rule of Law
• Separation of Powers
• Democratic self government
• Protection of Human Rights
• Independent Judiciary
• Transformative Constitutionalism
Constitutionalism is considered essential for a functional democratic
stateConstitutional Supremacy
Most definitive feature of SA post-apartheid constitutional
system is Constitutional Supremacy
• The foundation of our democratic constitutional
dispensation
• Is a Founding Value and a binding enforceable rule
- S1(c) (Value) ; S2 (binding rule)Constitutional Supremacy
• Constitutional supremacy renders the constitution judicable
o Any law or conduct can be tested against the provisions
of the constitution and must be declared unconstitutional
and invalid if they fail to comply with these provisions
o Given justiciability of Constitution – an important aspect of
constitutional supremacy is judicial review
o Judicial review enjoins court to declare any law/ conduct
inconstant with the Constitution invalid.Transformative
ConstitutionalismTransformative Constitutionalism:
• The 1996 Constitution is seen as inherently
transformative
o Because: the central aim of the Constitution is to move
from an unjust past to a just future
o The founding values in S1 confirm the intention to break
from the pastTransformative Constitutionalism:
S1 Values:
• Human dignity and equality,
• Non-racism and non-sexism,
• Supremacy of the Constitution,
• and Universal adult suffrage
Transformation as a principle is, therefore, foundational to
constitutional interpretationDefining Transformative Constitutionalism:
• No single fixed definition of Transformative Constitutionalism
• Most famous is from Prof Kare Klare:
Transformative constitutionalism:
• “Long-term project of constitutional enactment, interpretation and
enforcement committed (not in isolation, but in the historical context of
conducive political developments) to transforming [South Africa’s]
political and social institutions and power relationship in a democratic,
participatory, and egalitarian direction” (Kleyn et al page 52).Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
1) Long term – it will not happen overnight – is 30+ years enough to
address +250 years of colonial and apartheid history?
2) Interpretation and enforcement, not isolation but in context
3) Substantive equality: goes beyond formal legal rights to ensure
economic and social rights are realized, reducing structural inequality
4) Proactive role of the law: Unlike liberal traditions that see constitutions as static
shields, this approach views them as swords for social change and proactive
instruments for justice.Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
5) Rights Protections and Promotion: It encourages a social and
legal culture dedicated to upholding human dignity and democracy in
daily interactions.
6) Non-violent ”revolution”: It is often described as an "enterprise of
inducing large-scale social change through nonviolent political
processes grounded in lawDefining Transformative Constitutionalism:
• KK states TC is:
➢ Social
➢ redistributive,
➢ Caring,
➢ Positive,
➢ at least partly horizontal,
➢ participatory,
➢ egalitarian,
➢ multicultural and
➢ self-conscious about its
historical setting and
transformative role and
mission.
➢ ( see De Vos section 1.4)The Concept of Transformative Constitutionalism:
Constitutional Supremacy:
• Fundemental aspect of Transformative consitutionallism
• The Constitution is the highest law
o It should facilitate and enable fundamental political,
economic, social and cultural change
o
“Historical self consciousness” – redress and undoing of
the legacy of colonialism and Apartheid ( post-amble IC)
o Building a future – based on fundamental human rights,
democracy, and social justice (Preamble 1996 Constitution)The Concept of Transformative Constitutionalism:
• Value-based concept of democracy :
o S7(1) 1996 Constitution
o “This Bill of Rights is a cornerstone of democracy in
South Africa. It enshrines the rights of all people in our
country and affirms the democratic values of human
dignity, equality and freedom.
”
o Designed for social and structural changeTransformative Constitutionalism:
CJ P Langa:
• Paper was presented Annual Human Rights Lecture (Stellenbosch) 2006
• See the Constitution is a “bridge” (think back to post-amble discussion)
between the unjust, divided past and a future based on rights, equality,
and dignity
• He States the objective of the constitution is to establish a truly equal
society
• This includes provision of basic socio-economic rights to all
Transformation, therefore, looks at making a commitment to changeTransformative Constitutionalism
• Soobramoney v Minister of Health 1997 (CC) para 8: "We live in a
society in which there are great disparities in wealth. Millions of people are
living in deplorable conditions and in great poverty. There is a high level of
unemployment, inadequate social security, and many do not have access
to clean water or to adequate health services. These conditions already
existed when the Constitution was adopted and a commitment to
address them, and to transform our society into one in which there will
be human dignity, freedom and equality, lies at the heart of our new
constitutional order.
”
• Highlights that it is both backwards and forward lookingTransformative Constitutionalism:
CJ P Langa:
Culture of Justification: “The Constitution demands that all
decisions be capable of being substantively defended in terms of
rights and values that it enshrines. It is no longer sufficient for
judges to rely on the say-so of parliament or technical readings of
legislation as providing justifications for their decisions. Under a
transformative constitution, judges bear the ultimate
responsibility to justify their decisions not only by reference to
authority, but by reference to ideas and values.
”Transformative Constitutionalism:
CJ P Langa - Legal education and TC
o Cannot just blindly accept legal principles because of the authority
o Values of the Constitution must be instilled
o Must critically engage with constitutional vlaies
o “A truly transformative South Africa requires a new approach that
places constitutional dream at the very heart of legal education”
o Change in mindset – not just change of lawsTransformative Constitutionalism:
LLB standard:
• requires that “transformative constitutionalism” and its core
philosophy are suitable understood by law faculties, appropriately
embedded in curricula at all levels of the LLB programme and
internalised by students
• When you study
Theme 4: The
Constitution of 1996:
Basic Principles,
Concepts and
DoctrinesRecapUnderstanding the 1996 Constitution
• To understand the 1996 Constitution, you need to:
1) Understand the context in which it originates and operates
2) Understand the fundamental doctrines, concepts and
principles the constitution containsConstitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
• The theory of constitutional law
• Philosophy and doctrine that the governmental authority is
derived from, and limited by a body of (written) fundamental
law (ie a constitution)
• Ensures that rulers act according to binding boundaries and
not their own desiresConstitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
• In essence, constitutionalism is the notion that a constitution
must both STUCTURE and CONSTRAIN state power
o A constitution must establish the institutions and
structures of government and allocate power to them for
effective governing, AND
o It must limit and disperse that power among the I
institutions and structures in an attempt to ensure that
power will not be abusedConstitutional Supremacy
• Constitutional supremacy renders the constitution judicable
o Any law or conduct can be tested against the provisions
of the constitution and must be declared unconstitutional
and invalid if they fail to comply with these provisions
o Given justiciability of Constitution – an important aspect of
constitutional supremacy is judicial review
o Judicial review enjoins court to declare any law/ conduct
inconstant with the Constitution invalid.Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
• No single fixed definition of Transformative Constitutionalism
• Most famous is from Prof Kare Klare:
Transformative constitutionalism:
• “Long-term project of constitutional enactment, interpretation and
enforcement committed (not in isolation, but in the historical context of
conducive political developments) to transforming [South Africa’s]
political and social institutions and power relationship in a democratic,
participatory, and egalitarian direction” (Kleyn et al page 52).Transformative Constitutionalism
• Soobramoney v Minister of Health 1997 (CC) para 8: "We live in a
society in which there are great disparities in wealth. Millions of people are
living in deplorable conditions and in great poverty. There is a high level of
unemployment, inadequate social security, and many do not have access
to clean water or to adequate health services. These conditions already
existed when the Constitution was adopted and a commitment to
address them, and to transform our society into one in which there will
be human dignity, freedom and equality, lies at the heart of our new
constitutional order.
”
• Highlights that it is both backwards and forward lookingTransformative Constitutionalism: Criticism
• It is often praised for its ambitious goals, particularly in post-
apartheid South Africa
• BUT that does not mean it does not face several
significant criticismsCriticism: Persistent Inequality and Slow Pace
of Change
• The promised large scale social and economic transformation
remains unfulfilled despite a transformative legal framework
• Critics point to the persistent racialised poverty and inequality
as evidence that the project has failed to meet popular
expectations
• Critics claim that transformative constitutionalism cannot solve
deeply structural problems, such as land reformCriticism: Transformative Constitutionalism is
too Court Centric
• Critics argue that the project relies too heavily on the role of the
judiciary to achieve social change
• There is a burden of expectation placed on courts that courts cannot be
met through adjudicative means alone
• Krle Klares ' original concept of TC is seen as overly focused on the role of
lawyers and judges
• Counter-majoritarian Concerns: the focus on judicial intervention as the
main driver for change can be seen as a counter-majoritarian manifestation
that prevents more direct, political paths to social justiceCriticism: Transformative Constitutionalism is
too Court Centric
Counter-Majoritarian Dilemma Continued:
• the CMD is a legal and political concept describing the tension between
democratic majority rule and judicial review where unelected judges
invalidate laws created by elected representatives
• It questions why an unelected judiciary can override the will of the majority,
• Example: The constitutional Court overturning parliamentary actions to
align with the supreme constitutionCriticism: Transformative Constitutionalism is
too Court Centric
• IE Transformative constitutionalism, as the main theory to effect
change, is a court-driven process
• ‘Therefore, is it my contention that within the context of South Africa’s
prevailing conservative legal culture, the extent to which the success of
transformative constitutionalism as an enterprise depends on legal and
judicial interpretation leaves the project in danger of remaining and
incomplete project at best.
’ S Sibanda ‘Not Purpose Made …
’ 2011
Stell LR 493Criticism:
S Sibanda “Not yet Uhuru” Phd thesis Wits (2018) 224-225.
• Transformative constitutionalism has “not translated into much more
than rights or law-based approaches to driving change with little
evidence of other work within the discourse directed at
inculcating social, economic or cultural institutional or
structural power shifts or innovations beyond the courts”
…
transformative constitutionalism, as it has become to be understood
(as a strictly legal concept given meaning to by primarily the courts,
to the exclusion of other political actors) is not able to solve complex
questions such as those raised during the #Feesmustfall protests;
questions as to who is included in determining and shaping a
transformed society.
-Criticism: The Liberal Compromise
• A radical criticism is that the South African constitutional
arrangement represents an unacceptable compromise that
preserves the apartheid era socio-economic order rather
than achieving a true radical break
• Deconial critique: Some argue that transformative
constitutionalism is a misfit for the quest to decolonise, as it
may still be rooted in Western legal traditions and colonial
pedagogiesCriticism: “Fetishism of the Law”
• Some critics point to “constitutional fetishism” or
“constitutional worship”
• Some critics see the way we interact with the constitution in a
similar way to a religion, with its own “theology” (foundational
values), “priests” (judges), and “pieties” (legal protocols).
• Some argue that such “worship” can lead to form “anti-
intellectualism, where the constitution is treated as the ”exclusive
horizon” for all social and political change, silencing any alternative
radical or political ideasTask: Transformative Constitutionalism
Scenario: A group of residents in an informal settlement have been
living without access to adequate housing, water, or sanitation for
years.
They approach the courts, arguing that the government has failed
to realise their socio-economic rights under the constitutionTask: Discuss in Small Groups
1 )How could the doctrine of transformative constitutionalism support
the residents' claim
2) What role does the court play in this situation
3) What are some of the criticisms of using the Constitution in this way
• Are the courts overstepping into government decisions
• Is the transformation happening too slowly?
• Does law alone solve structural inequality
4) Do you think South Africa is being transformed by the constitution, or
is transformation more aspirational???
Theme 4: The
Constitution of 1996:
Basic Principles,
Concepts and
DoctrinesRecapTransformative Constitutionalism: Criticism
1) Persistent Inequality and Slow Pace of Change
2) Is too Court Centric
3) Liberal Compromise
4) Fetishism of the lawValue based constitutionalism
• Value-based constitutionalism is a legal concept that emphasises
that constitutions are not just legal, procedural documents but
are rooted in core ethical, moral, and social values.
• It prioritises these underlying principles to guide the
interpretation of rights and laws.
• Constitutional values are the foundational principles that underpin
a democratic state's legal framework and guide its governance.Value based constitutionalism
S1 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996
The Republic of South Africa is one, sovereign, democratic state founded on the
following values:
(a) Human dignity, the achievement of equality and the advancement of human
rights and freedoms.
(b) (b) Non-racialism and non-sexism.
(c) c) Supremacy of the constitution and the rule of law.(
(d) d) Universal adult suffrage, a national common voters' roll, regular elections and a
multi-party system of democratic government, to ensure accountability,
responsiveness and opennessValue based constitutionalism
Some Core Values and Application
• Human Dignity: Often positioned as the core value,
underpinning the right to self-worth.
• Equality: Demands substantive equality - addressing
structural barriers and historic disadvantage - rather
than just formal, equal treatment.
• Freedom: Includes liberty of thought, expression, and
action.Value based constitutionalism
• The values of human dignity, equality and freedom (and others) permeate the
legal system
• What does this mean in practice?
• Courts do not only ask “ what does the law say”
• They also ask “what outcome will best reflect the constitutional values
• Once again represents a break from the injustices of the past
• The Constitution aims to build a just, inclusive, and democratic society
(refer back to discussion on Transformative Constitutionalism)Value based constitutionalism
• Value-based constitutionalism, therefore, contrasts with
strict legal positivism
• Constitutional interpretation in South Africa is therefore seen
to be more moral, purposive, and transformative.Value based constitutionalism
Interpretation
• These values are used in the interpretation of the Bill of Rights
• S39(1): when interpreting the rights within the Bill of Rights... a
court…must promote the values that underlie an open and
democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom.
• Developing common law or customary law
• S39(2): When developing the common law or customary law,
every court… must promote the spirit, purport and objects of the
Bill of RightsValue based constitutionalism
• When interpreting legislation
• S39(2) when interpreting legislation, every court….must promote spirit, purport and objects
of the Bill of Rights
• Daniels v Campbell 2004 (5) SA 331 (CC):
• Case looked at where the term “spouse” as used in the Intestate Succession Act and
Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act includes a surviving spouse to a Muslim marriage
• Justice Sachs [para12]: “In the present matter the constitutional values of equality,
tolerance and respect for diversity point strongly in favour of giving the word ‘spouse'
[in Intestate Succession Act …] a broad and inclusive construction, the more so when it
corresponds with the ordinary meaning of the word.”Value based constitutionalism
Foundational Case: S v Makwayane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC)
• Facts:
• Makwanyane and Mchunu were convicted in the Witwatersrand Local Division on
four counts of murder and sentenced to death under section 277(1)(a) of
the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977.
• Their appeal raised a constitutional challenge under the Interim Constitution of
1993, arguing that the death penalty violated the rights to life (section 9), human
dignity (section 10), and protection against cruel, inhuman, or degrading
punishment (section 11(2))
• The case was referred to the newly created Constitutional Court, marking the first
constitutional review of legislation in post-apartheid South Africa.Value based constitutionalism
Foundational Case: S v Makwayane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC)
• The appellants contended that the death penalty was incompatible with
the Constitution’s foundational values of human rights .
• The State argued that deterrence, retribution, and public opinion
justified retaining the death penalty.
• The Court considered whether such justifications could limit
constitutional rights under the limitations clause and whether public
opinion could influence constitutional interpretationValue based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
• Rights are not absolute – they can in certain circumstances, be limited
• S36 contains a limitation clause – that ALLOWS for the
constitutionally valid limitation of rights in certain circumstances
• Limitation is determined by a two stage enquiry
• First court must established a right has been infringed upon
(limited)
• Second the court must determine whether it is justifiableValue based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
S36 Constitution, 1996 (S33 (1) IC)
• S36: The rights in the Bill of Rights may be limited only in terms of the law of
general application, to the extent that the limitation is reasonable and justifiable
in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality, and
freedom
• Factors to guide whether the limitation is reasonable and justifiable
• Nature of the right
• Importance and relationship between the purpose of limitation and the
limitation
• There are no less restrictive means to achieve the purposeValue based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
Re: S v Walters [para 26-27] : This is essentially a two-stage exercise. First, there is the threshold
enquiry aimed at determining whether or not the enactment in question constitutes a limitation on one or
other guaranteed right. This entails examining (a) the content and scope of the relevant protected right(s)
and (b) the meaning and effect of the impugned enactment to see whether there is any limitation of (a) by
(b). Subsections (1) and (2) of section 39 of the Constitution provide guidance on the interpretation of both
the rights and the enactment, essentially requiring that they be interpreted to promote the value system
of an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom. If upon such
analysis no limitation is found, that is the end of the matter. The constitutional challenge is dismissed there
and then.
If there is indeed a limitation, however, the second stage ensues. This is ordinarily called the limitations
exercise. In essence this requires a weighing-up of the nature and importance of the right(s) that are limited
together with the extent of the limitation as against the importance and purpose of the limiting enactment.Value based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
(Stage 2) the reasonable and justifiable enquiry
<Rieette.Venter@nwu.ac.za>Value based constitutionalism
S v Makwanyane
• The court found that the death penalty “Places persons beyond the pale of
humanity” and “uses a person as a tool for crime control”
• The death penalty violates the rights as found in the Bill of Rights (first leg of test)
• Was this limitation justifiable in terms of s36 (Second Leg of test)?
• Is the purpose of the limitation acceptable in an open and democratic
society based on values of human dignity, equality and freedom?Value based constitutionalism
S v Makwanyane
• Is there a justifiable limitation based on the stated purpose?
• Retribution
• Prevention
• Deterrence
• Constitutional Valid purpose of limitation?
• Rational connection between purpose and limitation?
• Less invasive means to achieve the purpose ?
• Proportionality – weighing up of the factorsValue based constitutionalism
S v Makwanyane
• The crux of it is that the court looked at the constitutional value of
human dignity to determine that there was no justifiable reason to
limit the Right to Life as found in the Bill of Rights through the use of the
death penaltyValue based constitutionalism
Balancing competing rights using values
• Courts balance competing rights by asking which outcome best reflects
constitutional values.
• Port Elizabeth Municipality v Various Occupiers2005 (1) SA 217 (CC))
• Competing rights – right to private property and right to housing
• Justice Sachs emphasised that fairness required considering both the
owners’ rights and the occupiers’ human dignity, especially in the
context of South Africa’s history of forced removals.Value-based constitutionalism
Values driving social transformation
• As discussed under Transformative Constitutionalism, one of the goals of the Constitution,
1996 is to change and transform society, not just resolve disputes.
• Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie 2006 (1) SA 524 (CC)
• Right to Equality and Same-sex marriage
• Justice Sachs Denying same-sex couples access to marriage contravened rights and
values of equality and human dignity. Excluding same-sex couples from marriage rendered
them “outsiders” to society’s central institution of love and commitment.
• Religious objections were rejected on the ground that South Africa’s democracy requires
the coexistence of sacred and secular spheres
• Framed marriage equality as integral to post-apartheid constitutional values of dignity,
equality, and freedom.Value-based constitutionalism
1. Normative
• The Constitution is based on moral values, not just legal rules
2. Interpretive
• Values guide how courts understand and apply rights
3. Transformative
• The Constitution aims to change society and address injustice
4. Contextual
• Must respond to and reflect South Africa’s social and historical context
5. Counter-majoritarian
• Courts can uphold values even against public opinionClass task:
Scenario:
• A group of 20 people has been living on unused municipal land for 3 years.
• The municipality now wants to evict them to allow for a private development project that
will bring jobs and infrastructure.
• The residents argue that eviction will leave them homeless.
Task 1 in small groups
• Identify relevant constitutional values
• Decide the outcome
• Should the eviction be allowed?
• Discuss which values should carry more weight
• How did your chosen values influence your decision

Constitution of 1996:

Concepts and
DoctrinesRecapValue Based Constitutionalism
• Value-based constitutionalism is a legal concept that emphasises
that constitutions are not just legal, procedural documents but are
rooted in core ethical, moral, and social values.
• What sections give us the Values in the 1996 Constitution?

rights– s36
- Rights are not absolute– can be limited
- What is the two-stage enquiry for the limitation of rights?
• Who can remind me how Constitutional values were used in S v
Makwenyane??Value-based constitutionalism
1. Normative
• The Constitution is based on moral values, not just legal rules
2. Interpretive
• Values guide how courts understand and apply rights
3. Transformative
• The Constitution aims to change society and address injustice
4. Contextual
• Must respond to and reflect South Africa’s social and historical context
5. Counter-majoritarian

Scenario:
• A group of 20 people has been living on unused municipal land for 3 years.
• The municipality now wants to evict them to allow for a private development project that
will bring jobs and infrastructure.
• The residents argue that eviction will leave them homeless.
Task 1 in small groups
• Identify relevant constitutional values
• Decide the outcome
• Should the eviction be allowed?
• Discuss which values should carry more weight
• How did your chosen values influence your decisionApplication of the
Bill of RightsBill of Rights
• Bill of Rights has been constructed in such a way to give effect
to the transformative vision of the Constitution, 1996
• It sets out a unique human rights vision for South Africa
• The broad range of rights is aimed at facilitating political and
socio-economic transformation in South Africa while
protecting the human dignity of all persons within the State
• It has broad application– both to the State and to private
partiesThe Application of the Bill of Rights
● When litigating the Bill of Rights, the Court
has to determine whether the BOR applies
○ Directly or Indirectly
○ Vertically or HorizontallyThe Application of the Bill of Rights
● Direct application:
○ Direct application of the Bill of Rights occurs when a person, company, or state
organ violates a constitutional right found in chp 2
○ Or when the ordinary rules of law (Legislation, common law, customary law) are
not consistent with the Bill of Rights
○ If they are not, the BOR if applied directly will override these rules of law – ie law
will be declared invalid by the courts
○ Example: company firing a woman due to pregnancy (violating section 9
equality rights), would be unconstitutional and invalid
○ Example: S v Mawanyane– Death Penalty declared unconstitutionalThe Application of the Bill of Rights
● Indirect application: the purpose is to determine whether the ordinary rules of the
law promote the values of the BOR
○ If they do not, the court will use the BOR to develop the rules of law (s39(2))
○ Example: the development of common law to align with constitutional values, as
seen in Carmichelev Minister of Safety and Security . (2001) CC: The Court used
s39(2) to interpret the law of delict to promote rights and constitutional values,
rather than directly invalidating a statute.
■ IE: Instead of declaring a law invalid (direct application), courts interpret
legislation or develop common law/customary law to conform with the Bill
of RightsThe application of the Bill of Rights
● The next question is then, is it a vertical or horizontal
application?
○ This refers to the different relationships and legal
situations in which the Bill of Rights is enforcedThe application of the Bill of Rights
Vertical application
● Governed by s8(1) – looks at the relationship between the state and private
individuals
● Imposes obligations on the state to respect, protect and fulfil rights in the BOR
● Acts an additional check on state power – therefore binds the legislative, executive,
judiciary and all organs of state
● Protects citizens from abuse of power by the government
● Example:
○ A person brings a claim against the police for unlawful arrest, or someone
who challenges a government policy that they claim violates their rightsThe application of the Bill of Rights
Examples of vertical application of rights :
● Right to Equality (Section 9): An individual sues a government department for
refusing to hire or promote them based on race, gender, or sexual orientation.
● Freedom of Expression (Section 16): A journalist or citizen challenges the police
for arresting them for participating in a lawful public protest.
● Right to Access Information (Section 32): A person uses the PAIA act to force a
public body, eg DHA, to disclose records held by the state.The application of the Bill of Rights
● Socio-economic Rights (Sections 26 & 27): Communities challenging the
government for failing to provide adequate, basic water services or, as in
the Grootboom case, reasonable access to housing.
● Right to Fair Trial (Section 35): An accused person argues that their rights were
violated by the police or prosecutor during their arrest or detention.
● Property Rights (Section 25): A landowner challenges the state's expropriation of
their property, arguing it was not done for a public purpose or without fair
compensation.The application of the Bill of Rights
Horizontal application
● Governed by s8(2) – requires considering the nature of the right and duty
imposed
● When applied horizontally, this imposes obligations between private persons
(individuals or companies) to respect the rights of the BOR (in certain
circumstances)
○ Protects citizens from violations of rights by private parties such as unfair
discrimination by an employer
○ IE you don’t have to rely on the common law or legislation – you can say
“this person has violated my constitutional right”The application of the Bill of Rights
Direct Horizontal application
● Governed by s8(2): The BOR applies directly to the conduct of private
individuals, allowing them to rely directly on a constitutional right for a
claim
Indirect Horizontal Application
● S39(2): The BOR influences private law by requiring courts to interpret
legislation or develop the common law in a way that promotes the sprite,
purport, and object of the BORThe application of the Bill of Rights
● Question to the class: Why is it important to have
direct horizontal application of the Bill of Rights?The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 1: Equality (S9)
● Scenario: A private employer refuses to hire someone based on their race,
gender, or disability.
● Even though this is a private employer (not the state) the right to equality
can apply directly
● The private individual can argue, “my constitutional right to equality has
been infringed by this private actor”
● Equality is a right that clearly makes sense in private relationships
(employment, services etc)
● Courts recognised that discrimination is not only a state problemThe application of the Bill of Rights
Example 2: Freedom of Expression (s16)
Scenario: A private media company refuses to publish an opinion article
● The private individual might try to rely on freedom of expression
● BUT the court will have to balance
○ The writers freedom of expression
○ The companies freedom to choose what it publishes
○ Rights can apply directly but can compete with other rights in
private relationshipsThe application of the Bill of Rights
Example 3: Right to housing (s26)
Scenario: A private land owner evicts people living on their land without following the legal
processes
● Those evicted can rely directly on the right to access housing
● They can argue “this eviction violates my right to housing”
● Rights will still apply between the private individuals
● The Court will ask
○ Is eviction just and equitable
○ What processes were followed
○ What is the impact on the vulnerable people
● Again we see competing rights of private individuals as the land owner has his own proterty
rights protected by s25The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 4: Right to education (s29)
Scenario: Private school refuses to admit a learner without a fair and lawful
reason (arbitrary exclusion)
● The learner or parent may rely directly on s29 (right to basic education)
● They can argue “The decision unjusrifably limites my right to education”
● Private schools are private individuals (not the state)The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 4: Right to education (s29)
Scenario: Private school refuses to admit a learner without a fair and lawful reason
(arbitrary exclusion)
● Again, the court will ask :
○ Is exclusion reasonable
○ Does it undermine the right to basic education
○ Are there other justifications such as contractual or policy justifications
○ Nuance: The right to basic education is a very strong right (immediately
realisable)
○ But the balance will be with the school's autonomy to decide who they admitThe application of the Bill of Rights
Key take aways from the examples:
● Rights can shape private relationships, especially where there is
○ A power imbalance
○ Basic human needs are effected
● Direct horizontal application means you can use the constitution itself in disputes with
other private parties – but courts will always ask whether it is appropriate nd how rights
should be balanced
● It will depend on
○ The nature of the right
○ The relationship between the parties
○ And the need to balance competing rightsThe application of the Bill of Rights
Class task:
● Look through the rights in Chapter 2 of the Constitution
● Discuss how they may be applied directly: vertically and
horizontally
○ Look at nature of right, who it affects, how it affects
them, etc

Theme 4: The
Constitution of 1996:
Basic Principles,
Concepts and
DoctrinesRecapThe Application of the Bill of Rights
● When litigating the Bill of Rights, the Court
has to determine whether the BOR applies
○ Directly or Indirectly
○ Vertically or Horizontally• What did we celebrate on Monday?
• What is its significance?
• How does it encapsulate what we have done
this semester?Democracy!
• What do you think is Democracy?
• How do we define democracy?Democracy!
• We have a “Constitutional Democracy”
• Pre-amble” ‘ A Society based on democratic values’
• S1(d): elections and a multi-party system of democratic
government, to ensure accountability, responsiveness
and opennessDemocracy!
• Undeniably one of the dominate and enduring political
ideas of modern times
• A CORE concept and value of the 1996 Constitution
• In the 1996 Constitution, the idea of democracy is so
prominent it permeates virtually all aspects of the
ConstitutionDemocracy!
• S1 ushers in democracy by declaring South Africa to be “a
sovereign, democratic state”.
• S1(d) Democratic values: “universal adult suffrage, a
national common voters' roll, regular elections and a
multi-party system of democratic government, to
ensure accountability, responsiveness and openness.How to define Democracy in
the 1996 Constitution Context
• Democracy – as a concept – defies singular definition
• However, we can still get an understanding of what democracy
entails.
• Theuys Roux : ‘The core idea – that decisions affecting the
members of a political community should be taken by the
members themselves, or at least by elected representatives
whose power to make those decisions ultimately derives from
the members– is more or less settled’How to define Democracy…
• Roux’s idea of democracy is linked to the notion that people should prevail
and have a say in how they are governed.
• However, it is not possible to have every individual vote on every decision,
so this conceptualisation of democracy highlights that modern democracy
is exercised through institutionalised politics that entails electing
individuals or organisations to represent their interests
• Roux’s definition also lends itself to understanding that democracy, as
found in the 1996 constitution, embodies different conceptions of
democracyTypes of Democracy
• Direct Democracy
• Representative democracy
• Participatory democracy
• Constitutional DemocracyDirect democracy
• Decisions affecting the members of a political community
should be taken by the members themselves = direct
democracy
• Historically considered the purest form of democracy.
• What are some elements of direct democracy in the
Constitution?Direct democracy
• Section 17: Right to assemble, demonstrate, picket and present
petitions, unarmed and peacefully
• Section 84(2)(g): President can call a national referendum
• Section 127(2)(f) Provincial premier can call a provincial
referendum
• Does SA have a substantive form of direct democracy?
• \ Look at discussion of Merafong city decision (De vos s2.5.3)Representative Democracy
• Most decisions are not made by direct involvement by the
citizenry
• Decisions affecting the members of a political community are
made by elected representatives whose power to make those
decisions ultimately derives from the members = representative
democracy
• Citizens elect representatives to govern for a limited timeRepresentative Democracy
• Section 42(3) :“The National Assembly is elected to represent
the people and to ensure government by the people
• Section 19(3)(a): Every adult citizen has the right to vote in
elections
• Role of political parties - our democracy is founded on a multi-
party system of government (S1(d))
• Link between citizens and political parties/representativesRepresentative Democracy
Multi-party government:
• A system where three or more political parties have the capacity to
gain control of the government, either separately or through a
coalition
• S19 read with s1(d) = MPG Is an integral part of our democracy
• It is characterised by competitive elections, proportional
representation, and usually a coalition of political parties working
together to form a majority in the legislationRepresentative Democracy
But in New Nation Movement v President of RSA 2020 CC
• CC found the Electoral Act unconstitutional as it violated citizens'
political rights (Section 19) by allowing only political parties to contest
national and provincial elections, invalidating the exclusion of
independent candidates.
• This decision necessitated fundamental electoral reform in South
Africa, moving towards a system that allows for individual candidacy
rather than exclusively party-based representation.
• Electoral Amendment Bill – signed 20 April 2023Representative Democracy
Electoral Amendment Act 1 of 2023
• Allows independent candidates (not afflicated to political parties) to
contest elections for the National Assembly and provincial legislatures
for the first time
• Came into effect for 2024 elections
• Independent candidates must prove support to qualify. Candidates need
to have 1,000 signatures in support of them.Representative Democracy
• 2024 elections = No Party got Majority – GNU government
• Democratic implications of the GNU
• Power sharing: inclusive governance through multi-party
collaboration
• Checks and Balances: No single majority ensures more balanced
policy-making
• Challenges: tensions over ideological differences ( VAT, NHI,
foreign policy)Limitations of Representative
Democracy
• Representative democracy is the only workable system…
• Failure to regulate political parties, elite-driven democracy
• Inability to directly influence elected members in between elections
• Influence of those not actively involved in political parties
• Has Electoral Amendment Act fixed this?
• One-party dominance
• Affected democratic accountability and limited democratic
participation, eroding separation between political parties and the stateParticipatory Democracy
• Tries to counteract the political exclusion of citizens' opinions in
decision-making
• Participatory democracy = affording citizens an opportunity to have
their voice heard when decisions are made that affect them
• Section 1(d) “system of democratic government to ensure
accountability, responsiveness and openness”
• Section 59(1)(a)and 72(1)(a), and 118: NA and NCOP MUST facilitate
public participation in law-making processesParticipatory Democracy
• Doctors for Life v Speaker of the National Assembly para 105-117
• South Africa has both representative and participatory democracy
• Which are are mutually supportive
• The participation by the public on a continuous basis provides
vitality to the functioning of representative democracy
• The court invalidated legislation in circumstances where there had
not been sufficient opportunity for public participation on
legislation that significancy affects the lives of peopleConstitutional Democracy
• A descriptive term, a decision affecting a political community made in
terms of a Constitution, and this Constitution has certain basic features
and characteristics
• Notions of democracy (centrality of democracy); Constitutional
supremacy, centrality of foundational values ( human dignity,
equality, freedom etc), culture of human rights, democratic ideas,
juridical review
• A purposive concept – if we adhere to these features, we will establish
the society envisaged by the ConstitutionClass task
• Scenario: The university is deciding whether to introduce a mandatory attendance
policy for all lectures.
• Discuss in groups
• 1. Direct democracy:
• How would this decision be made if all students voted directly?
• 2. Representative democracy:
• How would this decision be made if student representatives (e.g. SRC) decided?
• 3. Participatory democracy:
• How would this decision be made if students were consulted and involved, but did not
make the final decision?Defiance Campaign
• Resulted in a United Nations Commission to investigate the
unjust racial policies (international recognition)
• The period marked the beginning of non-racial cooperation in
the resistance to apartheid which was cemented by the
Congress Alliance in 1954, in the run-up to the Congress of
the peopleCongress Alliance
• Coalition of anti-apartheid organisations formed in the early 1950s to
coordinate resistance against apartheid laws
• Included:
• African National Congress
• South African Coloured Peoples Organization
• Congress of Democrats
• South African Congress of Trade Unions
• Among othersCongress Alliance
• It was explicitly NON-racial at a time when apartheid
enforced racial division
• It developed a shared constitutional vision of equality
and citizenship.
• Organised the Congress of the people 1955Congress of the People
• Held in Kliptown (Near JHB) on 26 June
1955
• 3000 delegates from across South Africa
Gathered
• Mass democratic process
• Started with a campaign asking
ordinary people what kind of South
Africa do you want
• Adopted the Freedom CharterFreedom Chater
• Declared “South Africa belongs to
all who live in it”
• Envisioned equality, shared
citizenship, and socio-economic
rights
• Became the normative precursor
to the 1996 Final ConstitutionFreedom Chater
• Key Principles
• Universal suffrage and democratic government
• Equality before the law
• Human rights and freedoms, including speech,
assembly and movement
• Redistribution of land and economic opportunity
• Access to housing, education and work
• Although not legally binding, Freedom Charter
became a foundational ideological document for the
liberation movementRoad to Sharpeville (1959 – March 1960)
• Anti-Pass campaign
• 6 Dec 1959 – ANC conference – Chief Albert
Luthuli announces 1960 as the “ Year of the Pass”
• 16 March 1960 – Robert Sobukwe and the PAC
announce that on 21 March 1960 there will be a
mass pass law protest
• PAC had recently split from the ANCRoad to Sharpeville (1959 – March 1960)
• 18 March 1960: PAC activists distribute circulars
calling on black South Africans to:
• Leave pass books at home
• Voluntarily present themselves at police
stations for arrest
• The aim was to overwhelm the apartheid system and
challenge pass laws directlySharpeville Massacre
• 21 March 1960: Thousands march peacefully to the
Sharpeville police station without their passbooks
• Police responded by opening fire on the crowed
• 69 people where killed
• Hundreds injured
• Witnesses later testified that police fired into an unarmed
crowd, and later when and placed weapons in the hands of
the deadSharpeville: Government Response
• 23 March 1960: Prime Minister Verwoed tells Parliament that
the protests were not about pass laws and praisesd thr
police response
• 23 March: Robert Sobukwe and PAC leaders are arrested
• Protests spread across the country in response
• 24 March: gatherings of 12 or more people are banned and
police surveillance increasesSharpeville: Government Response
• 30 March 1960: Government declares a state of emergency
• Used to suppress protests
• Resulted in the mass detention of thousands of people
• Resulted in the ANC and PAC being banned (Unlawful
Organisations Act )
• Lasted several months and marked a shift to the more
violent, repressive phase of apartheid
• Historical turning point and led to international criticism1961
Constitution1961 Constitution
• 5 October 1960: Referendum in which white-only voters
approve the move to become a Republic, separate from
Britain.
• The British Monarch would be removed as head of state
• South Africa wanted to be part of the Commonwealth but
due to the recent political violence was not accepted by
international community1961 Constitution
• 32 May 1961 SA became a Republic and left the
commonwealth
• Retained the parliamentary system from the 1910
constitution
• This constitution reinforced white minority dominance, and
continued to exclude black South Africans from the political
process1961 Constitution
• Most important change was that the Monarch would no
longer be the head of state, this would not vest with the
President, as elected by the people.
• First president was C R SwartRivonia Trial
• Suppression of political dissent
• Suppression of Communism Act (1950),
• Sabotage Act (1962),
• Carried the death penalty
• 90-Day Detention Law (1963)
• Allowed indefinite solitary confinement without
charge, access to lawyers, or contact with family.Rivonia Trial
• Held from 1963-1964
• Landmark legal proceeding that resulted n life
imprisonment of Nelson Mandela and other anti-
apartheid leaders
• Another historical turning point, which resulted in
international scrutiny on apartheid regimeRivonia Trial
• Trialists charged under laws specifically designed to
criminalize resistance to racial oppression
• Demonstrates how a legal system can be weaponised by those
in power against the very people it should protect
• Makes a case for why constitutions must entrench rights
that constrain legislative power, not just procedural rulesRivonia Trial
• Rather than mount a purely criminal defence, the accused chose to put
apartheid itself on trial.
• Mandela's famous "I am prepared to die" statement from the dock reframed
the proceedings as a question of political legitimacy:
• can a government that excludes the majority from political
participation claim the right to prosecute them for defying its laws?
• This connects directly to social contract theory and the question of what
gives law its moral authority.Rivonia Trial
• In short, the Rivonia Trial is a foundational case study in the difference
between law and justice, the role of courts in authoritarian systems, why
entrenched constitutional rights matter, and how the legacy of historical
abuse shapes constitutional design.
• It was a political win for the fight against apartheid, but with many of the
leaders now in jail, the resistance saw setbacks and stagnation for several
years following, in which time the oppression of the government continued
and escalated .1983 Constitution1983 Constitution
● Republic of South Africa Constitution Act No 110 of 1983
● Key legislative reform under Apartheid Regime – to entrench apartheid
rule and response to internal protest and international pressure
● Aimed to incorporate Coloured and Indian groups, to create a broader
base of support for the white minority and fracture the non-racial dissent
● Direct response to ever increasing urban protest and unrest, needed to
ensure white control was maintained
● Referendum November 2, 1983, with a 66.3% (whites only) yes vote for
change1983 Constitution
● Created the Tricameral Parliament: Parliament was restructured into
three separate houses
○ House of Assembly: For the white population group
○ House of Representatives: For the Coloured population group
○ House of Delegates: For the Indian population group
● Total exclusion of Majority of Black African population – complete
exclusion from any representation in the central government
● Created a hierarchy among the non-white race groups (similar to the
caste system in India?)1983 Constitution
● Competencies were categorised as “own” or “general” affairs
○ Own Affairs – handled by each separate house
○ General affairs – handled by full parliament
● The Office of the Prime Minister was abolished
○ Symbolic State President replaced with executive State president,
created consolidating power into an office not directly elected by
the public but by the electoral college dominated by white ruling
party
● Executive authority rested with the cabinetNext week ….

○ 1990s end of apartheid
○ First democratic elections
○ Interim Constitution
○ Final Constitution

Separation of Powers
Dr Christiaan van Schalkwyk
christiaanvs@sun.ac.za
Chair in Urban Law and SustainabilityStructure: Separation of Powers
1. Introduction
2. Concepts & principles
3. Historical context
4. Application in South Africa
5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma & deference
6. Conclusion
7. Class activity1. Introduction
• Our focus is on:
o Analysing the model of separation of powers
o Understanding the principles, concepts and historical context
