1. Theme 3 Source + Scope Audit
📘 What Theme 3 is really about

Theme 3 explains how South Africa moved from apartheid legality and parliamentary sovereignty into a negotiated constitutional democracy. The key story is not only “a new Constitution was written”. The deeper issue is how legitimacy was constructed through a two-stage transition: an interim negotiated settlement, followed by a democratically elected Constitutional Assembly, checked by pre-agreed Constitutional Principles and judicial certification.

Source / material
	How it matters for this docket
	Theme 3 lecture 10-13
	Provides the lecture roadmap: CODESA, MPNF, Interim Constitution, Constitutional Principles, First Certification, Second Certification, Final Constitution, amendments, and transformative nature.
	Interim Constitution Act 200 of 1993
	Primary legal text for the two-stage transition, Bill of Rights, Constitutional Assembly, certification mechanism, and Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles.
	Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles
	Binding benchmarks against which the Final Constitution had to be certified.
	First Certification judgment
	Major case for certification, legal legitimacy, role of Constitutional Court, and whether the New Text complied with the Constitutional Principles.
	Mureinik, “A Bridge to Where?”
	Key article for “historic bridge”, culture of authority, culture of justification, and why the Bill of Rights mattered.
	Langa, “Transformative Constitutionalism”
	Key article for transformative constitutionalism, substantive equality, legal culture, access to justice, and the Constitution as a long-term project of change.
	Constitutional Guidelines for a Democratic South Africa
	Political / constitutional vision document showing pre-1994 ideas about democracy, non-racialism, non-sexism, Bill of Rights, land, workers, women, and family.

2. Master Timeline of the Negotiated Constitutional Revolution
🧩 Timeline in one exam sentence

Collapse of apartheid legitimacy → CODESA I → central legitimacy and minority-protection deadlock → CODESA II failure → violence and mistrust, especially Boipatong → MPNF compromise → Interim Constitution → 1994 democratic election → Constitutional Assembly → First Certification failure → amended text → Second Certification → Mandela signs the Final Constitution → 1996 Constitution commences on 4 February 1997.

Stage
	Legal / constitutional meaning
	Exam trigger
	CODESA I
	Negotiations begin but legitimacy problem remains: negotiators were not elected in free and verifiable elections.
	Why could unelected negotiators not legitimately write the final constitution?
	CODESA II
	Second round in 1992 fails over voting thresholds and transitional government structure.
	Explain breakdown and why compromise became necessary.
	Political violence
	Boipatong, township violence, assassinations, IFP conflict and security force destabilisation deepened mistrust.
	Shows transition was negotiated under pressure, not peacefully inevitable.
	MPNF
	Successor to CODESA; established two-stage transition and election date.
	Role of Ramaphosa and Meyer; why MPNF succeeded.
	Interim Constitution
	Legal bridge: governs after first election and sets rules for drafting Final Constitution.
	Key features: GNU, Bill of Rights, Constitutional Court, CPs, certification.
	1994 election
	Democratic mandate created; Constitutional Assembly becomes legitimate constitution-making body.
	Why first election matters beyond symbolism.
	Certification
	Constitutional Court acts as independent legal arbiter of compliance with CPs.
	Judicial, not political, certification task.
	Final Constitution
	Product of democratic mandate + negotiated constraints + judicial certification.
	Why 1996 Constitution has special legitimacy.

3. Case Law Docket
🎯 How to use the case law in Theme 3

Theme 3 is not case-heavy in the ordinary criminal/private-law sense. Its most important “case” is the First Certification judgment because it explains the legal mechanics and legitimacy of the 1996 Constitution. The other cases appear mainly through Langa and the Certification judgment to support transformation, the bridge metaphor, access to justice, and the Court’s understanding of post-apartheid constitutionalism.

⚖️ Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 / Ex parte Chairperson of the Constitutional Assembly: In re Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 1996 (4) SA 744 (CC); 1996 (10) BCLR 1253 (CC)
Category in Theme 3: MAIN THEME 3 CASE - certification of the New Text
Source note: Source focus: study guide prescribes paragraphs 1-47; lecture also refers to objections on socio-economic rights, separation of powers, and non-compliance issues.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	The Constitutional Assembly adopted a new constitutional text on 8 May 1996 and transmitted it to the Constitutional Court for certification. Political parties and many private bodies objected to various provisions. The Court had to decide whether every provision of the New Text complied with the 34 Constitutional Principles in Schedule 4 to the Interim Constitution.
	Issue
	Whether the Constitutional Court could certify that all provisions of the proposed Final Constitution complied with the Constitutional Principles agreed during the negotiated transition.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The Court explained that certification was a judicial, not political, function. It compared the New Text to the Constitutional Principles, not to political preferences. The Court held that the CPs had to be interpreted purposively, holistically and without technical rigidity. The Court first asked whether the basic structure and premises of the New Text accorded with the CPs; then it examined whether the detailed provisions complied. The Court accepted the basic structure but found some details non-compliant.
	Judgment / outcome
	The Court refused to certify the first text as it stood because several provisions did not comply with the Constitutional Principles. The text had to go back to the Constitutional Assembly for amendment.
	Constitutional significance
	This judgment is central to the legitimacy of the 1996 Constitution. It proves that the Final Constitution was not merely a political deal; it was measured against a binding legal pact. It also shows how the two-stage transition balanced democratic legitimacy with negotiated safeguards.
	Exam use
	Use this case whenever asked about: the two-stage transition; the role of the Constitutional Court; the purpose of the 34 Constitutional Principles; why certification mattered; why the 1996 Constitution has special legitimacy; or why the Court’s task was legal rather than political.

⚖️ Certification of the Amended Text of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 / Second Certification Judgment
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 1996 (later Constitutional Court certification of Amended Text; lecture gives 4 December 1996)
Category in Theme 3: THEME 3 COMPLETION CASE - final legal hurdle
Source note: The uploaded lecture gives the core details; the full Second Certification judgment was not uploaded in this batch.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	After the Constitutional Court refused to certify the first text, the Constitutional Assembly amended the text to address the shortcomings identified in the First Certification judgment.
	Issue
	Whether the amended constitutional text now complied with the 34 Constitutional Principles and could therefore come into force.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The Court considered whether the defects identified in the First Certification judgment had been remedied. The lecture states that the Court unanimously certified the Amended Text as complying with the Constitutional Principles.
	Judgment / outcome
	The Amended Text was certified. This cleared the final legal hurdle for the 1996 Constitution. Mandela signed the Constitution into law on 10 December 1996 at Sharpeville, and it took effect on 4 February 1997.
	Constitutional significance
	This case completes the certification story. The Final Constitution is legitimate because it was produced by an elected Constitutional Assembly and certified by an independent Constitutional Court against pre-agreed principles.
	Exam use
	Use after First Certification to show the complete sequence: first draft rejected → amendments made → amended text certified → Final Constitution becomes law.

⚖️ Executive Council, Western Cape Legislature and Others v President of the Republic of South Africa and Others
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 1995 (4) SA 877 (CC); 1995 (10) BCLR 1289 (CC)
Category in Theme 3: Mentioned in First Certification judgment for transition complexity
Source note: Mentioned in First Certification judgment para 9 context.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	The First Certification judgment refers to this case while describing the enormous complexity of replacing apartheid-era government structures with a constitutional state. Four provincial governments, self-governing territories, and former TBVC structures ceased to exist when the Interim Constitution came into force.
	Issue
	In the broader transition context, the issue was how to manage constitutional, legislative, executive, administrative and judicial continuity while dismantling apartheid structures and creating new democratic institutions.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The case is used in the Certification judgment as context: it illustrates the practical difficulty of constitutional transition and decentralisation after apartheid.
	Judgment / outcome
	The case is not the main Theme 3 authority, but it supports the idea that the transition was legally and administratively complex, not just political.
	Constitutional significance
	It shows that constitutional transformation required institutional reconstruction, not only a new text.
	Exam use
	Use as supporting authority if discussing the complexity of the transition, the collapse of old structures, and the need for continuity under the Interim Constitution.

⚖️ Azanian Peoples Organisation (AZAPO) and Others v President of the Republic of South Africa and Others
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: Constitutional Court, CCT 17/96, 25 July 1996
Category in Theme 3: Mentioned in First Certification judgment for negotiated transition context
Source note: Mentioned in First Certification judgment para 10 context.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	The First Certification judgment refers to AZAPO when explaining that the overwhelming majority of South Africans realised the country had to be rescued from imminent disaster through a negotiated commitment to a fundamentally new constitutional order.
	Issue
	In the broader context, AZAPO dealt with the post-apartheid settlement and the legal consequences of national unity and reconciliation.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The Certification judgment uses AZAPO to support the historical point that South Africa moved from deep conflict and minority domination into a negotiated constitutional order based on open democracy and fundamental human rights.
	Judgment / outcome
	AZAPO is not the main Theme 3 case, but it is useful background for the transition and reconciliation logic.
	Constitutional significance
	It links Theme 3 to the idea that constitutional democracy was produced by negotiation, compromise and an attempt to avoid catastrophe.
	Exam use
	Use as a supporting case when discussing why negotiation, reconciliation and compromise mattered in the constitutional transition.

⚖️ S v Makwanyane
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC); 1995 (6) BCLR 665 (CC)
Category in Theme 3: Transformative constitutionalism / bridge case mentioned by Langa
Source note: Mentioned in Langa article footnote and later Theme 4 material; useful as cross-theme authority.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	The case concerned the constitutionality of the death penalty under the Interim Constitution. Langa cites it as an example of the Constitution expressly aspiring to transition from the unacceptable features of the past to a contrasting future.
	Issue
	Whether the death penalty was compatible with the values and rights in the Interim Constitution, especially life, dignity and protection against cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The Court used constitutional values to reject the death penalty. Langa uses the case to show that the Constitution is transformative and future-orientated.
	Judgment / outcome
	The death penalty was declared unconstitutional.
	Constitutional significance
	In Theme 3, use it not mainly for the death penalty itself, but to show that the Interim Constitution was already understood as a transformative bridge from past injustice to a rights-based future.
	Exam use
	Use when asked to “critically discuss the 1996 Constitution as a transformative document” or to link Theme 3’s bridge idea to constitutional values.

⚖️ Du Plessis v De Klerk
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 1996 (3) SA 850 (CC); 1996 (5) BCLR 658 (CC)
Category in Theme 3: Transformation and Bill of Rights application mentioned by Langa / Certification
Source note: Mentioned in Langa and First Certification judgment.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	The case is cited by Langa for the idea that the Constitution seeks to transform the previous legal order into a new order. The First Certification judgment also refers to it in relation to indirect horizontal application of rights under the Interim Constitution.
	Issue
	How the Bill of Rights interacts with private law/common law and how the Constitution changes the pre-1994 legal order.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The case forms part of the early constitutional jurisprudence around the application of the Bill of Rights and constitutional transformation.
	Judgment / outcome
	It confirmed that the Constitution marked a move away from the old order, even where the precise mechanics of horizontality were contested.
	Constitutional significance
	It helps show that transformative constitutionalism includes transformation of legal culture and private law, not merely replacement of parliamentary sovereignty.
	Exam use
	Use as supporting authority for the proposition that the Constitution seeks to transform the status quo ante into a new order.

⚖️ Soobramoney v Minister of Health, KwaZulu-Natal
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 1998 (1) SA 765 (CC); 1997 (12) BCLR 1696 (CC)
Category in Theme 3: Transformative constitutionalism and socio-economic context
Source note: Mentioned in Langa and Theme 3 / Theme 4 lecture material.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	The case concerned access to scarce healthcare resources. Langa cites it for Chaskalson CJ’s statement that the Constitution commits South Africa to address poverty, unemployment, inadequate social security, lack of clean water and inadequate health services.
	Issue
	How socio-economic realities fit into constitutional transformation and the interpretation of socio-economic rights.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The Court acknowledged the harsh socio-economic conditions existing when the Constitution was adopted and linked transformation to dignity, freedom and equality.
	Judgment / outcome
	The applicant did not receive the requested treatment, but the case became a foundational statement about the Constitution’s transformative commitment.
	Constitutional significance
	For Theme 3, it proves that the Final Constitution is not merely procedural. It is connected to material transformation and the struggle to remedy apartheid’s socio-economic legacy.
	Exam use
	Use in answers on transformative constitutionalism, especially when explaining that the Constitution is backward-looking and forward-looking.

⚖️ Rates Action Group v City of Cape Town
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 2004 (12) BCLR 1328 (C)
Category in Theme 3: Transformative Constitution - cited by Langa
Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	Langa cites this case for the idea that South Africa’s Constitution is not designed to obstruct modernity or prevent change, but to provide a mandate, framework and blueprint for transforming society from its racist and unequal past into one in which all can live with dignity.
	Issue
	What purpose the South African Constitution serves in a society emerging from apartheid.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The quoted reasoning contrasts South Africa’s Constitution with a static view of constitutionalism. It emphasises that the Constitution is meant to enable change.
	Judgment / outcome
	The case is used as a persuasive articulation of the Constitution’s transformative character.
	Constitutional significance
	It supports the Theme 3 idea that the 1996 Constitution is a transformative document produced by negotiated constitutionalism.
	Exam use
	Use as a supporting quote/example in an essay on transformative constitutionalism, especially to show the Constitution is a mandate and framework for change.

⚖️ City of Johannesburg v Rand Properties (Pty) Ltd
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 2006 (6) BCLR 728 (W)
Category in Theme 3: Transformative Constitution - cited by Langa
Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	Langa cites this case for the proposition that the State cannot be a passive bystander in shaping a society in which individuals can fully enjoy their rights.
	Issue
	Whether constitutional rights should be interpreted in light of social and economic context.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The case emphasised that the full power of the Bill of Rights is realised when rights are interpreted with reference to actual socio-economic conditions.
	Judgment / outcome
	The case supports a context-sensitive and transformative approach to constitutional rights.
	Constitutional significance
	It links Theme 3’s negotiated Constitution to concrete duties of social transformation.
	Exam use
	Use when explaining that transformative constitutionalism is not just symbolic; it demands state action and context-sensitive interpretation.

⚖️ Van Rooyen v S
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 2002 (8) BCLR 810 (CC)
Category in Theme 3: Transformation of institutions - cited by Langa
Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	Langa cites Van Rooyen for the idea that transformation involves changes not only in the legal order but also in the composition and character of institutions that were historically controlled largely by whites and, in particular, white men.
	Issue
	How constitutional transformation affects legal institutions and their composition.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The reasoning cited by Langa stresses that transformation is institutional as well as doctrinal.
	Judgment / outcome
	The case supports the proposition that constitutional transformation requires changing institutions, not only rules.
	Constitutional significance
	It helps deepen Theme 3 answers by showing that the negotiated Constitution aimed at structural transformation.
	Exam use

⚖️ Minister of Finance v Van Heerden
📌 Quick ID

Citation / reference: 2004 (11) BCLR 1125 (CC)
Category in Theme 3: Substantive equality - cited by Langa
Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

Element
	Detailed notes
	Facts
	Langa cites Sachs J in Van Heerden for a substantive approach to equality. Equality is not simply identical treatment; the real question is whether a measure advances or retards the equal enjoyment of rights in practice.
	Issue
	How equality should be understood in a society structured by historical disadvantage.
	Court reasoning / legal reasoning
	The reasoning cited by Langa roots equality in a transformative constitutional philosophy that confronts systemic race and gender disadvantage.
	Judgment / outcome
	The case supports remedial and substantive equality measures.
	Constitutional significance
	In Theme 3, it supports the argument that the 1996 Constitution is transformative because it aims to undo systemic disadvantage, not merely declare formal equality.
	Exam use
	Use when linking Constitutional Principles, the Final Constitution, and transformative constitutionalism to substantive equality.

4. Legislation / Constitutional Instrument Docket
📜 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 200 of 1993 (“Interim Constitution” / IC)
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Interim constitutional statute; assented to 25 January 1994; commenced 27 April 1994; later repealed/replaced by the 1996 Constitution.
	Key provisions / content
	Key provisions for Theme 3 include: Preamble and Postamble; s 4 supremacy of the Constitution; Chapter 3 Bill of Rights; Chapter 5 ss 68-74 on the adoption of the new Constitution; s 71 certification; Chapter 7 creating the Constitutional Court; Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles; Government of National Unity provisions.
	Role in Theme 3
	The IC is the legal bridge between apartheid parliamentary sovereignty and the Final Constitution. It governed the country after the 1994 election and set the rules for how the Final Constitution would be drafted and certified.
	Exam use
	Use in any Theme 3 answer on the two-stage transition, the “bridge”, the Constitutional Assembly, certification, Constitutional Principles, and the shift from parliamentary sovereignty to constitutional supremacy.
	Warning / nuance
	Do not confuse the Interim Constitution with the Final Constitution. The IC was drafted by unelected negotiators; the Final Constitution was drafted by an elected Constitutional Assembly and certified by the Constitutional Court.

📜 Chapter 5 of the Interim Constitution: ss 68-74
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Specific chapter regulating the adoption of the new constitutional text.
	Key provisions / content
	s 68 created the Constitutional Assembly by requiring the National Assembly and Senate to sit jointly for constitution-making. s 71 required Constitutional Court certification. s 73 regulated adoption of the new text, including the two-thirds majority requirement and fallback mechanisms. s 74 protected the Constitutional Principles and Chapter 5 from easy amendment.
	Role in Theme 3
	Chapter 5 is the legal engine of the second stage of the transition. It converts the political compromise into legal procedure.
	Exam use
	Use when asked to explain the rules for drafting the Final Constitution. Mention Constitutional Assembly = NA + Senate sitting jointly; two-year deadline; two-thirds support; certification; referendum fallback if relevant.
	Warning / nuance
	Exam trap: do not say CODESA drafted the Final Constitution. CODESA/MPNF produced the negotiated framework and IC; the elected Constitutional Assembly drafted the Final Constitution.

📜 Schedule 4 to the Interim Constitution: the 34 Constitutional Principles
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Binding principles agreed during negotiations and entrenched in the IC.
	Key provisions / content
	The Principles required, among other things: one sovereign democratic state; common citizenship; fundamental rights protected by entrenched and justiciable provisions; prohibition of discrimination; constitutional supremacy; equality before the law; separation of powers; independent judiciary; representative government; universal adult suffrage; common voters’ roll; proportional representation; freedom of information; formal legislative procedures; language and cultural diversity; traditional leadership and customary law; multi-level government; provincial and local powers; fiscal arrangements; independent institutions; non-partisan public service; security forces acting in the national interest; GNU until 1999; no national election before 30 April 1999 unless specific conditions arose; and self-determination possibilities.
	Role in Theme 3
	They solved the legitimacy/minority-fear deadlock: the elected body would draft the Final Constitution, but it had to remain within negotiated binding principles.
	Exam use
	Use as the heart of the two-stage transition answer. They are the legal benchmark used by the Constitutional Court in certification.
	Warning / nuance
	Critical phrase: the CPs were a “solemn pact”. Do not describe them as optional guidelines.

📜 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 / formerly Act 108 of 1996
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Final Constitution; formally enacted as Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 108 of 1996 and now referred to as the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996.
	Key provisions / content
	Drafted by the Constitutional Assembly; certified by the Constitutional Court; signed by Mandela on 10 December 1996; commenced on 4 February 1997. Important aspects include a justiciable Bill of Rights, universal adult suffrage, constitutional supremacy, rule of law, non-racialism and non-sexism, co-operative government, separation of powers, Chapter 9 institutions, traditional leaders and languages.
	Role in Theme 3
	The Final Constitution is the product of Theme 3. Its legitimacy rests on democratic election, negotiated principles, Constitutional Assembly drafting, and Constitutional Court certification.
	Exam use
	Use to conclude Theme 3 answers. Show that the Constitution is not just a statute but the culmination of a negotiated constitutional revolution.
	Warning / nuance
	Use correct name: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996.

📜 Constitutional Guidelines for a Democratic South Africa
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	ANC constitutional vision document, reproduced in 1989 SAJHR and simplified in the uploaded material.
	Key provisions / content
	The Guidelines proposed an independent, unitary, democratic, non-racial South Africa; one person one vote; one country, one people; a Bill of Rights based on the Freedom Charter; anti-racism; social and economic rights; mixed economy; land redress; workers’ charter; equal rights for women; protection of family rights; and a non-aligned foreign policy.
	Role in Theme 3
	The Guidelines show the pre-negotiation constitutional imagination of a democratic South Africa and how liberation-era constitutional ideas fed into the later negotiation process.
	Exam use
	Use as background when explaining the run-up to negotiations and the vision of a future democratic order.
	Warning / nuance
	This is not the same as the 34 Constitutional Principles. It is a political / constitutional guideline document, not the binding Schedule 4 certification benchmark.

📜 Electoral Act, 1993
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Legislation referred to in the Interim Constitution for regulating elections under the transitional framework.
	Key provisions / content
	The Interim Constitution refers to elections being held in accordance with the Electoral Act, 1993, including elections for the National Assembly.
	Role in Theme 3
	The Act matters because democratic elections were necessary to create a legitimate Constitutional Assembly.
	Exam use
	Use only briefly if discussing the legal machinery of the first democratic election.
	Warning / nuance
	Do not over-focus on this unless the question asks about election mechanics.

📜 Republic of South Africa Constitution Act 110 of 1983 / 1983 Constitution
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Pre-democratic Constitution under which the old Parliament still operated before the transition.
	Key provisions / content
	The lecture notes that the Interim Constitution was adopted in terms of the procedures and processes of the 1983 Constitution.
	Role in Theme 3
	This shows constitutional history matters: the new order was legally brought into being through the old order’s formal machinery, even though it broke substantively with parliamentary sovereignty and apartheid constitutionalism.
	Exam use
	Use to explain continuity + rupture: the transition used old legal forms to create a radically different constitutional order.
	Warning / nuance
	Exam trap: do not say the 1983 Constitution itself was democratic. It provided the old legal route through which the IC was enacted.

📜 Labour Relations Act, 1956 / Labour Relations Act reference in certification issues
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Ordinary labour legislation mentioned in the certification context, especially around attempts to shield legislation from constitutional scrutiny.
	Key provisions / content
	The Theme 3 lecture refers to NT 241(1) and the LRA in the context of immunising legislation from constitutional scrutiny. The concern was that ordinary laws cannot be insulated from constitutional review because CP IV requires constitutional supremacy.
	Role in Theme 3
	This is an example of why the First Certification Court refused to certify some provisions. If Parliament could shield ordinary legislation from constitutional scrutiny, constitutional supremacy would be undermined.
	Exam use
	Use in First Certification answers as an example of non-compliance with CP IV.
	Warning / nuance
	Keep the focus on constitutional supremacy, not labour law detail.

📜 Local Government Transition Act 209 of 1993
Element
	Detailed notes
	Nature / status
	Legislation appearing in the First Certification judgment index in relation to local government and provincial powers.
	Key provisions / content
	The Certification judgment considered local government powers and their relationship to Constitutional Principles concerning provincial powers.
	Role in Theme 3
	The Act is relevant mainly to the technical certification analysis of provincial/local government powers.
	Exam use
	Use only if asked about detailed Certification objections around provincial powers or local government. For ordinary Theme 3 answers, mention only if necessary.
	Warning / nuance
	Not a core memorise item unless your lecturer specifically emphasised provincial power objections.

5. Constitutional Principles Bank
🧠 What the 34 Constitutional Principles did

They were not ordinary political promises. They were legally binding benchmarks in Schedule 4 of the Interim Constitution. The Constitutional Assembly could choose among permissible models, but it could not draft a Final Constitution inconsistent with the Constitutional Principles. The Constitutional Court was the independent arbiter.

Principle(s)
	Exam-ready meaning
	I
	One sovereign state, common citizenship, democratic government, equality between men and women and all races.
	II
	Universally accepted fundamental rights, freedoms and civil liberties protected by entrenched and justiciable constitutional provisions.
	III
	Prohibition of racial, gender and other discrimination; promotion of racial and gender equality and national unity.
	IV
	Constitution as supreme law, binding all organs of state at all levels.
	V
	Equality before the law and equitable legal process, including affirmative measures.
	VI
	Separation of powers with checks and balances for accountability, responsiveness and openness.
	VII
	Independent, impartial judiciary with power to safeguard the Constitution and rights.
	VIII
	Representative government, multi-party democracy, regular elections, universal adult suffrage, common voters’ roll and proportional representation.
	IX-XV
	Open administration, formal legislative procedures, language/culture protection, civil society rights, traditional leadership, minority participation and special amendment procedures.
	XVI-XXVII
	Government structured at national, provincial and local levels; allocation of powers; provincial autonomy; local government; fiscal powers and equitable share.
	XXVIII-XXXI
	Labour rights, independent institutions, public service, and security forces serving the national interest.
	XXXII-XXXIV
	GNU until 1999, no early national election unless specified, and possible community self-determination within the broader national self-determination framework.

6. Exam Use: How to Write Theme 3 Answers
✍️ Model answer skeleton: two-stage transition

Intro: South Africa’s transition was not a simple handover of power; it was a negotiated constitutional revolution structured through a two-stage transition.
Point 1: Explain legitimacy problem at CODESA - unelected negotiators lacked democratic mandate.
Point 2: Explain minority fear problem - old government wanted safeguards, power-sharing and supermajorities.
Point 3: Explain compromise - Stage 1 IC by negotiators; Stage 2 Final Constitution by elected Constitutional Assembly.
Point 4: Explain safeguards - 34 CPs + Constitutional Court certification.
Conclusion: The 1996 Constitution’s legitimacy comes from both democratic election and legal compliance with negotiated principles.

✍️ Model answer skeleton: First Certification

Intro: The First Certification judgment was the legal mechanism that ensured the Final Constitution complied with the negotiated settlement.
Facts/context: Constitutional Assembly adopted New Text; it was sent to the Constitutional Court.
Issue: Did all provisions comply with the 34 Constitutional Principles?
Reasoning: The Court’s task was judicial, not political; it interpreted CPs purposively and holistically; it assessed both structure and details.
Outcome: Basic structure complied, but some detailed provisions did not; the Court refused certification.
Significance: Certification protected constitutional supremacy, democratic legitimacy and negotiated safeguards.

🧠 What to memorise

·           “Two-stage transition” = IC first, Final Constitution second.
·           “Solemn pact” = 34 Constitutional Principles.
·           Constitutional Assembly = National Assembly + Senate sitting jointly.
·           s 71(2) IC = new text had no force unless certified by the Constitutional Court.
·           First Certification = first text rejected.
·           Second Certification = amended text certified.
·           Mureinik = culture of authority → culture of justification.
·           Langa = transformative constitutionalism = substantive equality + legal culture + ongoing change.

Likely question
	Best authorities / instruments to use
	Explain the journey leading to the 1996 Constitution.
	CODESA, MPNF, IC, CPs, Constitutional Assembly, First + Second Certification, Final Constitution.
	Explain the two-stage transition and why it was necessary.
	IC ss 68-74; Schedule 4 CPs; First Certification paras 11-18 logic.
	What was the role of the Constitutional Court in certification?
	First Certification judgment; IC s 71(2) and s 71(3).
	Why was the Interim Constitution a bridge?
	IC Postamble; Mureinik article; Langa article.
	Critically discuss the 1996 Constitution as transformative.
	Langa; Soobramoney; Makwanyane; Van Heerden; Mureinik.

7. Do You Need More Textbook Pages?
✅ Honest answer

Yes - for the most complete, prescribed-source version, you should add more textbook/article pages if you can. This docket is strong for the uploaded Theme 3 lecture and uploaded readings, but your study guide lists prescribed sources that are not fully included in the upload batch.

Material still useful / possibly missing
	Why it matters
	Kleyn et al Beginner’s Guide pages 51-52, 156-167, 180
	Likely provides basic textbook framing of the transition, constitutionalism and 1996 Constitution.
	De Vos & Freedman sections 1.3, 1.4 and 2.2
	Prescribed for transition to democracy, the 1996 Constitution, and constitutionalism. This would deepen the legal context and give textbook phrasing.
	Sarkin, “The drafting of South Africa’s Final Constitution from a Human-Rights Perspective”
	Prescribed article likely adds detail on drafting process and human-rights choices in the Final Constitution.
	Klug, “Towards a sociology of constitutional transformation”
	Prescribed article likely adds deeper academic explanation of post-apartheid constitutional order.
	Full Second Certification judgment
	Would allow the Second Certification entry to be expanded with direct judgment detail rather than lecture-level summary.

🎯 Practical recommendation

For exam purposes, the most urgent missing items would be: (1) De Vos & Freedman sections 1.3 and 1.4; (2) Sarkin; (3) Klug; and (4) the full Second Certification judgment if your lecturer expects detail beyond “the amended text was certified”.

3. Detailed case bank
S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this for any answer on foundational values, limitation of rights, dignity, judicial review, constitutional supremacy, or value-
based interpretation.
Legal theme Value-based constitutionalism; limitation of rights; human dignity,
equality and freedom; judicial review of legislation.
Facts Makwanyane and Mchunu were convicted of murder and
sentenced to death under s 277(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure
Act 51 of 1977. They challenged the constitutionality of the death
penalty under the 1993 Interim Constitution. The case became the
first major constitutional review of legislation by the new
Constitutional Court.
Issue Whether the death penalty was compatible with the rights to life,
dignity and freedom from cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment,
and whether it could be justified under the limitation clause.
Court reasoning The Court treated the Constitution as a value-based document. It
did not only ask what the statute allowed; it asked whether the
death penalty could survive a constitutional system founded on
dignity, equality and freedom. The State relied on deterrence,
prevention, retribution and public opinion. The Court held that
public opinion cannot decide constitutional rights. Rights must be
interpreted through constitutional values. The death penalty
objectifies the condemned person and places the person outside
the protection of humanity.
Judgment / outcome The death penalty was declared unconstitutional and invalid.
Section 277(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act was invalid to the
extent that it authorised capital punishment.
Constitutional significance Foundational case for value-based constitutionalism. It shows that
courts can invalidate legislation inconsistent with the Constitution;
rights are not absolute but limitations must be reasonable and
justifiable; human dignity is central to constitutional interpretation.
Legislation / sections linked Interim Constitution ss 9, 10, 11(2), 33; Constitution 1996 ss 10,
11, 12, 36, 39; Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977 s 277(1)(a).
How to write it in the exam “In S v Makwanyane, the Constitutional Court used the values of
human dignity, equality and freedom to hold that the death penalty
could not be justified in a constitutional democracy, even if public
opinion supported it.”
S v Walters⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this when asked “explain the limitation clause” or “how do courts decide if a limitation is reasonable and justifiable?”.
Legal theme Limitation clause; two-stage enquiry; interpretation of rights and
impugned law.
Facts The Court considered whether a statutory provision limiting
constitutional rights could survive constitutional scrutiny. The case
is used in the lecture for the mechanics of the limitation enquiry.
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
Issue How must a court determine whether a right has been limited and,
if so, whether that limitation is constitutionally justifiable?
Court reasoning The Court explained a two-stage process. First, identify the
content and scope of the right and the meaning/effect of the
impugned law to see whether there is a limitation. If there is no
limitation, the challenge fails. If there is a limitation, the second
stage is the limitations exercise: weigh the nature and importance
of the right and the extent of limitation against the purpose and
importance of the limiting law.
Judgment / outcome The case provides the analytical structure for s 36 limitation
analysis rather than merely stating an outcome for Theme 4
purposes.
Constitutional significance High-yield because it gives the exam method for limitation
questions: right infringed first, justification second.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 36 and 39.
How to write it in the exam “Following S v Walters, the limitation analysis is a two-stage
enquiry: first determine whether the right is limited; then determine
whether the limitation is reasonable and justifiable under s 36.”
Daniels v Campbell 2004 (5) SA 331 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this for value-based constitutionalism, statutory interpretation, diversity, equality and religious/cultural inclusion.
Legal theme Value-based interpretation of legislation; s 39(2); equality,
tolerance and diversity.
Facts The case concerned whether the word “spouse” in the Intestate
Succession Act and the Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act
included a surviving spouse from a Muslim marriage.
Issue Whether statutes should be interpreted broadly and inclusively to
recognise a surviving spouse in a Muslim marriage.
Court reasoning Justice Sachs reasoned that constitutional values of equality,
tolerance and respect for diversity supported a broad and inclusive
interpretation of “spouse”. The Court used constitutional values to
interpret ordinary legislation in a way that promoted the spirit,
purport and objects of the Bill of Rights.
Judgment / outcome The Court held that “spouse” included a surviving spouse to a
Muslim marriage for the purposes of the relevant Acts.
Constitutional significance Shows s 39(2) in action: courts interpret legislation through
constitutional values instead of reading statutes narrowly in a way
that excludes vulnerable groups.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 s 39(2); Intestate Succession Act 81 of 1987;
Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act 27 of 1990.
How to write it in the exam “Daniels v Campbell illustrates that s 39(2) requires courts to
interpret legislation in a way that promotes equality, tolerance and
diversity.”
Port Elizabeth Municipality v Various Occupiers 2005 (1) SA 217 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this for values, limitation/balancing, housing, property, evictions, and the class task about municipal land.
Legal theme Balancing competing rights through constitutional values; property
vs housing; eviction justice.
Facts A municipality sought the eviction of unlawful occupiers. The
dispute required the Court to consider the interests of
landowners/municipality and the occupiers’ vulnerability and
potential homelessness.
Issue How should courts balance property rights and housing/dignityBuilt for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
interests when deciding whether eviction is just and equitable?
Court reasoning Justice Sachs emphasised that eviction law must be interpreted in
light of South Africa’s history of forced removals and
homelessness. Fairness requires attention to both the owners’
rights and the occupiers’ dignity. The Constitution does not allow
mechanical eviction; it requires a humane, context-sensitive
balancing exercise.
Judgment / outcome Eviction must only occur where it is just and equitable after
considering all relevant circumstances.
Constitutional significance Excellent case for showing that constitutional values operate when
rights conflict. It connects dignity, housing, property, transformative
constitutionalism and historical context.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 25 and 26; especially s 26(3) on evictions.
How to write it in the exam “Port Elizabeth Municipality shows that courts balance competing
rights by asking which outcome best reflects dignity, equality,
freedom and South Africa’s history of dispossession.”
Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie 2006 (1) SA 524 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this for transformative constitutionalism, value-based interpretation, equality, dignity and the role of courts in protecting
minorities.
Legal theme Transformative constitutionalism; equality and dignity; social
inclusion; values against majoritarian exclusion.
Facts Same-sex couples were excluded from the institution of civil
marriage. The applicants argued that this exclusion violated their
rights to equality and dignity.
Issue Whether excluding same-sex couples from marriage was
constitutionally permissible.
Court reasoning The Court held that exclusion from marriage rendered same-sex
couples outsiders to a central social institution of love and
commitment. Constitutional democracy requires equal concern and
respect. Religious objections could not justify state exclusion
because South Africa requires coexistence between sacred and
secular spheres.
Judgment / outcome The exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage was
unconstitutional. Parliament was given time to correct the defect,
leading to the Civil Union Act.
Constitutional significance Shows values driving social transformation. It links equality,
dignity, freedom, minority protection and the counter-majoritarian
role of courts.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 9, 10, 15, 36, 39; Civil Union Act 17 of 2006
as legislative response.
How to write it in the exam “Fourie shows that the Constitution aims not merely to regulate
society but to transform social institutions so that previously
excluded groups enjoy equal dignity and belonging.”
Carmichele v Minister of Safety and Security 2001 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this for direct vs indirect application and s 39(2) common-law development.
Legal theme Indirect application of Bill of Rights; development of common law;
state duties to protect rights.
Facts Ms Carmichele was attacked by a man who had been released
despite prior charges and warning signs. She claimed that police
and prosecutors had failed to protect her. The question was
whether the common law of delict should recognise liability in suchBuilt for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
circumstances.
Issue Whether courts must develop the common law of delict to reflect
constitutional rights and values.
Court reasoning The Court held that courts have a duty under s 39(2) to develop
the common law where it is deficient and inconsistent with the
spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights. The Constitution
influences private/common-law rules indirectly by requiring their
development in light of rights.
Judgment / outcome The matter was sent back for reconsideration in light of the
constitutional duty to develop the common law.
Constitutional significance Core case for indirect application. It shows that constitutional rights
transform ordinary law without necessarily invalidating a statute.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 7(2), 8, 12, 39(2).
How to write it in the exam “Carmichele is the key example of indirect application: instead of
invalidating law, the Court required the common law to be
developed to promote the Bill of Rights.”
Government of the Republic of South Africa v Grootboom 2000 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this for vertical application, socio-economic rights, housing, reasonableness and transformative constitutionalism.
Legal theme Vertical application of socio-economic rights; housing;
reasonableness review.
Facts A group of people living in desperate conditions sought emergency
shelter and access to housing. They challenged the government’s
housing programme.
Issue Whether the state had complied with its constitutional obligation to
take reasonable measures to progressively realise the right of
access to adequate housing.
Court reasoning The Court held that socio-economic rights are justiciable. The state
does not have to provide a house immediately to everyone, but its
programme must be reasonable and must make provision for
people in crisis or desperate need.
Judgment / outcome The government’s housing programme was constitutionally
defective because it failed to provide for those in desperate need.
Constitutional significance Core vertical application example. It shows courts reviewing state
policy against the Bill of Rights and demanding reasonableness
while respecting institutional limits.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 26 and 7(2).
How to write it in the exam “Grootboom shows that socio-economic rights are enforceable and
that government programmes must be reasonable, especially for
those in desperate need.”
Soobramoney v Minister of Health, KwaZulu-Natal 1997 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use this for transformative constitutionalism and the socio-economic context of the Constitution.
Legal theme Transformative constitutionalism; socio-economic context; scarce
resources; dignity, freedom and equality.
Facts Mr Soobramoney suffered from chronic renal failure and sought
access to dialysis at a public hospital. The hospital had limited
resources and criteria for treatment.
Issue Whether refusal to provide dialysis violated the rights to
emergency medical treatment and access to health care.
Court reasoning The Court recognised the severe inequality and poverty existing at
the birth of the Constitution. It held that transformation lies at the
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
heart of the constitutional order, but courts must consider resource
constraints and institutional competence when assessing socio-
economic rights.
Judgment / outcome The claim failed because the treatment did not fall within
emergency medical treatment and the hospital’s resource-based
policy was not shown to be unconstitutional.
Constitutional significance Often used for the famous statement that the Constitution is
committed to transforming society into one based on human
dignity, freedom and equality. It shows the promise and limits of
socio-economic rights litigation.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 27 and 36; also linked to values in s 1.
How to write it in the exam “Soobramoney shows that the transformative Constitution is both
backward-looking and forward-looking: it responds to existing
poverty while aiming toward dignity, freedom and equality.”
Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly 2016 (CC) [Nkandla / EFF 1]⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use for rule of law, accountability, constitutional supremacy, legality, Chapter 9 institutions and separation of
powers/accountability.
Legal theme Rule of law; constitutional supremacy; accountability; Public
Protector remedial action.
Facts The Public Protector investigated spending on upgrades at
President Zuma’s Nkandla residence and directed remedial action.
The President and National Assembly did not comply and
attempted to replace or second-guess the remedial action.
Issue Whether the Public Protector’s remedial action was binding and
whether the President and National Assembly acted inconsistently
with the Constitution.
Court reasoning The Court linked the rule of law, constitutional supremacy and
accountability. It held that no decision grounded in the Constitution
or law may be ignored merely because a person disagrees with it;
recourse must be had to a court. Ignoring binding remedial action
would amount to self-help, which is inconsistent with the rule of
law.
Judgment / outcome The remedial action was binding. The President’s non-compliance
and the National Assembly resolution absolving him were
unconstitutional and invalid.
Constitutional significance Major Theme 4 rule of law case. Shows that even the President
must obey the Constitution and lawful constitutional decisions.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 1(c), 2, 42(3), 55(2), 83(b), 181, 182.
How to write it in the exam “EFF v Speaker confirms that constitutionalism, accountability and
the rule of law prevent public officials from treating constitutional
obligations as optional.”
Fedsure Life Assurance Ltd v Greater Johannesburg Transitional Metropolitan Council 1998 ⚖️
(CC)
High-yield exam use
Use for rule of law and legality definition.
Legal theme Rule of law; legality; authorised public power.
Facts A local government body exercised public powers affecting
rates/levies. The case became an early authority on the principle
that all public power must be sourced in law.
Issue Whether organs of state may exercise powers beyond those
conferred by law.
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
Court reasoning The Court held that the rule of law includes the principle of legality:
the legislature and executive in every sphere may exercise no
power and perform no function beyond that conferred by law.
Judgment / outcome The legality principle was affirmed as a constitutional control on
public power.
Constitutional significance Foundational legality case. It gives the basic exam formula: public
power must be authorised by law.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 1(c) and 2.
How to write it in the exam “Fedsure establishes that legality is part of the rule of law: every
exercise of public power must be authorised by law.”
Affordable Medicines Trust v Minister of Health 2005 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use when explaining that legality is not just administrative-law language; it is constitutional law.
Legal theme Legality; control of public power; rationality.
Facts Regulations and licensing powers in the medicines/health context
were challenged. The case is used in Theme 4 for the general rule
that public power must comply with the Constitution and legality.
Issue What constitutional controls apply to the exercise of public power?
Court reasoning The Court held that the exercise of public power must comply with
the Constitution and the doctrine of legality. Legality is an incident
of the rule of law and one of the constitutional mechanisms for
controlling public power.
Judgment / outcome The Court affirmed legality as a foundation for the control of public
power.
Constitutional significance Use with Fedsure and Albutt to build the rule of law/legality line of
authority.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 1(c), 2 and 172.
How to write it in the exam “Affordable Medicines confirms that legality is an incident of the
rule of law and forms part of the constitutional control of public
power.”
Albutt v Centre for the Study of Violence and Reconciliation 2010 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use for legality, rationality, procedural fairness and public power.
Legal theme Legality and rationality; procedural rationality; presidential pardons.
Facts The President created a special process for pardons of offenders
convicted of politically motivated crimes who had not received
amnesty through the TRC process. Victims and families wanted to
make representations before pardons were granted, but were
excluded.
Issue Whether victims had to be afforded an opportunity to be heard
before the President could grant pardons under the special
dispensation.
Court reasoning The Court held that all public power must comply with legality and
rationality. Because the purpose of the special dispensation was
linked to national reconciliation, excluding victims from the process
was irrational. Rationality can require a fair procedure where the
process chosen must be rationally connected to the purpose.
Judgment / outcome Victims had to be given an opportunity to make representations
before pardons were granted.
Constitutional significance Key rule of law case for rationality. It shows that legality is not only
“is there authorisation?” but also whether the means chosen
rationally connect to a legitimate governmental purpose.
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 1(c), 2 and 84(2)(j).
How to write it in the exam “Albutt shows that the exercise of public power must be rationally
connected to its purpose; if reconciliation is the aim, excluding
victims from the pardon process is irrational.”
S v Dodo 2001 (3) SA 382 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use for separation of powers, judicial function and comparative law.
Legal theme Separation of powers; sentencing; judicial independence; foreign
law under s 39.
Facts The case concerned mandatory minimum sentences prescribed by
legislation and whether such sentencing laws impermissibly
interfered with judicial sentencing discretion.
Issue Whether mandatory minimum sentences violate the separation of
powers by limiting the judiciary’s sentencing function.
Court reasoning The Court considered comparative foreign law and observed that
many constitutional democracies permit the legislature to set
sentencing frameworks. Mere legislative involvement in sentencing
does not automatically violate separation of powers. The key
question is whether judicial power is undermined to an
unconstitutional degree.
Judgment / outcome Mandatory minimum sentencing does not, merely by existing,
violate separation of powers.
Constitutional significance Useful for separation of powers and s 39(1) foreign law. It shows
that separation of powers does not require absolute separation;
some overlap is constitutionally permissible.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 ss 12, 36, 39; Criminal Law Amendment Act
minimum sentencing framework as background.
How to write it in the exam “S v Dodo shows that separation of powers is not absolute:
legislative regulation of sentencing is permissible if it does not
destroy the judiciary’s constitutional role.”
H v Fetal Assessment Centre 2015 (2) SA 193 (CC)⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use only if a question mentions international/foreign law or comparative interpretation.
Legal theme Use of foreign law; development of common law; s 39.
Facts The case concerned whether South African law should recognise a
child’s claim relating to negligent failure to detect serious foetal
abnormalities. It is used in the textbook extract for principles on
using foreign law.
Issue How should foreign law be used in constitutional interpretation and
common-law development?
Court reasoning The Court explained that foreign law can be useful when
approaching constitutional problems, but it must be used carefully
and contextually. South African courts must not transplant foreign
rules without considering local constitutional values and conditions.
Judgment / outcome The case developed the law cautiously while clarifying principles
for comparative legal reasoning.
Constitutional significance Not a core lecture case, but useful if a question asks about s 39(1)
(c) and the role of foreign law.
Legislation / sections linked Constitution 1996 s 39(1)(c) and s 39(2).
How to write it in the exam “H v Fetal Assessment Centre reminds us that foreign law may
assist constitutional reasoning, but South African courts must
adapt it to local constitutional values.”
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
Ex Parte Chairperson of the Constitutional Assembly: Certification judgments⚖️
High-yield exam use
Use when linking Theme 3 to Theme 4: the doctrines in Theme 4 were not accidental; they were constitutional commitments
certified by the Court.
Legal theme Background link to 1996 Constitution; constitutional supremacy;
separation of powers; legitimacy.
Facts The Constitutional Court had to certify whether the constitutional
text complied with the Constitutional Principles agreed during the
transition. The Theme 4 lectures refer back to certification as part
of understanding how the 1996 Constitution came into force.
Issue Whether the Final Constitution complied with the binding
Constitutional Principles.
Court reasoning The Court treated certification as a legal/judicial task rather than a
political preference exercise. The text had to comply with agreed
principles such as constitutional supremacy, justiciable rights,
democracy and separation of powers.
Judgment / outcome The first text was not fully certified; after amendment, the
constitutional text was certified and the Constitution came into
force on 4 February 1997.
Constitutional significance Useful background case for why the 1996 Constitution has legal
legitimacy and why its doctrines are binding.
Legislation / sections linked Interim Constitution Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles;
Constitution 1996 generally.
How to write it in the exam “The Certification judgments show that the 1996 Constitution’s
core principles were legally tested against agreed Constitutional
Principles before the Constitution came into force.”
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
4. Legislation, constitutional sections and legal instruments bank
Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 Central legal source for Theme 4. Prescribed sections: 1, 2, 8, 9,
10, 36, 39, 172. Lecture examples also use ss 7, 12, 16, 25, 26,
27, 32, 35, 74, 83, 84, 181 and 182.
What it says / does Supreme law of the Republic; creates values, rights, institutions,
limitations, interpretation duties and remedies for invalid
law/conduct.
Why it matters Theme 4 is essentially about how the 1996 Constitution structures,
constrains and transforms public and private power.
Cases linked Makwanyane, Daniels, PE Municipality, Fourie, Carmichele,
Grootboom, Soobramoney, EFF, Fedsure, Affordable Medicines,
Albutt, Dodo.
Exam sentence “The Constitution is both a founding-value document and a binding
supreme law: s 1 states the values, while s 2 gives them
enforceable supremacy.”
Section 1 - Founding values📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 Value-based constitutionalism and rule of law sections.
What it says / does South Africa is founded on dignity, equality, human rights, non-
racialism, non-sexism, supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law,
universal adult suffrage, regular elections, multi-party democracy,
accountability, responsiveness and openness.
Why it matters These values permeate interpretation, limitation, democracy, rule
of law and separation of powers.
Cases linked Makwanyane, Soobramoney, Fourie, EFF, Fedsure.
Exam sentence “Section 1 makes constitutional values foundational, meaning
courts must interpret law consistently with dignity, equality,
freedom, accountability and the rule of law.”
Section 2 - Supremacy of the Constitution📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 Constitutional supremacy.
What it says / does The Constitution is the supreme law; law or conduct inconsistent
with it is invalid; obligations imposed by it must be fulfilled.
Why it matters Makes judicial review possible and separates South Africa from
parliamentary sovereignty.
Cases linked Makwanyane, EFF, Fedsure, Affordable Medicines, Albutt.
Exam sentence “Section 2 converts constitutional supremacy into a binding rule:
inconsistent law or conduct is invalid.”
Section 7 - Rights📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 Bill of Rights framework.
What it says / does Bill of Rights is a cornerstone of democracy; the state must
respect, protect, promote and fulfil rights; rights are subject to
limitations.
Why it matters Links transformative constitutionalism and the state’s positive
obligations.
Cases linked Grootboom, Carmichele, Soobramoney.
Exam sentence “Section 7(2) means the state must not only avoid violating rights
but must actively protect, promote and fulfil them.”
Section 8 - Application of the Bill of Rights📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 Direct/indirect and vertical/horizontal application.
What it says / does The Bill of Rights applies to all law and binds the legislature,
executive, judiciary and organs of state. It may bind natural and
juristic persons depending on the nature of the right and duty.
Why it matters Core section for explaining vertical and horizontal application.
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
Cases linked Exam sentence Carmichele; equality examples; private discrimination examples.
“Section 8 is the gateway provision for deciding whether the Bill of
Rights applies vertically, horizontally, directly or indirectly.”
Section 9 - Equality📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Value-based constitutionalism; horizontal application examples.
Everyone is equal before the law; unfair discrimination by the state
and by private persons is prohibited; national legislation must
prevent/prohibit unfair discrimination.
Shows substantive equality and direct horizontal application.
Makwanyane, Fourie, Daniels; linked to PEPUDA.
“Section 9 is especially important because it expressly applies to
private persons through s 9(4), supporting horizontal application.”
Section 10 - Human dignity📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Foundational value/right; Makwanyane; Fourie; PE Municipality.
Everyone has inherent dignity and the right to have dignity
respected and protected.
Often treated as a core value in South African constitutionalism.
Makwanyane, Fourie, PE Municipality, Soobramoney.
“Dignity is both a right and an organising value that shapes
interpretation, limitation and remedies.”
Section 36 - Limitation of rights📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Limitations clause.
Rights may be limited only by law of general application to the
extent reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic
society based on dignity, equality and freedom. Factors include
nature of right, purpose, extent, relationship between limitation and
purpose, and less restrictive means.
Core exam structure for limitation questions.
Makwanyane, Walters, Fourie, Dodo.
“A s 36 answer must first identify the infringement, then weigh
whether the limitation is reasonable and justifiable.”
Section 39 - Interpretation of the Bill of Rights / legislation / common law / customary law📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Value-based interpretation; indirect application.
When interpreting the Bill of Rights, courts must promote dignity,
equality and freedom; must consider international law; may
consider foreign law. When interpreting legislation or developing
common/customary law, courts must promote the spirit, purport
and objects of the Bill of Rights.
Central to value-based constitutionalism and indirect application.
Daniels, Carmichele, H v Fetal Assessment Centre, S v Walters.
Exam sentence “Section 39(2) is the bridge between constitutional values and
ordinary law.”
Section 172 - Constitutional invalidity and remedies📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Constitutional supremacy and judicial review.
When deciding a constitutional matter, a court must declare
inconsistent law/conduct invalid to the extent of inconsistency and
may make a just and equitable order.
This is the remedial consequence of constitutional supremacy.
Makwanyane, EFF, Affordable Medicines.
“Section 172 gives courts the remedial power that makes
constitutional supremacy practical.”
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
Interim Constitution of 1993📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Makwanyane and s 33 limitation comparison.
The transitional constitution containing an interim Bill of Rights and
limitation clause.
Why it matters Several early Constitutional Court cases, including Makwanyane,
were decided under the Interim Constitution, but the principles
remain foundational.
Cases linked Exam sentence Makwanyane, Certification judgments.
“The Interim Constitution introduced justiciable rights and began
the shift from parliamentary sovereignty to constitutional
supremacy.”
Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977 - s 277(1)(a)📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does S v Makwanyane.
Authorised the death penalty for certain crimes before
constitutional invalidation.
Why it matters Shows how old-order legislation was tested against the new
constitutional order.
Cases linked Exam sentence S v Makwanyane.
“Makwanyane invalidated the death penalty provision in the
Criminal Procedure Act because it was inconsistent with
constitutional rights and values.”
Intestate Succession Act 81 of 1987📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Daniels v Campbell.
Regulates inheritance where a person dies without a will. The term
“spouse” was interpreted to include a surviving spouse in a Muslim
marriage.
Shows values-based statutory interpretation and inclusion.
Daniels v Campbell.
“Daniels shows that ordinary statutory words must be interpreted
through constitutional values where possible.”
Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act 27 of 1990📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Daniels v Campbell.
Allows claims for maintenance by surviving spouses. “Spouse”
was interpreted inclusively.
Works with Intestate Succession Act in Daniels.
Daniels v Campbell.
“The Acts were read inclusively to avoid exclusion inconsistent
with equality, tolerance and diversity.”
Disaster Management Act 57 of 2002 - s 27📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Rule of law lecture example on lockdown regulations.
Allows the responsible Minister, after a national state of disaster, to
make regulations or issue directions on matters such as
movement, resources, evacuation, traffic, premises, alcohol,
communication, procurement and other steps necessary to prevent
escalation.
Why it matters Cases linked Used to explain legality and rationality: is there authority, and is
there a rational relationship between the regulation and legitimate
government purpose?
Rule-of-law example; linked conceptually to Fedsure, Affordable
Medicines and Albutt.
Exam sentence “The Disaster Management Act example shows that lawful public
power requires both authorisation and rational connection to a
legitimate purpose.”
Built for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
Promotion of Access to Information Act 2 of 2000 (PAIA)📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Vertical application example for s 32 access to information.
Legislation giving effect to the right of access to information.
Shows how a constitutional right is implemented through national
legislation and enforced against public bodies.
Not a core Theme 4 case; used in examples.
“PAIA is the statutory mechanism used to give effect to s 32
access-to-information rights.”
Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000 (PEPUDA)📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Horizontal equality and s 9(4).
National legislation enacted to prevent or prohibit unfair
discrimination.
Why it matters Shows how the Constitution requires legislation to regulate private
discrimination.
Cases linked Exam sentence Linked to equality and horizontal application examples.
“PEPUDA operationalises s 9(4), which prohibits unfair
discrimination by private persons.”
Common law and customary law under s 39(2)📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Why it matters Cases linked Indirect application and Carmichele.
Courts must develop common law and customary law to promote
the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights.
This is how the Bill of Rights transforms ordinary legal rules
without always invalidating legislation.
Carmichele; H v Fetal Assessment Centre.
Exam sentence “Indirect application occurs when courts develop common law or
customary law under s 39(2) to align it with constitutional values.”
Civil Union Act 17 of 2006📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Consequence of Fourie.
Legislation enacted after Fourie to provide legal recognition for
same-sex unions.
Why it matters Shows how a Constitutional Court decision can require Parliament
to correct unconstitutional exclusion.
Cases linked Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie.
Exam sentence “Fourie resulted in legislative reform, showing the Constitution’s
transformative effect on social institutions.”
Promotion of Administrative Justice Act 3 of 2000 (PAJA)📜
Where it appears in Theme 4 What it says / does Background to administrative justice; not central in your Theme 4
slide extracts but useful if s 33/legality is raised.
National legislation giving effect to the constitutional right to just
administrative action.
Why it matters Cases linked Exam sentence Do not confuse PAJA review with legality review: legality is used
where no specific review route applies or where broad public
power is assessed.
Albutt, Affordable Medicines and Fedsure are legality/rule-of-law
cases rather than ordinary PAJA case examples in your lecture.
“If a question is about rule of law/legality rather than administrative
action, focus on authorisation and rationality rather than defaulting
to PAJA.”

6. What to memorise before a Theme 4 test
Memory list
Constitutionalism = government authority is derived from and limited by a constitution; it must structure and constrain state
power.
Constitutional supremacy = Constitution is supreme; inconsistent law/conduct is invalid; courts can review law/conduct.
Rule of law / legality = public power must be authorised by law and exercised rationally.
Values = dignity, equality, freedom, non-racialism, non-sexism, accountability, responsiveness, openness and rule of law
permeate interpretation and limitation.
s 36 method = right limited? If yes, is limitation reasonable and justifiable? Apply nature of right, purpose, extent, relation and
less restrictive means.
s 39 method = interpret rights and ordinary law to promote dignity, equality and freedom and the spirit, purport and objects of
the Bill of Rights.
Application = direct/indirect + vertical/horizontal. Always identify both in a rights problem.
Use Makwanyane for values and limitation; Daniels for s 39 interpretation; Carmichele for common-law development;
EFF/Fedsure/Affordable Medicines/Albutt for rule of law; PE Municipality/Fourie for balancing and transformation.
7. Mini model answer templates
5-mark: Explain constitutional supremacy
Constitutional supremacy means the Constitution is the highest law. Section 2 provides that law or conduct inconsistent with it is
invalid and that constitutional obligations must be fulfilled. This makes the Constitution justiciable: courts may test laws and
conduct against it. It also rejects parliamentary sovereignty because Parliament is bound by the Constitution. Cases such as S v
Makwanyane and EFF v Speaker show that courts may invalidate old legislation or unlawful conduct when inconsistent with
constitutional rights, values and obligations.
5-mark: Explain rule of law and legality
The rule of law is a founding value in s 1(c). At minimum, it requires that public power must be authorised by law and exercised
rationally. Fedsure states that the legislature and executive may exercise no power beyond that conferred by law. Affordable
Medicines confirms that legality is part of the constitutional control of public power. Albutt shows that rationality may require aBuilt for exam revision | Cases, Acts, sections + how to use themIntro to Constitutional Law 178 | Theme 4 Case + Legislation Doc
fair process where the process must be connected to the purpose. EFF v Speaker shows that no constitutional decision may
simply be ignored without court challenge.
10/15-mark: Application of the Bill of Rights structure
1. Identify the right and section involved.
2. State whether the Bill of Rights applies directly or indirectly.
3. State whether it applies vertically or horizontally.
4. If direct: explain that the right itself is relied upon and inconsistent law/conduct may be invalid.
5. If indirect: use s 39(2) to interpret legislation or develop common/customary law.
6. If vertical: state actor/state organ is bound by s 8(1).
7. If horizontal: private actor may be bound under s 8(2), considering nature of right and duty.
8. Add example/case: Makwanyane for direct invalidity; Carmichele for indirect development; Grootboom for vertical socio-
economic rights; equality examples/PEPUDA for horizontal discrimination.
