34  Paragraph (d) uses the word 'justifiable'  instead of'reasonable'. The wording derives from dissension
during the  drafting.  In  one of their early  reports,  the  drafters of  the  Bill  opposed the  entrenchment
of  review  of  administrative  decisions  for  unreasonableness  on  the  ground  that  that  would  have
'far-reaching  consequences  for  South  African  administrative  law'  (Technical  Committee  on
Fundamental  Rights during the Transition  Seventh Progress Report (29 July  1993)  6).  This was a very
curious  objection  - after  all,  much  of the Bill,  and the  Constitution  of which  it  is part,  will  have
cataclysmic  consequences  for  South  African law -
At that stage there  appeared to be two sources  of resistance among political negotiators  to the notion
anxiety  that  that idea
of review  for unreasonableness.  The one  was  the usual -
might be abused by the  courts to usurp  the policymaking prerogatives of the executive.  The other was
an anxiety  arising from  a  somewhat irrational  distrust  of the word  'reasonable'.
In an effort  to allay these  concerns,  I proposed  a compromise  administrative justice clause to certain
political negotiators.  The compromise  clause  tried to meet  the first anxiety by defining  the  scope of
the review jurisdiction in a way which  attempted to guard against the kind of abuse feared. Paragraphs
(2)  and  (3)  of the  compromise  clause  (below)  embody this  effort.  And  it  tried to meet  the  second
anxiety by replacing  the word  'reasonable'  with 'justifiable',  which I take to mean  the same thing,  but
which is  apparently  freer of the connotations  which  dismay  those  who  fear  'reasonableness'.
The compromise  clause  read  as follows:
'Compromise  Administrative  Justice Clause:
18.(1)  Every person shall have the  right not to be affected adversely by a decision made in the exercise
of public  power which is  unlawful,  procedurally unfair,  or not justifiable.
(2)  A  decision  shall  not be considered  justifiable  unless:
(a)  a plausible  answer can  be given  to any reasonable  objection  to the  decision;
(b)  a plausible  explanation  can be given  why  the decision  was chosen  in  preference to  any arguably
superior alternative;  and
(c)  a rational connection  can be shown between the premises  of the decision (including  any evidence
or argument  on which it  purports  to  be based)  and the decision  itself.
(3)  In  deciding  whether  a  decision  is  justifiable,  the  [designated  authority]  shall  not  usurp  the
prerogative  of  the  decisionmaker  to  make  such  policy  choices  as  the  decisionmaker  considers
desirable in  the  interests  of good governance,  and it  shall respect and  uphold every  such  choice.
(4) Every  person shall have  the  right to be  furnished  with reasons  in  writing for  any decision,  made
in the exercise  of public power,  which  affects  him or  her adversely.'

In the end, as can be seen from the administrative  justice clause  actually enacted  (quoted in the text
above),  the legitimate anxiety  was  ignored,  and no wording  was adopted to guard  against  it; but the
irrational  anxiety  was met,  and  the word  'justifiable',  the  sole survivor  of  the  compromise  clause,
somehow  found its way  into the  final  product.
(The expression 'designated  authority' was  used to fit with the text then current.  At that stage it  was
still  an open question which courts would be  entrusted with  the enforcement  of the  Bill.)


INTRODUCING  THE  INTERIM  BILL OF  RIGHTS

to develop a theory of what makes a decision justifiable,  and what makes
it  unjustifiable.  A  good  starting  point  would  be  to  recognize  that  the
justifiability  of  an  administrative  decision  is  a  matter  not  of  second-
guessing  the policy choices  that it  entails,  which  is the  prerogative of the
decisionmaker,  but  rather  of  the  soundness  of the  process  of deciding
which went into its making. It is suggested that an administrative  decision
cannot  be  taken  to  be  justifiable  unless  (a)
the  decisionmaker  has
considered  all  the  serious  objections  to  the  decision  taken  and  has
answers  which  plausibly  meet  them;  (b)  the  decisionmaker  has  consi-
dered all the serious alternatives to the  decision taken,  and has discarded
them for plausible reasons; and (c)  there is a rational connection  between
premises  and  conclusion  -
between  the  information  (evidence  and
argument)  before  the  decisionmaker  and  the  decision  taken.35  A
decisionmaker  who  is  conscious,  while  deciding,  that  a  court  may
eventually  scrutinize  his  or her  decisions  under  these  criteria  is  under
serious  pressure  to  deploy  a  thorough  and  disciplined  decisionmaking
process;  one likely  to yield  wise  decisions. 36

So  understood,  s  24(d)  would  lift the  shutters  that  now veil  the  inner
workings of so  much administrative decisionmaking,  and expose it to the
lights of the ethic of justification. In one respect, however,  s 24(d) may be
thought  to  render  administrative  action  excessively  vulnerable:
it
requires administrative  action to be justifiable 'in  relation to the reasons
given for it'.  This qualification  might be read as referring  back to s 24(c),
which entitles one to demand reasons in writing for administrative  action.
If s  24(d)  requires  administrative  action  to  be justifiable  by  the reasons
supplied  in response  to a  demand  made  under s  24(c),  that might wreak
administrative  havoc,  for  it  would  require  officials  to  supply  reasons
under  s  24(c) which  are carefully  enough  drafted to  take  the  decision in
due  course  past judicial  review  under s  24(d).

Suppose,  in  other  words,  that  an  official,  faced  with  some  urgent
demand  for  written  reasons  under  paragraph  (c),  responds  carelessly,
omits one of the reasons  which actually moved the decisionmaker  to take
the decision,  and consequently furnishes a set of written reasons  which  is
not full  enough  to  demonstrate  justifiability under  paragraph  (d).  If on
judicial  review  under  paragraph  (d)  the  decisionmaker  has  to show  the
decision to be justifiable on the basis of the careless statement of reasons,
the court would  have to strike down  the decision,  even although  it is one
which  might  in  fact be  justifiable,  just  because  the  written  statement  is
incomplete.  On this reading of s 24,  the decision would stand or fall by the
written statement of reasons,  and that statement  could not be augmented
with  reasons  not  mentioned  in  it  but  which  did  actually  move  the

35  See,  further,  my 'Reconsidering  Review:  Participation  and Accountability'  1993  Acta Juridica 35  at

40-43.

36  Which  is not to say  that the  idea  of justifiability entitles  a court  to strike down  a decision  merely  on

the ground of  its unwisdom.


SOUTH  AFRICAN  JOURNAL  ON  HUMAN  RIGHTS

decisionmaker  to take  the  decision and  which,  together with  the  written
reasons,  do in  fact show  the decision  to  be justifiable.

So the drafters,  who initially resisted the idea of entrenching review for
unreasonableness  altogether, 37 have,  somewhat  perversely,  in  the  end
embodied  it  in  a  form  which  may  be  read  as  being  among  the  most
demanding  versions  possible  of  that  idea.  Indeed,  this  version  is  so
demanding  that  it  may sabotage  the  idea  altogether.  There  can  be few
civil  services  anywhere  which  have  the  capacity  regularly  to  produce
statements of reasons that, without pre-litigation revision,  are sufficiently
meticulously drafted to assure passage past judicial review.  Our own civil
service,  in  the  nature  of the transition  that South  Africa  is  undergoing,
will be relatively  inexperienced,  and it will be  dealing with  a great tide of
expectations,  and an immense volume of work. To burden it with the kind
of  rigour  which  this  reading  requires  might  undermine  government
altogether.

And  that  might  put  the  very  idea  of  review  for  unreasonableness  in
jeopardy, because it would give the government a case for a constitutional
amendment  to  free  itself  of the  burden  imposed  by  this  reading.  The
result  might well  be the  repeal  altogether  of s  24(d).  And  that would  of
course  gravely  subvert  the  contribution that s 24 makes  to  the  advent of
a culture  of justification.

If  the  courts  can  read  the  Bill  of  Rights  in  a  way  which  averts  this
consequence,  they should:  if the point of the Bill is  to foster a  culture of
justification,  it is  the  courts'  duty  to  read the  Bill  in the  way which  best
preserves  its  capacity  to  do  that.  And  there  are  ways  of  avoiding  the
reading of s 24(d) which would  put the Bill's contribution to such a culture
in jeopardy. The  courts might note, for  instance,  that s 24(c)  and  s 24(d)
govern  different  classes  of  administrative  action:  the  right  to  written
reasons  in  s  24(c)  applies  to  administrative  action  which  affects  one's
rights  or interests,  but the right  to  justifiable decisions in s 24(d)  applies
to  administrative  action  which  affects  or  threatens  one's  rights.  This
discrepancy is  a cogent argument  for refusing to  read the two paragraphs
together;  for refusing  to read 'justifiable  in relation to the  reasons given
for  it'  in  paragraph  (d)  as  referring  to  the  written  reasons  made
compulsory by paragraph  (c).  That would free a court to read 'the reasons
given for it' in paragraph (d)  as referring to the reasons supplied in judicial
review  itself by  way  of justifying  the  decision.  The  effect  would  be  to
make  s 24 an  instrument for improving  governance,  not frustrating  it.  A
reading  of s 24  which  achieves  that is  plainly to  be preferred.

This point draws attention to the most conspicuous idiosyncrasy  in s 24:
that each  of the  four  rights that it  confers  applies  to  a  different  class  of
administrative  action:  paragraph (a)  confers a right to  lawful administra-
tive  action  where  one's  rights  or  interests  are  affected  or  threatened;

37  See  note  34  above.


INTRODUCING  THE  INTERIM  BILL  OF  RIGHTS

paragraph  (b)  confers  a  right  to  procedurally  fair  administrative  action
where one's rights or legitimate  expectations (but  not one's interests) are
affected  or threatened;  paragraph  (c)  confers  a  right  to  written reasons
where  one's  rights  or  interests  are  affected  (but  not  threatened);  and
paragraph  (d)  confers  a  right  to  justifiable  administrative  action  where
one's  rights  (but  not  one's  interests  or  legitimate  expectations)  are
affected or threatened.  The courts will have their work cut out developing
a coherent  theory  to account  for these  variations.

Freedom of Information

The  drafting  is  also  problematic  in  s 23,  the  right  of  access  to  official
information.  Access  to  official  information  is  a  matter  of  the  utmost
importance  to  any  effort  to  bring  about  a  culture  of  justification.  A
government  which can close its files will be under much  weaker pressure
to justify  its decisions  than one  which has  to  open them.

If the  Bill  of Rights  entrenched  a  general  right  to  information,  that
would  of course  not  expose  all  official  information  to  public  scrutiny.
Even  the  most  committed  advocates  of open  government  acknowledge
that  there  are  always  sensitive  classes  of  information  -
such  as
information  necessary  to  protect  personal  privacy,  or  commercial
confidentiality,  or  national  security,  or  law  enforcement  - which
government is entitled to conceal. But the limitation clause is available  to
protect  such  information:  government  could  procure  legislation  to
preserve  the  confidentiality  of these  classes  of  information,  and  then
justify that legislation under the limitation clause.  Such  legislation would
be of the same form as a typical Freedom  of Information  Act.  The main
value  of a  general  right  to information  would  consequently  be  to force
government  to  define  and  defend  the  classes  of  information  which  it
asserts have to be secret.  Have the drafters bequeathed us a general right
of information?

Section  23  gives  every person  a  'right  of access  to all information  held
by the  state or any of its organs at any level  of government';  but only  'in
so far as such information is required for the exercise or protection of any
of his or her rights'. The drafters' decision to limit the right to information
required for the exercise  or protection of one's rights is unfortunate. 38 It
invites  a  conservative  court  to  read  the  right  as  merely  ancillary  to
litigation:  as conferring entitlement  only to  the  information  necessary to
no  more,  in  other  words,  than  a
vindicate  one's  rights  at  law  -

38  The limitation  appears  to be  derived  from Hugh  Corder et al A  Charter for Social Justice (1992)  54.

In  that work  the  authors propose  the  following access-to-information  clause:
'(1)  Everyone  has the right  of access  to information  held by any  authority performing  governmental
functions.
(2)  Everyone has the  right of access  to that information which  is necessary  for the implementation  of
his  or her rights.'


SOUTH  AFRICAN  JOURNAL  ON  HUMAN  RIGHTS

constitutional  right  to  discovery.  There  is nothing,  however,  in  the  text
which precludes the courts from reading the right more broadly.  One may
seek  to exercise or protect one's rights by means  other  than litigation -
for instance through  publicity or by resort  to the  political process -
and
information may be required for that purpose. On that, broader,  reading,
s 23 would come substantially closer to conferring a general right of access
to  official  information.

In choosing between  a narrower reading  and a broader  one, the courts
should have regard to the point of the Bill of Rights -
to foster a  culture
of justification. That point will usually argue for a broader reading.  So the
drafting is not entirely  irretrievable,  although  it is to be regretted that the
opportunity  to  enact  an  unambiguous  general  right  to  information  was
squandered.

Special Immunities: Labour and Religion

Despite  these deficiencies,  the rights in Chapter 3,  as the  above  account
reveals,  do comprise  a set of principles  with  considerable  power to  fuel a
vigorous  inquiry into the  justification  of decisions  within  their purview;
too  much  power  for  some,  as  the  efforts  of various  lobbies  to procure
special  exemptions  from such  inquiry  attests. 39 The  impact  of two such
lobbies  is  conspicuous  in  the  Bill.  Section  33(5)(a)  states  that  the
'provisions  of a  law in  force  at the  commencement  of  this  Constitution
promoting  fair  employment  practices,  orderly  and  equitable  collective
bargaining and the regulation of industrial action shall remain of full force
and effect until repealed or amended by the  legislature'.  The intention  is
apparently  to insulate existing  labour legislation  from inquiry  under the
Bill into  its justification,  although  the  apparently  deliberate  elimination
of wording expressly  giving this exemption  primacy over the rights in the
Bill,40  which was present  until  late  in the  drafting process, 41 might,  on a
theory which attached  importance to the drafting history, 42 be thought to
weaken  the evidence  of that  intention.

The other lobby is  the  religious.  Section  14(1)  guarantees  the  right to
freedom  of religion.  That idea might  be thought to entail  freedom  from
governmental  practices  which  favour  one  religious  perspective  over
another. 43  If  it  did,  it  would  open  inquiry  into  the  justification  of

non-adherents  which  may  be  considered  coercion. 46  Furthermore,  the
exemption  applies only where religious observances  'are  conducted on an
equitable  basis'.  But state  endorsement  of a  religious perspective  might
be  thought inequitable  to any  who do  not share  that perspective.

governmental  pressure,  since

it  comes  from  the  state  -

The result is that a religious observance can be taken to be safely within
the exemption  in s 14(2)  only where the state does not endorse a religious
perspective,  whether  explicitly  or  tacitly.  It  will  seldom  be  easy  to
structure  a  religious  observance  at  a  state  or  state-aided  institution  to
meet  this condition.

What  is  more,  the  exemption  in  s  14(2)  is  not framed  to  prevail  over
freedom of religion; nor, for that matter over the freedoms of conscience,
thought,  belief  and  opinion.  On  the  contrary,  it  is  expressed  not  to

Exercise Clause ('Congress  shall  make  no law  ...  prohibiting  the  free exercise  [of  religion]').  From
the  particular  textual  shape  of  the  First Amendment,  however,  it does not  follow  that  the question
cannot  arise  under the concept  of freedom  of  religion,  properly  understood.

44  Potentially more  succesful  is  s  14(3),  which  provides:

'Nothing  in  this Chapter  shall preclude  legislation  recognizing -
(a)  a  system  of personal  and family law  adhered  to  by persons  professing  a particular  religion;  and
(b)  the  validity  of  marriages  concluded  under  a  system  of  religious  law  subject  to  specified
procedures.'
The main point of this subsection  is  apparently  to  insulate the religious  practices  within its purview
from  challenge  under  the guarantee  of gender  equality  in  s 8.

45  Cf  Wallace v  Jaffree 472  US 38  (1984)  at  69 (O'Connor J).

46  Cf Lee  v  Weisman (1992)  120 L  Ed 2d  467  (S  Ct).


SOUTH  AFRICAN  JOURNAL  ON  HUMAN  RIGHTS

derogate from the generality of those freedoms. 47 This weakens  the force
of the  exemption.  Nor  is  there  any  indication  that  the  exemption  is  to
prevail over  the  prohibition  in s  8 - known  as the  equality  clause - on
unfair  discrimination,  direct  and  indirect,  on  the  ground  of  religion,
conscience  or  belief. 48  This  weakens  even  further  the  capacity  of  the
exemption  to  insulate  from  scrutiny  state  practices  that  favour  certain
religious  perspectives  over others.

There  is  therefore  ample  support  in  the  Bill  for  a  reading  of s 14(2)
which  gives it a narrow effect.  And a court  should be inclined  to give that
support  great  weight.  Special  exemptions  from the rights  in the  Bill  are
special  immunities  from the  standards  of justification  that it announces.
They  tend,  therefore,  to  undermine  the  Bill's  primary  object  of
inaugurating  a  culture  of  justification.  They  should  consequently  be
construed  as narrowly  as possible.  It follows  that any  textual  support  in
the Bill for a  narrow reading of the exemptions  should be given as  much
weight  as possible.

Resolving Ambiguity: Affirmative Action

The  same kind  of approach,  as  I have  already  suggested,  should  govern
any  ambiguity  in the  Bill:  any  ambiguity  should  be  resolved  in the way
which  optimizes  the Bill's  capacity  to  foster a  culture  of justification.

One such  ambiguity may be thought  to arise in the  field of affirmative
action. Section 8 (the equality clause) guarantees  both equality before the
law  and equal  protection of the law,  and prohibits  unfair discrimination
both generally and on the particular grounds of race,  gender,  sex,  ethnic
or  social  origin,  colour,  sexual  orientation,  age,  disability,  religion,
conscience,  belief,  culture  or language.  It then  continues:

'This section shall not preclude measures designed to achieve the adequate protection and
advancement  of  persons  or  groups  or  categories  of  persons  disadvantaged  by  unfair
discrimination,  in  order  to  enable  their  full  and  equal  enjoyment  of  all  rights  and
freedoms.'49

This  provision  is  intended  to  save  affirmative  action  programmes  -
programmes  to  undo  the  disadvantages  caused  by  apartheid  -
from
challenge  under  the equality clause.  The desirability  of such a  provision
was not very controversial  during the drafting  process. All three political
parties  which  published  proposed  bills  of  rights  prior  to  the  process
affirmed  the  need for  such  a  provision. 50  But an  important  controversy

47  The exemption  granted by s 14(2) is prefaced with the words,  'Without  derogating from the generality
of subsection (1)...'. Subsection (1) guarantees the freedoms of conscience,  religion, thought, belief
and opinion.
48  Section  8(2).
49  Section  8(3)(a).
50  See  the  African  National  Congress's  Draft  Bill of Rights  (Preliminary  Revised  Version February


INTRODUCING  THE INTERIM  BILL  OF  RIGHTS

during  the  drafting  process  raised  the  question  how  closely  a  court
applying  this  provision  could  scrutinize  something  purporting  to  be  an
affirmative  action  measure  to  make  sure  that  it  really  was one.

The controversy  was sparked  by an earlier draft,  in which the place  of
the  words  'designed  to  achieve'  was  taken  by  the  words  'aimed  at'. 51
Those  words  raised  the  concern  that  they  could  be  understood  to
authorize  a  court  to  ask  whether  a  measure  was  aimed  at  undoing
disadvantage,  but not whether it was actually likely to undo disadvantage.
The concern,  in  other words,  was that the  provision might  be  construed
to  empower  the  court  to  review  the  intentions  of  the  authors  of  the
measure,  but not its effects.  If, say,  the government  reserved  95  per cent
of senior civil  service jobs for Africans,  it might be impossible  to contest
the  government's  assertion  that  its  aim  was  to  protect  and  advance
categories  of persons  disadvantaged  by unfair discrimination,  in order to
enable  their  full  and  equal  enjoyment  of all  rights and  freedoms;  but  it
might  be  a  lively  question  whether  that  was  the probable  effect  of  the
reservation.  The anxiety was that the courts would have been confined to
scrutinizing the ends sought by the authors of the measure,  and precluded
from  scrutinizing  the means chosen  to  realize  those ends.

It was to meet this concern that the words 'aimed at' were replaced with
the  words 'designed  to  achieve'.  On  its face,  however,  the  new wording
is  far  from  an  unambiguous  resolution  of  the  controversy.  The  words
'designed  to achieve'  can  mean  (a)  'intended  to  achieve',  in which  case
they mean much the same as 'aimed  at'; or (b) they can mean 'constructed
so as to achieve'.  In this latter sense,  the wording refers to measures which
are  not  only  intended  to  achieve  something,  but  the  design  of  which
makes  it  objectively  probable  that  they  will  in  fact  achieve  that
something; which are structured, in other words,  to achieve that thing. In
this sense 'designed  to'  embodies much of the ambivalence  of 'calculated
to', which,  although  it can mean  'intended  to', the  courts often interpret
as  'likely  to';5 2  indeed,  it incorporates  both  those meanings.

In which sense is 'designed  to achieve'  used here:  (a)  or (b)? For what
it  is worth,  the  drafting  history  rules  out  (a);  if  that  had  been  the  sense
intended,  there  would  have  been  no  point  in  discarding  the  original
wording,  'aimed at'. 53 But a court  may,  and probably should,  decide  that

1993)  Art  14;  the  National  Party's  Government's Proposals on  a Charter of Fundamental Rights
(2  February 1993)  s 6  (3);  the  Democratic Party's Draft Bill of Rights (May  1993)  Art 2  (2).  See  also
the  KwaZulu  Legislative  Assembly's  proposed  Constitution  of  the  State  of  KwaZulu/Natal
(1 December  1992)  clause  10  (b).

51  Technical Committee  on Fundamental Rights during  the Transition Seventh Progress Report (29 July

1993)  clause  2  (3).  In  this earlier draft,  there  were  also other  differences  in wording.

52  Or some minor variation  on that expression:  see,  for  example,  Amoils v  Johannesburg City  Council
1943  TPD 386 at  389;  R v  Lord 1926 CPD  262 at  264;  Brink v  Lichtenburg Liquor Licensing Board
1944 TPD 161  at  171; Johannesburg Liquor Licensing Board v Short 1946 AD 713  at 722-3; Rossouw
v Norton NO  1950  (2)  SA 1  (C)  at  5;  S  v  Beyleveld 1964  (1)  SA  269  (T) at 272-3.

53  What  is  more,  the  political  negotiators  who  settled  the  wording  declined  to  insert  the  word


SOUTH  AFRICAN  JOURNAL  ON  HUMAN  RIGHTS

the  drafting  history is  irrelevant. 54  A  better  reason  for preferring  sense
(b)  over  sense  (a)  is  simply  that,  since  it  brings  not  only  ends  but  also
means under judicial  scrutiny, it brings the whole measure,  rather than an
arbitrary  fragment  of  it  (the  mere  intentions  of  its  authors)  into  the
enterprise  of  justification.  Sense  (b)  consequently  makes  the  provision
operate as a fuller and more coherent  contribution to the cultivation of an
ethic of justification.  That is a powerful  reason for preferring it over sense
(a).  On this  view,  the point of the Bill of Rights -
to  foster a  culture  of
justification -
is again  a resource  which helps  resolve ambiguities  in the
Bill's text.

CONCLUSION

The point of the Bill of Rights  is to  foster a culture  of justification.  This
is  something which  appears not only  from our history,  but from  the  text
of  the  Bill  itself.  Measured  against  that  point,  the  Bill  suffers  from
significant  weaknesses.  Fortunately,  the point  of the Bill  of Rights  is not
just  a  criterion  for  evaluating  the  Bill,  but  also  a  powerful  guide  for
answering  the questions  of interpretation  that  it generates.  If the  courts
use that guide  properly, they can overcome most of the deficiencies in the
Bill,  and  make  of it a  potent  weapon  for bringing  about  democracy.

'reasonable'  before 'measures'  or the word 'reasonably'  before 'designed',  evidently because they had
been  assured by  the technical committee  which  drafted the  Bill  that 'the  rationality  of the measures
is sufficiently catered  for by the qualification  which follows the words "in order to"  ' (unpublished  and
undated drafts generated  by  the Technical  Committee on Fundamental  Rights during the Transition
during September  1993).  Whatever one thinks of the soundness  of the technical committee's  opinion,
it seems clear that its effect was  that the  wording finally adopted  was accepted  on the understanding
that the  rationality  of  affirmative  action  measures  was to be  reviewable.  That  would  entitle  a court
to scrutinize not just the intentions of the authors of the  measures, but also the effects  of the measures.
Consequently,  so  far  as  a court  considers  the drafting  history  relevant,  this  feature  of  that history
appears  to demonstrate  that  the  text  was  adopted  on the  understanding  that  not  just  the  ends  of
affirmative  action  measures,  but also  their means,  were  to be  amenable  to judicial review.

54  For several  reasons,  among them that people  governed by  a text  are entitled  to order their lives  on
the strength  of  what  they  can  see;  on  the  strength,  in  other  words,  of  the published  words  and
published  authoritative  commentary,  without  having  to  burrow  among  obscure  and  inaccessible
drafting sources.  Other reasons for discounting the  drafting history appear from a rich literature.  See,
for example,  Ronald  Dworkin  Law's Empire (1986)  chapter  10;  Life's  Dominion (1993)  chapter 5.

Parliamentary Sovereignty & Judicial Review

Core Idea: Parliamentary Sovereignty

• Parliament was the SUPREME law maker

• Could make or unmake any law

• No Higher law

• Courts could not strike down acts of parliament based on substance

Judicial Role (Very Limited)

• Judicial review is when a court reviews a decision by parliament, focusing on whether the

correct Procedure was followed

• During Apartheid, Courts could  declare Acts of Parliament invalid (limited to procedure)

• Cannot review law based on law


Parliamentary Sovereignty & Judicial
review (Apartheid Era)

Why this matters

• Enabled Apartheid legislation

• No effective legal check and balances on Parliament


Constitutional Crisis & Parliamentary
Supremacy (Sovereignty)

● The 1910 Constitution had two entrenched provisions

○ 1) Language
○ 2) Limited voting rights of for Black  South Africans
○ To amend an entrenched provision – must have 2/3rds majority in parliament

● 1951 – Parliament passed the Separate Representation of Voters Act

○ Purpose – Parliament attempts to remove Black and Coloured voters from the

common roll

○ Houses sitting separately, adopted by a simple majority (thinking they did not

have to follow the procedural rules)


Harris v Minister of the Interior [Harris I]

● Legal Question

○ Could parliament validly remove Black and Coloured voters from the common

role WITHOUT complying with the entrenched amendment procedure?

● Decision

○ Appellant Division said NO
○ Even under parliamentary sovereignty, Parliament must follow the manner

and form requirements laid down in the Constitution (Judicial Review)

● Key Principle

○ Parliament is sovereign, but when altering entrenched provisions, it must

comply with the prescribed procedure

○ The Act was declared invalid


Harris v Minister of the Interior [Harris 1]

● Why Harris I matters

○ Recognised that procedural limits on Parliament are

enforceable by courts

○ Confirmed the idea of “manner and form” limitations

○ Strengthened the role of courts in protecting the constitutional

structure


Minister of the Interior v Harris (Harris II]

● The government refused to accept defeat in Harris I

● It attempted to bypass the Decision of the Appellate Division by:

○ Passed the High Court of Parliament Act 35 of 1952

○ This new body

■ Composed of Members of Parliament

■ Had the power to “review and overturn decisions” of the Appellate

Division

■ Could declare court judgments invalid

○ Parliament tried to make itself the final court of appeal over

constitutional matters


Minister of the Interior v Harris (Harris II]

Why is this problematic?

● Under the 1910 Constitution, there was

○ Parliamentary Sovereignty

○ But also a separation between legislative and judicial functions

(SOP)

● Even under PS – parliament could not simply

○ Convert itself into a court

○ Set aside judicial decisions retroactively

● Violated core structural principles of the constitutional order


Minister of the Interior v Harris (Harris II]

● The Appellate Division declared the High Court of Parliament Act

invalid

Reasoning

1. Parliament cannot confer judicial power on itself in a way

inconsistent with the constitutional structure

2. Judicial power is vested in the courts

3. Parliament cannot overturn a court judgment by simply declaring

it wrong

● This was a major assertion of judicial independence


Collins v Minister of the Interior

● Another attempt to ensure racial disenfranchisement

● Parliament

○ Expanded the senate to obtain the required majority

○ Passed the amendment to the Act through a joint sitting

● This case challenged the validity of the change to the Senate. The

Argument was such that parliament manipulated its own composition to

achieve the constitutional majority


Collins v Minister of the Interior

● The Appellate Division upheld the validity of the Senate Act and

constitutional amendments

Reasoning:

1. Parliament had complied with the formal “manner and form”

requirements

2. The Court would not inquire into Parliament's political motives

3. Once the proper procedure was followed, the amendment to the Senate

was valid

● If the formal constitutional procedure is satisfied, the courts will not

question how Parliament secured that majority


Collins v Minister of the Interior

● What this tells us

○ “courts were subservient and subordinate to Parliament. The

Court could only test the manner and form in which legislation

was promulgated. This means that only formal requirements

could be tested. The content or Substance of legislation could

not be tested. The Court could not use the fact that certain

guaranteed rights were violated as. a ground for its decision

(Kleyn et al )


Summary

● Harris  I = Parliament must follow the rules of the

Constitution

● Harris II – High Court of Parliament – Parliament cannot

turn itself into a court …  (SOP considerations)

● Collins = If Parliament follows the rules, courts cannot

question what it does


Parliamentary Sovereignty versus
Constitutional Supremacy

○ Parliament has final say

■ No substantive review

○ The Constitution is the final say!

■ Substantive review ( Judiciable BOR)


Two stage Transition Solution

• CODESA I

• CODESA II

• MPNF

→ IC

→ First elections

→ Constitutional Assembly

→ Certification

→ Final Text = Consitution of the Republic of South Africa


Two stage Transition Solution

The negotiators  (CODESA) devised a two-stage transition

solution:

• Stage 1: Unelected negotiating parties draft and adopt the IC; an

interim government and the IC would govern the country after

the first election

• Stage 2: A democratically elected Constitutional Assembly

drafts the Final Constitution after the election.

HAVE. A FANTASTIC VACATION

Bilateral Treaties
These are agreements between South Africa and one other specific country.
1. South Africa–China Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2024/2025 Framework):
This is a cornerstone of South Africa’s economic policy. In late 2025/early 2026, the two
nations signed the Framework Agreement on Joint Development Economic
Partnership. This agreement focuses on increasing bilateral trade (which reached over
$53 billion in 2025), expanding market access for South African agricultural goods, and
collaborating on "New Quality Productive Forces" like green energy and digital
technology.
2. South Africa–United States Extradition Treaty (2001):
A long-standing and active legal agreement that allows for the formal surrender of
persons accused or convicted of crimes between the two nations. This treaty is
frequently cited in high-profile international legal cases and is supported by a related
Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty (MLAT) to share evidence in criminal investigations.
Multilateral Treaties
These are agreements involving South Africa and three or more other countries.
1. African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA):
South Africa is a leading member of this landmark agreement, which aims to create a
single continental market for goods and services. In January 2024, South Africa officially
began trading under the AfCFTA preferences, sending its first shipment of locally
manufactured goods to other African ports. It is designed to eliminate 90% of tariffs on
intra-African trade over time.
2. SADC Protocol on Trade (and its updates):
As a member of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), South Africa
is bound by this protocol which established a Free Trade Area among 16 Southern
African nations. It governs the duty-free movement of goods within the region and is a
primary tool for South Africa’s regional economic integration.

(2025)

# Source: CON178-A2-S1-Hub/exports/cleaned_sources/03_theme_3_negotiated_revolution/theme_3_case_and_legislation_doc_intro_to_con_law_1.md

**INTRO TO CONSTITUTIONAL LAW 178**

**THEME 3 CASE + LEGISLATION DOCKET**

*Negotiated Constitutional “Revolution”*

- ---
- **🎯 Purpose of this docket**
- This document does the same job as the Theme 4 docket: it gathers the cases, laws, constitutional texts, constitutional principles, and legally important instruments mentioned or directly relied on in Theme 3.   * It is not a replacement for the full Meganotes. * It is a case + legislation bank for exam use. * It flags what you can cite, how to use it, and what textbook / prescribed pages may still be needed.

- ---
- **⚠️ Coverage honesty note**
- I used the uploaded Theme 3 lecture, Interim Constitution, Constitutional Principles, Constitutional Guidelines, First Certification judgment, Mureinik article, and Langa article.  The study guide also lists additional prescribed materials that were not all uploaded here, including Kleyn pages, De Vos & Freedman sections 1.3, 1.4 and 2.2, Sarkin, and Klug. Those should be added if you want a completely prescribed-source version.

# **📑 Table of Contents**

1. 1. Theme 3 source + scope audit
2. 2. Master timeline of the negotiated constitutional revolution
3. 3. Case law docket
4. 4. Legislation / constitutional instrument docket
5. 5. Constitutional Principles bank
6. 6. Exam use: how to write Theme 3 answers
7. 7. Do you need more textbook pages?

# **1. Theme 3 Source + Scope Audit**

- ---
- **📘 What Theme 3 is really about**
- Theme 3 explains how South Africa moved from apartheid legality and parliamentary sovereignty into a negotiated constitutional democracy. The key story is not only “a new Constitution was written”. The deeper issue is how legitimacy was constructed through a two-stage transition: an interim negotiated settlement, followed by a democratically elected Constitutional Assembly, checked by pre-agreed Constitutional Principles and judicial certification.

- **Source / material** **How it matters for this docket**
- Theme 3 lecture 10-13 Provides the lecture roadmap: CODESA, MPNF, Interim Constitution, Constitutional Principles, First Certification, Second Certification, Final Constitution, amendments, and transformative nature.
- Interim Constitution Act 200 of 1993 Primary legal text for the two-stage transition, Bill of Rights, Constitutional Assembly, certification mechanism, and Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles.
- Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles Binding benchmarks against which the Final Constitution had to be certified.
- First Certification judgment Major case for certification, legal legitimacy, role of Constitutional Court, and whether the New Text complied with the Constitutional Principles.
- Mureinik, “A Bridge to Where?” Key article for “historic bridge”, culture of authority, culture of justification, and why the Bill of Rights mattered.
- Langa, “Transformative Constitutionalism” Key article for transformative constitutionalism, substantive equality, legal culture, access to justice, and the Constitution as a long-term project of change.
- Constitutional Guidelines for a Democratic South Africa Political / constitutional vision document showing pre-1994 ideas about democracy, non-racialism, non-sexism, Bill of Rights, land, workers, women, and family.

# **2. Master Timeline of the Negotiated Constitutional Revolution**

- ---
- **🧩 Timeline in one exam sentence**
- Collapse of apartheid legitimacy → CODESA I → central legitimacy and minority-protection deadlock → CODESA II failure → violence and mistrust, especially Boipatong → MPNF compromise → Interim Constitution → 1994 democratic election → Constitutional Assembly → First Certification failure → amended text → Second Certification → Mandela signs the Final Constitution → 1996 Constitution commences on 4 February 1997.

- **Stage** **Legal / constitutional meaning** **Exam trigger**
- CODESA I Negotiations begin but legitimacy problem remains: negotiators were not elected in free and verifiable elections. Why could unelected negotiators not legitimately write the final constitution?
- CODESA II Second round in 1992 fails over voting thresholds and transitional government structure. Explain breakdown and why compromise became necessary.
- Political violence Boipatong, township violence, assassinations, IFP conflict and security force destabilisation deepened mistrust. Shows transition was negotiated under pressure, not peacefully inevitable.
- MPNF Successor to CODESA; established two-stage transition and election date. Role of Ramaphosa and Meyer; why MPNF succeeded.
- Interim Constitution Legal bridge: governs after first election and sets rules for drafting Final Constitution. Key features: GNU, Bill of Rights, Constitutional Court, CPs, certification.
- 1994 election Democratic mandate created; Constitutional Assembly becomes legitimate constitution-making body. Why first election matters beyond symbolism.
- Certification Constitutional Court acts as independent legal arbiter of compliance with CPs. Judicial, not political, certification task.
- Final Constitution Product of democratic mandate + negotiated constraints + judicial certification. Why 1996 Constitution has special legitimacy.

# **3. Case Law Docket**

- ---
- **🎯 How to use the case law in Theme 3**
- Theme 3 is not case-heavy in the ordinary criminal/private-law sense. Its most important “case” is the First Certification judgment because it explains the legal mechanics and legitimacy of the 1996 Constitution. The other cases appear mainly through Langa and the Certification judgment to support transformation, the bridge metaphor, access to justice, and the Court’s understanding of post-apartheid constitutionalism.

## **⚖️ Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 / Ex parte Chairperson of the Constitutional Assembly: In re Certification of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 1996 (4) SA 744 (CC); 1996 (10) BCLR 1253 (CC)  Category in Theme 3: MAIN THEME 3 CASE - certification of the New Text  Source note: Source focus: study guide prescribes paragraphs 1-47; lecture also refers to objections on socio-economic rights, separation of powers, and non-compliance issues.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts The Constitutional Assembly adopted a new constitutional text on 8 May 1996 and transmitted it to the Constitutional Court for certification. Political parties and many private bodies objected to various provisions. The Court had to decide whether every provision of the New Text complied with the 34 Constitutional Principles in Schedule 4 to the Interim Constitution.
- Issue Whether the Constitutional Court could certify that all provisions of the proposed Final Constitution complied with the Constitutional Principles agreed during the negotiated transition.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The Court explained that certification was a judicial, not political, function. It compared the New Text to the Constitutional Principles, not to political preferences. The Court held that the CPs had to be interpreted purposively, holistically and without technical rigidity. The Court first asked whether the basic structure and premises of the New Text accorded with the CPs; then it examined whether the detailed provisions complied. The Court accepted the basic structure but found some details non-compliant.
- Judgment / outcome The Court refused to certify the first text as it stood because several provisions did not comply with the Constitutional Principles. The text had to go back to the Constitutional Assembly for amendment.
- Constitutional significance This judgment is central to the legitimacy of the 1996 Constitution. It proves that the Final Constitution was not merely a political deal; it was measured against a binding legal pact. It also shows how the two-stage transition balanced democratic legitimacy with negotiated safeguards.
- Exam use Use this case whenever asked about: the two-stage transition; the role of the Constitutional Court; the purpose of the 34 Constitutional Principles; why certification mattered; why the 1996 Constitution has special legitimacy; or why the Court’s task was legal rather than political.

## **⚖️ Certification of the Amended Text of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 / Second Certification Judgment**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 1996 (later Constitutional Court certification of Amended Text; lecture gives 4 December 1996)  Category in Theme 3: THEME 3 COMPLETION CASE - final legal hurdle  Source note: The uploaded lecture gives the core details; the full Second Certification judgment was not uploaded in this batch.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts After the Constitutional Court refused to certify the first text, the Constitutional Assembly amended the text to address the shortcomings identified in the First Certification judgment.
- Issue Whether the amended constitutional text now complied with the 34 Constitutional Principles and could therefore come into force.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The Court considered whether the defects identified in the First Certification judgment had been remedied. The lecture states that the Court unanimously certified the Amended Text as complying with the Constitutional Principles.
- Judgment / outcome The Amended Text was certified. This cleared the final legal hurdle for the 1996 Constitution. Mandela signed the Constitution into law on 10 December 1996 at Sharpeville, and it took effect on 4 February 1997.
- Constitutional significance This case completes the certification story. The Final Constitution is legitimate because it was produced by an elected Constitutional Assembly and certified by an independent Constitutional Court against pre-agreed principles.
- Exam use Use after First Certification to show the complete sequence: first draft rejected → amendments made → amended text certified → Final Constitution becomes law.

## **⚖️ Executive Council, Western Cape Legislature and Others v President of the Republic of South Africa and Others**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 1995 (4) SA 877 (CC); 1995 (10) BCLR 1289 (CC)  Category in Theme 3: Mentioned in First Certification judgment for transition complexity  Source note: Mentioned in First Certification judgment para 9 context.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts The First Certification judgment refers to this case while describing the enormous complexity of replacing apartheid-era government structures with a constitutional state. Four provincial governments, self-governing territories, and former TBVC structures ceased to exist when the Interim Constitution came into force.
- Issue In the broader transition context, the issue was how to manage constitutional, legislative, executive, administrative and judicial continuity while dismantling apartheid structures and creating new democratic institutions.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The case is used in the Certification judgment as context: it illustrates the practical difficulty of constitutional transition and decentralisation after apartheid.
- Judgment / outcome The case is not the main Theme 3 authority, but it supports the idea that the transition was legally and administratively complex, not just political.
- Constitutional significance It shows that constitutional transformation required institutional reconstruction, not only a new text.
- Exam use Use as supporting authority if discussing the complexity of the transition, the collapse of old structures, and the need for continuity under the Interim Constitution.

## **⚖️ Azanian Peoples Organisation (AZAPO) and Others v President of the Republic of South Africa and Others**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: Constitutional Court, CCT 17/96, 25 July 1996  Category in Theme 3: Mentioned in First Certification judgment for negotiated transition context  Source note: Mentioned in First Certification judgment para 10 context.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts The First Certification judgment refers to AZAPO when explaining that the overwhelming majority of South Africans realised the country had to be rescued from imminent disaster through a negotiated commitment to a fundamentally new constitutional order.
- Issue In the broader context, AZAPO dealt with the post-apartheid settlement and the legal consequences of national unity and reconciliation.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The Certification judgment uses AZAPO to support the historical point that South Africa moved from deep conflict and minority domination into a negotiated constitutional order based on open democracy and fundamental human rights.
- Judgment / outcome AZAPO is not the main Theme 3 case, but it is useful background for the transition and reconciliation logic.
- Constitutional significance It links Theme 3 to the idea that constitutional democracy was produced by negotiation, compromise and an attempt to avoid catastrophe.
- Exam use Use as a supporting case when discussing why negotiation, reconciliation and compromise mattered in the constitutional transition.

## **⚖️ S v Makwanyane**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC); 1995 (6) BCLR 665 (CC)  Category in Theme 3: Transformative constitutionalism / bridge case mentioned by Langa  Source note: Mentioned in Langa article footnote and later Theme 4 material; useful as cross-theme authority.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts The case concerned the constitutionality of the death penalty under the Interim Constitution. Langa cites it as an example of the Constitution expressly aspiring to transition from the unacceptable features of the past to a contrasting future.
- Issue Whether the death penalty was compatible with the values and rights in the Interim Constitution, especially life, dignity and protection against cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The Court used constitutional values to reject the death penalty. Langa uses the case to show that the Constitution is transformative and future-orientated.
- Judgment / outcome The death penalty was declared unconstitutional.
- Constitutional significance In Theme 3, use it not mainly for the death penalty itself, but to show that the Interim Constitution was already understood as a transformative bridge from past injustice to a rights-based future.
- Exam use Use when asked to “critically discuss the 1996 Constitution as a transformative document” or to link Theme 3’s bridge idea to constitutional values.

## **⚖️ Du Plessis v De Klerk**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 1996 (3) SA 850 (CC); 1996 (5) BCLR 658 (CC)  Category in Theme 3: Transformation and Bill of Rights application mentioned by Langa / Certification  Source note: Mentioned in Langa and First Certification judgment.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts The case is cited by Langa for the idea that the Constitution seeks to transform the previous legal order into a new order. The First Certification judgment also refers to it in relation to indirect horizontal application of rights under the Interim Constitution.
- Issue How the Bill of Rights interacts with private law/common law and how the Constitution changes the pre-1994 legal order.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The case forms part of the early constitutional jurisprudence around the application of the Bill of Rights and constitutional transformation.
- Judgment / outcome It confirmed that the Constitution marked a move away from the old order, even where the precise mechanics of horizontality were contested.
- Constitutional significance It helps show that transformative constitutionalism includes transformation of legal culture and private law, not merely replacement of parliamentary sovereignty.
- Exam use Use as supporting authority for the proposition that the Constitution seeks to transform the status quo ante into a new order.

## **⚖️ Soobramoney v Minister of Health, KwaZulu-Natal**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 1998 (1) SA 765 (CC); 1997 (12) BCLR 1696 (CC)  Category in Theme 3: Transformative constitutionalism and socio-economic context  Source note: Mentioned in Langa and Theme 3 / Theme 4 lecture material.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts The case concerned access to scarce healthcare resources. Langa cites it for Chaskalson CJ’s statement that the Constitution commits South Africa to address poverty, unemployment, inadequate social security, lack of clean water and inadequate health services.
- Issue How socio-economic realities fit into constitutional transformation and the interpretation of socio-economic rights.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The Court acknowledged the harsh socio-economic conditions existing when the Constitution was adopted and linked transformation to dignity, freedom and equality.
- Judgment / outcome The applicant did not receive the requested treatment, but the case became a foundational statement about the Constitution’s transformative commitment.
- Constitutional significance For Theme 3, it proves that the Final Constitution is not merely procedural. It is connected to material transformation and the struggle to remedy apartheid’s socio-economic legacy.
- Exam use Use in answers on transformative constitutionalism, especially when explaining that the Constitution is backward-looking and forward-looking.

## **⚖️ Rates Action Group v City of Cape Town**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 2004 (12) BCLR 1328 (C)  Category in Theme 3: Transformative Constitution - cited by Langa  Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts Langa cites this case for the idea that South Africa’s Constitution is not designed to obstruct modernity or prevent change, but to provide a mandate, framework and blueprint for transforming society from its racist and unequal past into one in which all can live with dignity.
- Issue What purpose the South African Constitution serves in a society emerging from apartheid.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The quoted reasoning contrasts South Africa’s Constitution with a static view of constitutionalism. It emphasises that the Constitution is meant to enable change.
- Judgment / outcome The case is used as a persuasive articulation of the Constitution’s transformative character.
- Constitutional significance It supports the Theme 3 idea that the 1996 Constitution is a transformative document produced by negotiated constitutionalism.
- Exam use Use as a supporting quote/example in an essay on transformative constitutionalism, especially to show the Constitution is a mandate and framework for change.

## **⚖️ City of Johannesburg v Rand Properties (Pty) Ltd**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 2006 (6) BCLR 728 (W)  Category in Theme 3: Transformative Constitution - cited by Langa  Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts Langa cites this case for the proposition that the State cannot be a passive bystander in shaping a society in which individuals can fully enjoy their rights.
- Issue Whether constitutional rights should be interpreted in light of social and economic context.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The case emphasised that the full power of the Bill of Rights is realised when rights are interpreted with reference to actual socio-economic conditions.
- Judgment / outcome The case supports a context-sensitive and transformative approach to constitutional rights.
- Constitutional significance It links Theme 3’s negotiated Constitution to concrete duties of social transformation.
- Exam use Use when explaining that transformative constitutionalism is not just symbolic; it demands state action and context-sensitive interpretation.

## **⚖️ Van Rooyen v S**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 2002 (8) BCLR 810 (CC)  Category in Theme 3: Transformation of institutions - cited by Langa  Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts Langa cites Van Rooyen for the idea that transformation involves changes not only in the legal order but also in the composition and character of institutions that were historically controlled largely by whites and, in particular, white men.
- Issue How constitutional transformation affects legal institutions and their composition.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The reasoning cited by Langa stresses that transformation is institutional as well as doctrinal.
- Judgment / outcome The case supports the proposition that constitutional transformation requires changing institutions, not only rules.
- Constitutional significance It helps deepen Theme 3 answers by showing that the negotiated Constitution aimed at structural transformation.
- Exam use Use in an essay on transformative constitutionalism or when explaining why the transition required institutional reconstruction.

## **⚖️ Minister of Finance v Van Heerden**

- ---
- **📌 Quick ID**
- Citation / reference: 2004 (11) BCLR 1125 (CC)  Category in Theme 3: Substantive equality - cited by Langa  Source note: Mentioned in Langa article.

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Facts Langa cites Sachs J in Van Heerden for a substantive approach to equality. Equality is not simply identical treatment; the real question is whether a measure advances or retards the equal enjoyment of rights in practice.
- Issue How equality should be understood in a society structured by historical disadvantage.
- Court reasoning / legal reasoning The reasoning cited by Langa roots equality in a transformative constitutional philosophy that confronts systemic race and gender disadvantage.
- Judgment / outcome The case supports remedial and substantive equality measures.
- Constitutional significance In Theme 3, it supports the argument that the 1996 Constitution is transformative because it aims to undo systemic disadvantage, not merely declare formal equality.
- Exam use Use when linking Constitutional Principles, the Final Constitution, and transformative constitutionalism to substantive equality.

# **4. Legislation / Constitutional Instrument Docket**

## **📜 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 200 of 1993 (“Interim Constitution” / IC)**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Interim constitutional statute; assented to 25 January 1994; commenced 27 April 1994; later repealed/replaced by the 1996 Constitution.
- Key provisions / content Key provisions for Theme 3 include: Preamble and Postamble; s 4 supremacy of the Constitution; Chapter 3 Bill of Rights; Chapter 5 ss 68-74 on the adoption of the new Constitution; s 71 certification; Chapter 7 creating the Constitutional Court; Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles; Government of National Unity provisions.
- Role in Theme 3 The IC is the legal bridge between apartheid parliamentary sovereignty and the Final Constitution. It governed the country after the 1994 election and set the rules for how the Final Constitution would be drafted and certified.
- Exam use Use in any Theme 3 answer on the two-stage transition, the “bridge”, the Constitutional Assembly, certification, Constitutional Principles, and the shift from parliamentary sovereignty to constitutional supremacy.
- Warning / nuance Do not confuse the Interim Constitution with the Final Constitution. The IC was drafted by unelected negotiators; the Final Constitution was drafted by an elected Constitutional Assembly and certified by the Constitutional Court.

## **📜 Chapter 5 of the Interim Constitution: ss 68-74**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Specific chapter regulating the adoption of the new constitutional text.
- Key provisions / content s 68 created the Constitutional Assembly by requiring the National Assembly and Senate to sit jointly for constitution-making. s 71 required Constitutional Court certification. s 73 regulated adoption of the new text, including the two-thirds majority requirement and fallback mechanisms. s 74 protected the Constitutional Principles and Chapter 5 from easy amendment.
- Role in Theme 3 Chapter 5 is the legal engine of the second stage of the transition. It converts the political compromise into legal procedure.
- Exam use Use when asked to explain the rules for drafting the Final Constitution. Mention Constitutional Assembly = NA + Senate sitting jointly; two-year deadline; two-thirds support; certification; referendum fallback if relevant.
- Warning / nuance Exam trap: do not say CODESA drafted the Final Constitution. CODESA/MPNF produced the negotiated framework and IC; the elected Constitutional Assembly drafted the Final Constitution.

## **📜 Schedule 4 to the Interim Constitution: the 34 Constitutional Principles**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Binding principles agreed during negotiations and entrenched in the IC.
- Key provisions / content The Principles required, among other things: one sovereign democratic state; common citizenship; fundamental rights protected by entrenched and justiciable provisions; prohibition of discrimination; constitutional supremacy; equality before the law; separation of powers; independent judiciary; representative government; universal adult suffrage; common voters’ roll; proportional representation; freedom of information; formal legislative procedures; language and cultural diversity; traditional leadership and customary law; multi-level government; provincial and local powers; fiscal arrangements; independent institutions; non-partisan public service; security forces acting in the national interest; GNU until 1999; no national election before 30 April 1999 unless specific conditions arose; and self-determination possibilities.
- Role in Theme 3 They solved the legitimacy/minority-fear deadlock: the elected body would draft the Final Constitution, but it had to remain within negotiated binding principles.
- Exam use Use as the heart of the two-stage transition answer. They are the legal benchmark used by the Constitutional Court in certification.
- Warning / nuance Critical phrase: the CPs were a “solemn pact”. Do not describe them as optional guidelines.

## **📜 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 / formerly Act 108 of 1996**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Final Constitution; formally enacted as Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 108 of 1996 and now referred to as the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996.
- Key provisions / content Drafted by the Constitutional Assembly; certified by the Constitutional Court; signed by Mandela on 10 December 1996; commenced on 4 February 1997. Important aspects include a justiciable Bill of Rights, universal adult suffrage, constitutional supremacy, rule of law, non-racialism and non-sexism, co-operative government, separation of powers, Chapter 9 institutions, traditional leaders and languages.
- Role in Theme 3 The Final Constitution is the product of Theme 3. Its legitimacy rests on democratic election, negotiated principles, Constitutional Assembly drafting, and Constitutional Court certification.
- Exam use Use to conclude Theme 3 answers. Show that the Constitution is not just a statute but the culmination of a negotiated constitutional revolution.
- Warning / nuance Use correct name: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996.

## **📜 Constitutional Guidelines for a Democratic South Africa**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status ANC constitutional vision document, reproduced in 1989 SAJHR and simplified in the uploaded material.
- Key provisions / content The Guidelines proposed an independent, unitary, democratic, non-racial South Africa; one person one vote; one country, one people; a Bill of Rights based on the Freedom Charter; anti-racism; social and economic rights; mixed economy; land redress; workers’ charter; equal rights for women; protection of family rights; and a non-aligned foreign policy.
- Role in Theme 3 The Guidelines show the pre-negotiation constitutional imagination of a democratic South Africa and how liberation-era constitutional ideas fed into the later negotiation process.
- Exam use Use as background when explaining the run-up to negotiations and the vision of a future democratic order.
- Warning / nuance This is not the same as the 34 Constitutional Principles. It is a political / constitutional guideline document, not the binding Schedule 4 certification benchmark.

## **📜 Electoral Act, 1993**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Legislation referred to in the Interim Constitution for regulating elections under the transitional framework.
- Key provisions / content The Interim Constitution refers to elections being held in accordance with the Electoral Act, 1993, including elections for the National Assembly.
- Role in Theme 3 The Act matters because democratic elections were necessary to create a legitimate Constitutional Assembly.
- Exam use Use only briefly if discussing the legal machinery of the first democratic election.
- Warning / nuance Do not over-focus on this unless the question asks about election mechanics.

## **📜 Republic of South Africa Constitution Act 110 of 1983 / 1983 Constitution**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Pre-democratic Constitution under which the old Parliament still operated before the transition.
- Key provisions / content The lecture notes that the Interim Constitution was adopted in terms of the procedures and processes of the 1983 Constitution.
- Role in Theme 3 This shows constitutional history matters: the new order was legally brought into being through the old order’s formal machinery, even though it broke substantively with parliamentary sovereignty and apartheid constitutionalism.
- Exam use Use to explain continuity + rupture: the transition used old legal forms to create a radically different constitutional order.
- Warning / nuance Exam trap: do not say the 1983 Constitution itself was democratic. It provided the old legal route through which the IC was enacted.

## **📜 Labour Relations Act, 1956 / Labour Relations Act reference in certification issues**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Ordinary labour legislation mentioned in the certification context, especially around attempts to shield legislation from constitutional scrutiny.
- Key provisions / content The Theme 3 lecture refers to NT 241(1) and the LRA in the context of immunising legislation from constitutional scrutiny. The concern was that ordinary laws cannot be insulated from constitutional review because CP IV requires constitutional supremacy.
- Role in Theme 3 This is an example of why the First Certification Court refused to certify some provisions. If Parliament could shield ordinary legislation from constitutional scrutiny, constitutional supremacy would be undermined.
- Exam use Use in First Certification answers as an example of non-compliance with CP IV.
- Warning / nuance Keep the focus on constitutional supremacy, not labour law detail.

## **📜 Local Government Transition Act 209 of 1993**

- **Element** **Detailed notes**
- Nature / status Legislation appearing in the First Certification judgment index in relation to local government and provincial powers.
- Key provisions / content The Certification judgment considered local government powers and their relationship to Constitutional Principles concerning provincial powers.
- Role in Theme 3 The Act is relevant mainly to the technical certification analysis of provincial/local government powers.
- Exam use Use only if asked about detailed Certification objections around provincial powers or local government. For ordinary Theme 3 answers, mention only if necessary.
- Warning / nuance Not a core memorise item unless your lecturer specifically emphasised provincial power objections.

# **5. Constitutional Principles Bank**

- ---
- **🧠 What the 34 Constitutional Principles did**
- They were not ordinary political promises. They were legally binding benchmarks in Schedule 4 of the Interim Constitution. The Constitutional Assembly could choose among permissible models, but it could not draft a Final Constitution inconsistent with the Constitutional Principles. The Constitutional Court was the independent arbiter.

- **Principle(s)** **Exam-ready meaning**
- I One sovereign state, common citizenship, democratic government, equality between men and women and all races.
- II Universally accepted fundamental rights, freedoms and civil liberties protected by entrenched and justiciable constitutional provisions.
- III Prohibition of racial, gender and other discrimination; promotion of racial and gender equality and national unity.
- IV Constitution as supreme law, binding all organs of state at all levels.
- V Equality before the law and equitable legal process, including affirmative measures.
- VI Separation of powers with checks and balances for accountability, responsiveness and openness.
- VII Independent, impartial judiciary with power to safeguard the Constitution and rights.
- VIII Representative government, multi-party democracy, regular elections, universal adult suffrage, common voters’ roll and proportional representation.
- IX-XV Open administration, formal legislative procedures, language/culture protection, civil society rights, traditional leadership, minority participation and special amendment procedures.
- XVI-XXVII Government structured at national, provincial and local levels; allocation of powers; provincial autonomy; local government; fiscal powers and equitable share.
- XXVIII-XXXI Labour rights, independent institutions, public service, and security forces serving the national interest.
- XXXII-XXXIV GNU until 1999, no early national election unless specified, and possible community self-determination within the broader national self-determination framework.

# **6. Exam Use: How to Write Theme 3 Answers**

- ---
- **✍️ Model answer skeleton: two-stage transition**
- Intro: South Africa’s transition was not a simple handover of power; it was a negotiated constitutional revolution structured through a two-stage transition.  Point 1: Explain legitimacy problem at CODESA - unelected negotiators lacked democratic mandate.  Point 2: Explain minority fear problem - old government wanted safeguards, power-sharing and supermajorities.  Point 3: Explain compromise - Stage 1 IC by negotiators; Stage 2 Final Constitution by elected Constitutional Assembly.  Point 4: Explain safeguards - 34 CPs + Constitutional Court certification.  Conclusion: The 1996 Constitution’s legitimacy comes from both democratic election and legal compliance with negotiated principles.

- ---
- **✍️ Model answer skeleton: First Certification**
- Intro: The First Certification judgment was the legal mechanism that ensured the Final Constitution complied with the negotiated settlement.  Facts/context: Constitutional Assembly adopted New Text; it was sent to the Constitutional Court.  Issue: Did all provisions comply with the 34 Constitutional Principles?  Reasoning: The Court’s task was judicial, not political; it interpreted CPs purposively and holistically; it assessed both structure and details.  Outcome: Basic structure complied, but some detailed provisions did not; the Court refused certification.  Significance: Certification protected constitutional supremacy, democratic legitimacy and negotiated safeguards.

- ---
- **🧠 What to memorise**
- * “Two-stage transition” = IC first, Final Constitution second. * “Solemn pact” = 34 Constitutional Principles. * Constitutional Assembly = National Assembly + Senate sitting jointly. * s 71(2) IC = new text had no force unless certified by the Constitutional Court. * First Certification = first text rejected. * Second Certification = amended text certified. * Mureinik = culture of authority → culture of justification. * Langa = transformative constitutionalism = substantive equality + legal culture + ongoing change.

- **Likely question** **Best authorities / instruments to use**
- Explain the journey leading to the 1996 Constitution. CODESA, MPNF, IC, CPs, Constitutional Assembly, First + Second Certification, Final Constitution.
- Explain the two-stage transition and why it was necessary. IC ss 68-74; Schedule 4 CPs; First Certification paras 11-18 logic.
- What was the role of the Constitutional Court in certification? First Certification judgment; IC s 71(2) and s 71(3).
- Why was the Interim Constitution a bridge? IC Postamble; Mureinik article; Langa article.
- Critically discuss the 1996 Constitution as transformative. Langa; Soobramoney; Makwanyane; Van Heerden; Mureinik.

# **7. Do You Need More Textbook Pages?**

- ---
- **✅ Honest answer**
- Yes - for the most complete, prescribed-source version, you should add more textbook/article pages if you can. This docket is strong for the uploaded Theme 3 lecture and uploaded readings, but your study guide lists prescribed sources that are not fully included in the upload batch.

- **Material still useful / possibly missing** **Why it matters**
- Kleyn et al Beginner’s Guide pages 51-52, 156-167, 180 Likely provides basic textbook framing of the transition, constitutionalism and 1996 Constitution.
- De Vos & Freedman sections 1.3, 1.4 and 2.2 Prescribed for transition to democracy, the 1996 Constitution, and constitutionalism. This would deepen the legal context and give textbook phrasing.
- Sarkin, “The drafting of South Africa’s Final Constitution from a Human-Rights Perspective” Prescribed article likely adds detail on drafting process and human-rights choices in the Final Constitution.
- Klug, “Towards a sociology of constitutional transformation” Prescribed article likely adds deeper academic explanation of post-apartheid constitutional order.
- Full Second Certification judgment Would allow the Second Certification entry to be expanded with direct judgment detail rather than lecture-level summary.

- ---
- **🎯 Practical recommendation**
- For exam purposes, the most urgent missing items would be: (1) De Vos & Freedman sections 1.3 and 1.4; (2) Sarkin; (3) Klug; and (4) the full Second Certification judgment if your lecturer expects detail beyond “the amended text was certified”.

# **Source Notes Used for This Docket**

* Theme 3 lecture 10-13: CODESA, MPNF, IC, CPs, First Certification, Second Certification, Final Constitution, amendments and transformative constitutionalism.
* Interim Constitution Act 200 of 1993: preamble, supremacy, Bill of Rights, Chapter 5 ss 68-74, Constitutional Court and Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles.
* First Certification judgment: historical context, legal context, nature of certification function, CP interpretation, structural compliance and objections.
* Mureinik “A Bridge to Where?”: culture of authority, culture of justification, Bill of Rights as chief strut of the bridge.
* Langa “Transformative Constitutionalism”: transformative Constitution, substantive equality, legal culture, ongoing change, access to justice and cited cases.
* Constitutional Guidelines: constitutional vision for a free, democratic, non-racist, non-sexist South Africa.

Theme 3:
Negotiated
Constitutional
“Revolution”
