rights
o Procedural → Substantive2. Concepts & principles
• Four principles
o 1.) Division of government power
o 2.) Separation of functions
o 3.) Separation of personnel
o 4.) System of checks and balances3. Historical background
• Origins in 17th Century enlightenment political philosophy
o *though perhaps an oversimplification
o Development from Hobbes, to Locke
o To Charles Badron de Montestuieu, to Jean Jacques
Rosseau, and USA
o Specific histories of monarchical and tyrannical governments
o Rise of liberalism and negative conceptions of freedom
o Rise of constitutionalism
• In principle the same, but incremental developments
o E.g. overlaps; new public institutions (*see Ch 9 institutions)3. Historical background
• Why is historical background important?4. Application in South Africa
• No express mention in Final Constitution
o Constitutional Principle VI from Interim Constitution
o Constitutional Court = Implicit in Final Constitution
• South African model
o PoD: No universal model
o Historical understanding and appreciation
▪ E.g. Westminster system & parliamentary sovereignty in apartheid era
o CC in De Lange v Smuts4. Application in South Africa
• Legislature
o Chapter 4 of Constitution
o National Assembly (NA) & National Council of Provinces4. Application in South Africa
• Legislature
o Overlap with executive rationale= Policy power to legislation
o Inherited from Westminster system
• Executive Council of Western Cape Legislature v
President of the Republic of South Africa
o Delegation of law making authority
o Permissible (to some degree)
▪ Limitations to nature + extent
o But specialisation, democracy, and concentration of power?4. Application in South Africa
• Legislature
o Chapter 4 of Constitution
o National Assembly (NA) & National Council of Provinces
o Members of Parliament
o Overlap with executive = Policy power to legislation
• Executive Council of Western Cape Legislature v
President of the Republic of South Africa
o Delegation of law-making authority
o Permissible (to some degree)
▪ Limitations to nature + extent
o But specialisation, democracy, and concentration of power?4. Application in South Africa
• Executive
o Ss 84 and 85 of Constitution
o Cabinet composition of Ministers
o Obligation to select cabinet from NA
o Commissions of enquiry
• NA exercises oversight
o Can recall executive
o Initiate votes of no confidence (impeachment, s 89)
o Accountability to NA– s 55(2) of Constitution
o Oversight of the executive and hold it accountable,
particularly in the implementation of legislation4. Application in South Africa
• Judiciary
o Chapter 8 of Constitution
o Hierarchy of courts
o Appointment of judges– Judicial Services Commission
o Manner of appointment involves all 3 branches
o Ensures (or is supposed to) impartiality and independence4. Application in South Africa
• Judicial review
o S 172 provides for competent courts to declare that any law
inconsistent with the Constitution is invalid to the extent of
its decision whether an Act of Parliament, a provincial Act or
conduct of the President is constitutional (section 167(5))
o Certain principles in the Constitution to limit litigation of
legislature and executive against one another4. Application in South Africa
• Judicial independence and impartiality
o CC confirmation in SA Association of Personal Injury Lawyers v
Heath
o JSC code of conduct and removals
o Power to initiate proceedings for the removal of judges via
the JSC (and involvement of 3 branches)
o Only possible on limited grounds of incapacity, gross
incompetence or gross misconduct
o E.g. Removal of J Hlope by Pres Ramaphosa4. Application in South Africa
• Chapter 9 Institutions
o Unique set of institutions that do not fall within classic model
o E.g. Public Protector; South African Human Rights Commission
o Also exercise oversight
o But due to falling outside 3 branches, in unique position
o Independence and introduces another layer of checks and
balances
o Problems? Critiques?

▪ E.g. NA calling executive; Judicial review5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma
• Focus: Judiciary
• Parliamentary sovereignty → constitutional supremacy
• Power of judicial review (s 172)
o Function to interpret law
o BUT sometimes interpreting law requires adjustments,
declarations of invalidity, and providing remedies
o Hence, practical problems arise
▪ Judges can make law
▪ OR declare law supported by a majority invalid
o Judges not (democratically) elected representatives5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma
• We spoke yesterday of how the CC has interpreted
Separation of Powers
o Problems?5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma
• Judicial decisions against the political will
o Similarly, we spoke yesterday how impeachment has built-in
safeguards against abuse as a political move
• Encroachment of Judiciary on domain of Legislature and
Executive – permissible to some degree
• Question of nature + extent
• Spectrum of responses
• Some view irreconcilable
• Some as necessary limit in democracy
• Some as legitimizing (camp in which SA mostly falls)5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma
• Responses to the following, in favour of judicial review:
• Judicial decisions based on personal, political, religious
opinion?
o Safeguards
o Substantive: Starre decisis, s 39 of Constitution
o Procedural: Appeal & review
• Majoritarian politics not necessarily representative
• Pluralism & proportional representation
• Human rights beneficiaries – everyone, citizens, permanent
residents etc.
• Some as necessary limit in democracy
• Some as legitimizing (camp in which SA mostly falls)5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma
• Responses to the following, in favour of judicial review:
• Judicial decisions based on personal, political, religious
opinion?
o There are built-in safeguards
o Substantive: Starre decisis, s 39 of Constitution
o Procedural: Appeal & review5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma
• Responses to the following, in favour of judicial review:
• Majoritarian politics not necessarily representative
• Pluralism & proportional representation
• Human rights beneficiaries – everyone, citizens, permanent
residents etc.
• Independence of judiciary
• Specialisation aspect of separation of powers
• Courts can enhance democracy
• Deliberative democracy, contestory politics, diologic SoP
• Critical legal theorists: Courts perpetuate neo-liberal paradigm5. Deference
• Focus: Judiciary
• ‘Paying deference to the legislature and executive’
• Non-interference with legislative and executive domain
• Recognition of functional divisions
• Question of a policy and political nature, not constitutional
• Application of counter-majoritarian dilemma
• Most pertinent e.g. budgeting, allocation of resources
• But – transformative constitutionalism?6. Conclusion
• SoP provides framework of government functioning
• The classical model is adapted based on
• Historical and normative context
• Political system
• While focus is on functionality and efficiency
• Oversight and accountability are the guiding principles
• Particularly in the SA context
• Know the mechanisms each branch of government has
• Understand problems in applying the SoP model7. Class activity
• Division of class ito: Executive, Legislature, Judiciary
• We are going to look at a factual circumstance
• Then explain how you would exercise oversight over the
other branches7. Class activity
The Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and Environment (the
executive) has approved plans for the construction of a new
1200 MW coal-fired powerplant. This comes after a meeting
of the Minister with select foreign energy companies. Only a
small environmental impact assessment was carried out.
The Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) and Carbon Act (CA)
developed by parliament (the legislature) makes provision
for coal fired powerplants. This is provided the
environmental impacts are not serious, and jobs are
prioritised for South Africans. Some MPs that drew up the
policy and act have shares in the energy companies that
attended the meeting. The Minister was not aware of this.7. Class activity
A group of concerned environmentalists have taken the
matter to court (the judiciary). They argue that a new coal-
fired powerplant infringes their environmental right in
section 24 of the Constitution. Further, they argue
government should be prioritising building new cleaner forms
of energy production in the IRP and the CA.7. Class activity
Questions
• Executive:
• How would you exercise oversight over the legislature?
• What would your response be in court to justify your decision to
approve the construction?
• Legislature
• How would you exercise oversight over the executive?
• What would your response be in court to justify the provisions of the
IRP and the CA?
• Judiciary
• How would you proceed to review the decision of the Minister?
• How would you proceed to review the contents of the IRP and
the CA?

# Source: CON178-A2-S1-Hub/exports/cleaned_sources/04_theme_4_core_principles/theme_4_lecture_15.md

Theme 4: The
Constitution of 1996:
Basic Principles,
Concepts and
Doctrines

Admin!
Tutorials…16th April
A1… 16th April
Emails… Please be polite

Recap: Theme 3
● We looked at the transition period that led to our 1996 Constitution
● We looked at the IC, and its characteristics
● We looked at the Constitutional Negotiations
● We looked at the two-stage transition
● We looked at the Constitutional Assembly
● We looked at the Certification Judgment
● We looked at the introduction of the 1996 Constitution

The way forward: Theme 4 RoadMap
● Be able to provide a comprehensive explanation of the term ‘constitutionalism’
● Be able to explain constitutional supremacy and its impact on South African
law
● Be able to explain Transformative Constitutionalism
● Know the foundational values of the Constitution and how it permeates
through the Constitution, specifically in the interpretation and limitation of rights
contained in the bill of rights
● Understand the concept of the horizontal application of the Bill of Rights
● Be able to explain the rule of law principle and how it has found application in
South African law
● Be able to explain the different conceptions of democracy
● Know and be able to explain the principles upon which the separation of
powers is based

The Constitution, 1996.
• Formally enacted as: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa
Act 108 of 1996
• Is now referred to as: Constitution of the Republic of South
Africa, 1996
• Drafted by the Constitutional Assembly
• Finally certified by the Constitutional Court (Second Certification
Judgment
• Took effect: 4 February 1997 (replacing 1993 Interim Constitution)

Important aspects of the 1996 Constitution
• Basic Rights for everyone are contained in a justiciable Bill of Rights
• Universal adult suffrage
• Constitutional Supremacy and the Rule of Law
• Non-racialism and non-sexism
• Co-operative government (national, provincial and local)
• Separation of powers (Legislative, executive and judicial authority)
• State institutions supporting constitutional democracy (Chp 9 institutions
like the auditor General or the Public Protector)
• Traditional leaders
• Languages

Understanding the 1996 Constitution
• To understand the 1996 Constitution, you need to
1) Understand the context in which it originates and operates
2) Understand the fundamental doctrines, concepts and principles
the constitution contains

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
• The theory of constitutional law
• Philosophy and doctrine that the governmental authority is
derived from, and limited by a body of (written) fundamental
law (ie a constitution)
• Ensures that rulers act according to binding boundaries and
not their own desires

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
• In essence, constitutionalism is the notion that a constitution
must both STUCTURE and CONSTRAIN state power
- A  constitution must establish the institutions and
o
- structures of government and allocate power to  them
for effective governing AND
- It  must limit and  disperse that power among the  I
o
 institutions and structures in an attempt to ensure power
will not be abused

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Characteristics of Constitutionalism
1. Identifies and establishes institutions and structures of
government
2. Formal and legal distribution of power to these institutions
and structures in terms of a written constitution
3. Describes nature and basis of relationship between the
institutions and structures

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Characteristics of Constitutionalism
4. Provides the creation of binding rules/ laws for institutions
and those who they govern
5. Places limits on exercise of public (state power)
6. Structure state and award and constrain power

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Descriptive understanding of Constitutionalism
• Factual description of structures and institutions
- • Focus on  EXPLAINING how these institutions work,
inter4act with each other, share and distribute power etc
- • Without reference to  norms or  normative values on
which constitutional system is evaluated by
• Focused on form rather than substance
• Colonial / Apartheid South Africa Constitutionalism

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Prescriptive understanding of Constitutionalism
• With reference to norms / normative values on which
the constitutional system is based
• Constitutional system should adhere to some basic
doctrines, principles etc
• This is the approach the new Democratic South Africa
takes

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
Key Aspects of Prescriptive Constitutionalism
• Constitutional Supremacy
• Limited Government
• Rule of Law
• Separation of Powers
• Democratic self government
• Protection of Human Rights
• Independent Judiciary
• Transformative Constitutionalism
Constitutionalism is considered essential for a functional democratic
state

Constitutional Supremacy
Most definitive feature of SA post-apartheid constitutional
system is Constitutional Supremacy
- • The foundation of  our democratic constitutional
dispensation
• Is a Founding Value and a binding enforceable rule
- - S1(c) (Value) ; S2 (binding rule)

Constitutional Supremacy
• Constitutional supremacy renders the constitution judicable
o Any law or conduct can be tested against the provisions
of the constitution and must be declared unconstitutional
and invalid if they fail to comply with these provisions
o Given justiciability of Constitution – an important aspect of
constitutional supremacy is judicial review
o Judicial review enjoins court to declare any law/ conduct
inconstant with the Constitution invalid.

Transformative
Constitutionalism

Transformative Constitutionalism:
The 1996 Constitution is seen as inherently
•
transformative
o Because: the central aim of the Constitution is to move
from an unjust past to a just future
o The founding values in S1 confirm the intention to break
from the past

Transformative Constitutionalism:
S1 Values:
• Human dignity and equality,
• Non-racism and non-sexism,
• Supremacy of the Constitution,
• and Universal adult suffrage
Transformation as a principle is, therefore, foundational to
constitutional interpretation

Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
No single fixed definition of Transformative Constitutionalism
•
Most famous is from Prof Kare Klare:
•
Transformative constitutionalism:
• “Long-term project of constitutional enactment, interpretation and
enforcement committed (not in isolation, but in the historical context of
conducive political developments) to transforming [South Africa’s]
political and social institutions and power relationship in a democratic,
participatory, and egalitarian direction” (Kleyn et al page 52).
•

Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
1) Long term – it will not happen overnight – is 30+ years enough to
address +250 years of colonial and apartheid history?
2) Interpretation and enforcement, not isolation but in context
3) Substantive equality: goes beyond formal legal rights to ensure
economic and social rights are realized, reducing structural inequality
4) Proactive role of the law: Unlike liberal traditions that see constitutions as static
shields, this approach views them as swords for social change and proactive
instruments for justice.

Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
5) Rights Protections and Promotion: It encourages a social and
legal culture dedicated to upholding human dignity and democracy in
daily interactions.
6) Non-violent ”revolution”: It is often described as an "enterprise of
inducing large-scale social change through nonviolent political
processes grounded in law

Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
KK states TC is:
•
➢ Social ➢ egalitarian,
➢ redistributive, ➢ multicultural and
➢ Caring, ➢ self-conscious about its
➢ Positive, historical setting and
➢ at least partly horizontal, transformative role and
➢ participatory, mission.
➢ ( see De Vos section 1.4)

The Concept of Transformative Constitutionalism:
Constitutional Supremacy:
• Fundemental aspect of Transformative consitutionallism
• The Constitution is the highest law
o It should facilitate and enable fundamental political,
economic, social and cultural change
o “Historical self consciousness” – redress and undoing of
the legacy of colonialism and Apartheid ( post-amble IC)
o Building a future – based on fundamental human rights,
democracy, and social justice (Preamble 1996 Constitution)

The Concept of Transformative Constitutionalism:
• Value-based concept of democracy :
o S7(1) 1996 Constitution
o “This Bill of Rights is a cornerstone of democracy in
South Africa. It enshrines the rights of all people in our
country and affirms the democratic values of human
dignity, equality and freedom.”
o Designed for social and structural change

Transformative Constitutionalism:
CJ P Langa:
• Paper was presented Annual Human Rights Lecture (Stellenbosch) 2006
• See the Constitution is a “bridge” (think back to post-amble discussion)
between the unjust, divided past and a future based on rights, equality,
and dignity
• He States the objective of the constitution is to establish a truly equal
society
• This includes provision of basic socio-economic rights to all
Transformation, therefore, looks at making a commitment to change
•

Transformative Constitutionalism
• Soobramoney v Minister of Health 1997 (CC) para 8: "We live in a
society in which there are great disparities in wealth. Millions of people are
living in deplorable conditions and in great poverty. There is a high level of
unemployment, inadequate social security, and many do not have access
to clean water or to adequate health services. These conditions already
existed when the Constitution was adopted and a commitment to
address them, and to transform our society into one in which there will
be human dignity, freedom and equality, lies at the heart of our new
constitutional order.”
• Highlights that it is both backwards and forward looking

Transformative Constitutionalism:
CJ P Langa:
Culture of Justification: “The Constitution demands that all
decisions be capable of being substantively defended in terms of
rights and values that it enshrines. It is no longer sufficient for
judges to rely on the say-so of parliament or technical readings of
legislation as providing justifications for their decisions. Under a
transformative constitution, judges bear the ultimate
responsibility to justify their decisions not only by reference to
authority, but by reference to ideas and values.”
•

Transformative Constitutionalism:
CJ P Langa - Legal education and TC
o Cannot just blindly accept legal principles because of the authority
o Values of the Constitution must be instilled
o Must critically engage with constitutional vlaies
o “A truly transformative South Africa requires a new approach that
places constitutional dream at the very heart of legal education”
o Change in mindset – not just change of laws
•

Transformative Constitutionalism:
LLB standard:
• requires that “transformative constitutionalism” and its core
philosophy are suitable understood by law faculties, appropriately
embedded in curricula at all levels of the LLB programme and
internalised by students
• When you study

# Source: CON178-A2-S1-Hub/exports/cleaned_sources/04_theme_4_core_principles/theme_4_lecture_16.md

Theme 4: The
Constitution of 1996:
Basic Principles,
Concepts and
Doctrines

Recap

Understanding the 1996 Constitution
•
,
- To understand the 1996 Constitution you need to:
1) Understand the context in which it originates and operates
- 2) Understand the fundamental doctrines, concepts and
principles the constitution contains

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
•
The theory of constitutional law
•
Philosophy and doctrine that the governmental authority is
derived from, and limited by a body of (written) fundamental
law (ie a constitution)
•
Ensures that rulers act according to binding boundaries and
not their own desires

Constitutionalism (de Vos 2.2)
•
In  essence,  constitutionalism  is  the  notion  that  a  constitution
must both STUCTURE and CONSTRAIN state power
o
- A  constitution must establish the institutions and
- structures of government and allocate power to them for
effective governing, AND
o
- It  must limit and disperse that power among the  I
  institutions  and  structures  in  an  attempt  to  ensure  that
power will not be abused

Constitutional Supremacy
• Constitutional supremacy renders the constitution judicable
o Any law or conduct can be tested against the provisions
of the constitution and must be declared unconstitutional
and invalid if they fail to comply with these provisions
o Given justiciability of Constitution – an important aspect of
constitutional supremacy is judicial review
o Judicial review enjoins court to declare any law/ conduct
inconstant with the Constitution invalid.

Defining Transformative Constitutionalism:
No single fixed definition of Transformative Constitutionalism
•
Most famous is from Prof Kare Klare:
•
Transformative constitutionalism:
• “Long-term project of constitutional enactment, interpretation and
enforcement committed (not in isolation, but in the historical context of
conducive political developments) to transforming [South Africa’s]
political and social institutions and power relationship in a democratic,
participatory, and egalitarian direction” (Kleyn et al page 52).
•

Transformative Constitutionalism
• Soobramoney v Minister of Health 1997 (CC) para 8: "We live in a
society in which there are great disparities in wealth. Millions of people are
living in deplorable conditions and in great poverty. There is a high level of
unemployment, inadequate social security, and many do not have access
to clean water or to adequate health services. These conditions already
existed when the Constitution was adopted and a commitment to
address them, and to transform our society into one in which there will
be human dignity, freedom and equality, lies at the heart of our new
constitutional order.”
• Highlights that it is both backwards and forward looking

Transformative Constitutionalism: Criticism
• It is often praised for its ambitious goals, particularly in post-
apartheid South Africa
- • BUT that does not mean it  does not face several
significant criticisms

Criticism: Persistent Inequality and Slow Pace
of Change
• The promised large scale social and economic transformation
remains unfulfilled despite a transformative legal framework
• Critics point to the persistent racialised poverty and inequality
as evidence that the project has failed to meet popular
expectations
• Critics claim that transformative constitutionalism cannot solve
deeply structural problems, such as land reform

Criticism: Transformative Constitutionalism is
too Court Centric
• Critics argue that the project relies too heavily on the role of the
judiciary to achieve social change
• There is a burden of expectation placed on courts that courts cannot be
met through adjudicative means alone
• Krle Klares ' original concept of TC is seen as overly focused on the role of
lawyers and judges
• Counter-majoritarian Concerns: the focus on judicial intervention as the
main driver for change can be seen as a counter-majoritarian manifestation
that prevents more direct, political paths to social justice

Criticism: Transformative Constitutionalism is
too Court Centric
Counter-Majoritarian Dilemma Continued:
• the CMD is a legal and political concept describing the tension between
democratic majority rule and judicial review where unelected judges
invalidate laws created by elected representatives
• It questions why an unelected judiciary can override the will of the majority,
• Example: The constitutional Court overturning parliamentary actions to
align with the supreme constitution

Criticism: Transformative Constitutionalism is
too Court Centric
• IE Transformative constitutionalism, as the main theory to effect
change, is a court-driven process
• ‘Therefore, is it my contention that within the context of South Africa’s
prevailing conservative legal culture, the extent to which the success of
transformative constitutionalism as an enterprise depends on legal and
judicial interpretation leaves the project in danger of remaining and
incomplete project at best.’ S Sibanda ‘Not Purpose Made …’ 2011
Stell LR 493

Criticism:
S Sibanda “Not yet Uhuru” Phd thesis Wits (2018) 224-225.
• Transformative constitutionalism has “not translated into much more
than rights or law-based approaches to driving change with little
evidence of other work within the discourse directed at
inculcating social, economic or cultural institutional or
structural power shifts or innovations beyond the courts” …
transformative constitutionalism, as it has become to be understood
(as a strictly legal concept given meaning to by primarily the courts,
to the exclusion of other political actors) is not able to solve complex
questions such as those raised during the #Feesmustfall protests;
questions as to who is included in determining and shaping a
transformed society. -

Criticism: The Liberal Compromise
• A radical criticism is that the South African constitutional
arrangement represents an unacceptable compromise that
preserves the apartheid era socio-economic order rather
than achieving a true radical break
• Deconial critique: Some argue that transformative
constitutionalism is a misfit for the quest to decolonise, as it
may still be rooted in Western legal traditions and colonial
pedagogies

Criticism: “Fetishism of the Law”
• Some critics point to “constitutional fetishism” or
“constitutional worship”
• Some critics see the way we interact with the constitution in a
similar way to a religion, with its own “theology” (foundational
values), “priests” (judges), and “pieties” (legal protocols).
• Some argue that such “worship” can lead to form “anti-
intellectualism, where the constitution is treated as the ”exclusive
horizon” for all social and political change, silencing any alternative
radical or political ideas

Task: Transformative Constitutionalism
Scenario: A group of residents in an informal settlement have been
living without access to adequate housing, water, or sanitation for
years.
They approach the courts, arguing that the government has failed
to realise their socio-economic rights under the constitution

Task: Discuss in Small Groups
1 )How could the doctrine of transformative constitutionalism support
the residents' claim
2) What role does the court play in this situation
3) What are some of the criticisms of using the Constitution in this way
• Are the courts overstepping into government decisions
• Is the transformation happening too slowly?
• Does law alone solve structural inequality
4) Do you think South Africa is being transformed by the constitution, or
is transformation more aspirational???

---

# Source: CON178-A2-S1-Hub/exports/cleaned_sources/04_theme_4_core_principles/theme_4_lecture_17.md

Theme 4: The
Constitution of 1996:
Basic Principles,
Concepts and
Doctrines

Recap

Transformative Constitutionalism: Criticism
- 1) Persistent Inequality and Slow Pace of Change
- 2) Is too Court Centric
- 3) Liberal Compromise
- 4) Fetishism of the law

Value based constitutionalism
• Value-based constitutionalism is a legal concept that emphasises
that constitutions are not just legal, procedural documents but
are rooted in core ethical, moral, and social values.
• It prioritises these underlying principles to guide the
interpretation of rights and laws.
• Constitutional values are the foundational principles that underpin
a democratic state's legal framework and guide its governance.

Value based constitutionalism
S1 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996
The Republic of South Africa is one, sovereign, democratic state founded on the
following values:
(a) Human dignity, the achievement of equality and the advancement of human
rights and freedoms.
(b) (b) Non-racialism and non-sexism.
(c) c) Supremacy of the constitution and the rule of law.(
(d) d) Universal adult suffrage, a national common voters' roll, regular elections and a
multi-party system of democratic government, to ensure accountability,
responsiveness and openness

Value based constitutionalism
Some Core Values and Application
• Human Dignity: Often positioned as the core value,
underpinning the right to self-worth.
- • Equality: Demands substantive equality - addressing
- structural barriers and historic disadvantage - rather
than just formal, equal treatment.
- • Freedom: Includes liberty of thought, expression, and
action.

Value based constitutionalism
• The values of human dignity, equality and freedom (and others) permeate the
legal system
• What does this mean in practice?
• Courts do not only ask “ what does the law say”
• They also ask “what outcome will best reflect the constitutional values
• Once again represents a break from the injustices of the past
• The Constitution aims to build a just, inclusive, and democratic society
(refer back to discussion on Transformative Constitutionalism)

Value based constitutionalism
• Value-based constitutionalism, therefore, contrasts with
strict legal positivism
• Constitutional interpretation in South Africa is therefore seen
to be more moral, purposive, and transformative.

Value based constitutionalism
Interpretation
• These values are used in the interpretation of the Bill of Rights
• S39(1): when interpreting the rights within the Bill of Rights... a
court…must promote the values that underlie an open and
democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom.
• Developing common law or customary law
• S39(2): When developing the common law or customary law,
every court… must promote the spirit, purport and objects of the
Bill of Rights

Value based constitutionalism
• When interpreting legislation
• S39(2) when interpreting legislation, every court….must promote spirit, purport and objects
of the Bill of Rights
• Daniels v Campbell 2004 (5) SA 331 (CC):
• Case looked at where the term “spouse” as used in the Intestate Succession Act and
Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act includes a surviving spouse to a Muslim marriage
• Justice Sachs [para12]: “In the present matter the constitutional values of equality,
tolerance and respect for diversity point strongly in favour of giving the word ‘spouse'
[in Intestate Succession Act …] a broad and inclusive construction, the more so when it
corresponds with the ordinary meaning of the word.”

Value based constitutionalism
Foundational Case: S v Makwayane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC)
• Facts:
• Makwanyane and Mchunu were convicted in the Witwatersrand Local Division on
four counts of murder and sentenced to death under section 277(1)(a) of
the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977.
• Their appeal raised a constitutional challenge under the Interim Constitution of
1993, arguing that the death penalty violated the rights to life (section 9), human
dignity (section 10), and protection against cruel, inhuman, or degrading
punishment (section 11(2))
• The case was referred to the newly created Constitutional Court, marking the first
constitutional review of legislation in post-apartheid South Africa.

Value based constitutionalism
Foundational Case: S v Makwayane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC)
• The appellants contended that the death penalty was incompatible with
the Constitution’s foundational values of human rights .
• The State argued that deterrence, retribution, and public opinion
justified retaining the death penalty.
• The Court considered whether such justifications could limit
constitutional rights under the limitations clause and whether public
opinion could influence constitutional interpretation

Value based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
• Rights are not absolute – they can in certain circumstances, be limited
• S36 contains a limitation clause – that ALLOWS for the
constitutionally valid limitation of rights in certain circumstances
• Limitation is determined by a two stage enquiry
• First court must established a right has been infringed upon
(limited)
• Second the court must determine whether it is justifiable

Value based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
S36 Constitution, 1996 (S33 (1) IC)
• S36: The rights in the Bill of Rights may be limited only in terms of the law of
general application, to the extent that the limitation is reasonable and justifiable
in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality, and
freedom
• Factors to guide whether the limitation is reasonable and justifiable
• Nature of the right
• Importance and relationship between the purpose of limitation and the
limitation
• There are no less restrictive means to achieve the purpose

Value based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
Re: S v Walters [para 26-27] : This is essentially a two-stage exercise. First, there is the threshold
enquiry aimed at determining whether or not the enactment in question constitutes a limitation on one or
other guaranteed right. This entails examining (a) the content and scope of the relevant protected right(s)
and (b) the meaning and effect of the impugned enactment to see whether there is any limitation of (a) by
(b). Subsections (1) and (2) of section 39 of the Constitution provide guidance on the interpretation of both
the rights and the enactment, essentially requiring that they be interpreted to promote the value system
of an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom. If upon such
analysis no limitation is found, that is the end of the matter. The constitutional challenge is dismissed there
and then.
If there is indeed a limitation, however, the second stage ensues. This is ordinarily called the limitations
exercise. In essence this requires a weighing-up of the nature and importance of the right(s) that are limited
together with the extent of the limitation as against the importance and purpose of the limiting enactment.

Value based constitutionalism
The limitations Clause
(Stage 2) the reasonable and justifiable enquiry
<Rieette.Venter@nwu.ac.za>

Value based constitutionalism
S v Makwanyane
• The court found that the death penalty “Places persons beyond the pale of
humanity” and “uses a person as a tool for crime control”
• The death penalty violates the rights as found in the Bill of Rights (first leg of test)
• Was this limitation justifiable in terms of s36 (Second Leg of test)?
• Is the purpose of the limitation acceptable in an open and democratic
society based on values of human dignity, equality and freedom?

Value based constitutionalism
S v Makwanyane
• Is there a justifiable limitation based on the stated purpose?
• Retribution
• Prevention
• Deterrence
• Constitutional Valid purpose of limitation?
• Rational connection between purpose and limitation?
• Less invasive means to achieve the purpose ?
• Proportionality – weighing up of the factors

Value based constitutionalism
S v Makwanyane
• The crux of it is that the court looked at the constitutional value of
human dignity to determine that there was no justifiable reason to
limit the Right to Life as found in the Bill of Rights through the use of the
death penalty

Value based constitutionalism
Balancing competing rights using values
• Courts balance competing rights by asking which outcome best reflects
constitutional values.
• Port Elizabeth Municipality v Various Occupiers2005 (1) SA 217 (CC))
• Competing rights – right to private property and right to housing
• Justice Sachs emphasised that fairness required considering both the
owners’ rights and the occupiers’ human dignity, especially in the
context of South Africa’s history of forced removals.

Value-based constitutionalism
Values driving social transformation
• As discussed under Transformative Constitutionalism, one of the goals of the Constitution,
1996 is to change and transform society, not just resolve disputes.
• Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie 2006 (1) SA 524 (CC)
• Right to Equality and Same-sex marriage
• Justice Sachs Denying same-sex couples access to marriage contravened rights and
values of equality and human dignity. Excluding same-sex couples from marriage rendered
them “outsiders” to society’s central institution of love and commitment.
• Religious objections were rejected on the ground that South Africa’s democracy requires
the coexistence of sacred and secular spheres
• Framed marriage equality as integral to post-apartheid constitutional values of dignity,
equality, and freedom.

Value-based constitutionalism
1. Normative
• The Constitution is based on moral values, not just legal rules
2. Interpretive
• Values guide how courts understand and apply rights
3. Transformative
• The Constitution aims to change society and address injustice
4. Contextual
• Must respond to and reflect South Africa’s social and historical context
5. Counter-majoritarian
• Courts can uphold values even against public opinion

Class task:
Scenario:
• A group of 20 people has been living on unused municipal land for 3 years.
• The municipality now wants to evict them to allow for a private development project that
will bring jobs and infrastructure.
• The residents argue that eviction will leave them homeless.
Task 1 in small groups
• Identify relevant constitutional values
• Decide the outcome
• Should the eviction be allowed?
• Discuss which values should carry more weight
• How did your chosen values influence your decision

Theme 4: The
Constitution of 1996:
Basic Principles,
Concepts and
Doctrines

Recap

Value Based Constitutionalism
•
Value-based constitutionalism is a legal concept that emphasises
that constitutions are not just legal, procedural documents but are
- rooted in core ethical, moral, and social values.
•
- What sections give us the Values in the 1996 Constitution?
•
- What were some of the values discussed?

Value Based Constitutionalism
•
We looked at how courts uses these values in the interpretation of
- rights – s39
•
We looked at how courts use these values in the limitation of
- rights – s36
- - Rights are not absolute – can be limited
- What is the two-stage enquiry for the limitation of rights?
•
- Who can remind me how Constitutional values were used in S v
Makwenyane??

Value-based constitutionalism
1. Normative
• The Constitution is based on moral values, not just legal rules
2. Interpretive
• Values guide how courts understand and apply rights
3. Transformative
• The Constitution aims to change society and address injustice
4. Contextual
• Must respond to and reflect South Africa’s social and historical context
5. Counter-majoritarian
• Courts can uphold values even against public opinion

Class task:
Scenario:
• A group of 20 people has been living on unused municipal land for 3 years.
• The municipality now wants to evict them to allow for a private development project that
will bring jobs and infrastructure.
• The residents argue that eviction will leave them homeless.
Task 1 in small groups
• Identify relevant constitutional values
• Decide the outcome
• Should the eviction be allowed?
• Discuss which values should carry more weight
• How did your chosen values influence your decision

Application of the
Bill of Rights

Bill of Rights
•
Bill of Rights has been constructed in such a way to give effect
- to the transformative vision of the Constitution, 1996
- • It sets out a unique human rights vision for South Africa
• The broad range of rights is aimed at facilitating political and
- socio-economic transformation in South Africa while
- protecting the human dignity of all persons within the State
• It has broad application – both to the State and to private
parties

The Application of the Bill of Rights
When litigating the Bill of Rights, the Court
●
has to determine whether the BOR applies
Directly or Indirectly
○
Vertically or Horizontally
○

The Application of the Bill of Rights
● Direct application:
○ Direct application of the Bill of Rights occurs when a person, company, or state
organ violates a constitutional right found in chp 2
○ Or when the ordinary rules of law (Legislation, common law, customary law) are
not consistent with the Bill of Rights
○ If they are not, the BOR if applied directly will override these rules of law – ie law
will be declared invalid by the courts
○ Example: company firing a woman due to pregnancy (violating section 9
equality rights), would be unconstitutional and invalid
○ Example: S v Mawanyane – Death Penalty declared unconstitutional

The Application of the Bill of Rights
● Indirect application: the purpose is to determine whether the ordinary rules of the
law promote the values of the BOR
○ If they do not, the court will use the BOR to develop the rules of law (s39(2))
○ Example: the development of common law to align with constitutional values, as
seen inCarmichelev Minister of Safety and Security. (2001) CC: The Court used
s39(2) to interpret the law of delict to promote rights and constitutional values,
rather than directly invalidating a statute.
■ IE: Instead of declaring a law invalid (direct application), courts interpret
legislation or develop common law/customary law to conform with the Bill
of Rights

The application of the Bill of Rights
● The next question is then, is it a vertical or horizontal
application?
○ This refers to the different relationships and legal
situations in which the Bill of Rights is enforced

The application of the Bill of Rights
Vertical application
● Governed by s8(1) – looks at the relationship between the state and private
individuals
● Imposes obligations on the state to respect, protect and fulfil rights in the BOR
● Acts an additional check on state power – therefore binds the legislative, executive,
judiciary and all organs of state
● Protects citizens from abuse of power by the government
● Example:
○ A person brings a claim against the police for unlawful arrest, or someone
who challenges a government policy that they claim violates their rights

The application of the Bill of Rights
Examples of vertical application of rights :
● Right to Equality (Section 9): An individual sues a government department for
refusing to hire or promote them based on race, gender, or sexual orientation.
● Freedom of Expression (Section 16): A journalist or citizen challenges the police
for arresting them for participating in a lawful public protest.
● Right to Access Information (Section 32): A person uses the PAIA act to force a
public body, eg DHA, to disclose records held by the state.

The application of the Bill of Rights
● Socio-economic Rights (Sections 26 & 27): Communities challenging the
government for failing to provide adequate, basic water services or, as in
the Grootboom case, reasonable access to housing.
● Right to Fair Trial (Section 35): An accused person argues that their rights were
violated by the police or prosecutor during their arrest or detention.
● Property Rights (Section 25): A landowner challenges the state's expropriation of
their property, arguing it was not done for a public purpose or without fair
compensation.

The application of the Bill of Rights
Horizontal application
● Governed by s8(2) – requires considering the nature of the right and duty
imposed
● When applied horizontally, this imposes obligations between private persons
(individuals or companies) to respect the rights of the BOR (in certain
circumstances)
○ Protects citizens from violations of rights by private parties such as unfair
discrimination by an employer
○ IE you don’t have to rely on the common law or legislation – you can say
“this person has violated my constitutional right”

The application of the Bill of Rights
Direct Horizontal application
● Governed by s8(2): The BOR applies directly to the conduct of private
individuals, allowing them to rely directly on a constitutional right for a
claim
Indirect Horizontal Application
● S39(2): The BOR influences private law by requiring courts to interpret
legislation or develop the common law in a way that promotes the sprite,
purport, and object of the BOR

The application of the Bill of Rights
● Question to the class: Why is it important to have
direct horizontal application of the Bill of Rights?

The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 1: Equality (S9)
● Scenario: A private employer refuses to hire someone based on their race,
gender, or disability.
● Even though this is a private employer (not the state) the right to equality
can apply directly
● The private individual can argue, “my constitutional right to equality has
been infringed by this private actor”
● Equality is a right that clearly makes sense in private relationships
(employment, services etc)
● Courts recognised that discrimination is not only a state problem

The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 2: Freedom of Expression (s16)
Scenario: A private media company refuses to publish an opinion article
● The private individual might try to rely on freedom of expression
● BUT the court will have to balance
○ The writers freedom of expression
○ The companies freedom to choose what it publishes
○ Rights can apply directly but can compete with other rights in
private relationships

The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 3: Right to housing (s26)
Scenario: A private land owner evicts people living on their land without following the legal
processes
●
Those evicted can rely directly on the right to access housing
●
They can argue “this eviction violates my right to housing”
●
Rights will still apply between the private individuals
●
The Court will ask
○
Is eviction just and equitable
○
What processes were followed
○
What is the impact on the vulnerable people
●
Again we see competing rights of private individuals as the land owner has his own proterty
rights protected by s25

The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 4: Right to education (s29)
Scenario: Private school refuses to admit a learner without a fair and lawful
reason (arbitrary exclusion)
● The learner or parent may rely directly on s29 (right to basic education)
● They can argue “The decision unjusrifably limites my right to education”
● Private schools are private individuals (not the state)

The application of the Bill of Rights
Example 4: Right to education (s29)
Scenario: Private school refuses to admit a learner without a fair and lawful reason
(arbitrary exclusion)
● Again, the court will ask :
○ Is exclusion reasonable
○ Does it undermine the right to basic education
○ Are there other justifications such as contractual or policy justifications
○ Nuance: The right to basic education is a very strong right (immediately
realisable)
○ But the balance will be with the school's autonomy to decide who they admit

The application of the Bill of Rights
Key take aways from the examples:
●
Rights can shape private relationships, especially where there is
○
A power imbalance
○
Basic human needs are effected
●
Direct horizontal application means you can use the constitution itself in disputes with
other private parties – but courts will always ask whether it is appropriate nd how rights
should be balanced
●
It will depend on
○
The nature of the right
○
The relationship between the parties
○
And the need to balance competing rights

The application of the Bill of Rights
Class task:
● Look through the rights in Chapter 2 of the Constitution
● Discuss how they may be applied directly: vertically and
horizontally
○ Look at nature of right, who it affects, how it affects
them, etc

# Democracy!
S1 ushers in democracy by declaring South Africa to be “a sovereign, democratic state”.
S1(d) Democratic values: “universal adult suffrage, a national common voters' roll, regular elections and a multi-party system of democratic government, to ensure accountability, responsiveness and openness.

### Notes:
S1 does not define what democracy means in SA, but shows us the elements that are paramount in the South African Constitutional Context

<!-- Slide number: 11 -->
# How to define Democracy in the 1996 Constitution Context
Democracy – as a concept – defies singular definition
However, we can still get an understanding of what democracy entails.
 Theuys Roux : ‘The core idea – that decisions affecting the members of a political community should be taken by the members themselves, or at least by elected representatives whose power to make those decisions ultimately derives from the members – is more or less settled’

### Notes:
There is not one idea of democracy, but different conceptions of democracy

<!-- Slide number: 12 -->
# How to define Democracy…
Roux’s idea of democracy is linked to the notion that people should prevail and have a say in how they are governed.
However,  it is not possible to have every individual vote on every decision, so this conceptualisation of democracy highlights that modern democracy is exercised through institutionalised politics that entails electing individuals or organisations to represent their interests
Roux’s definition also lends itself to understanding that democracy, as found in the 1996 constitution, embodies different conceptions of democracy

### Notes:
There is not one idea of democracy, but different conceptions of democracy

# Direct democracy
Decisions affecting the members of a political community should be taken by the members themselves = direct democracy
Historically considered the purest form of democracy.
What are some elements of direct democracy in the Constitution?

<!-- Slide number: 15 -->
# Direct democracy

Section 127(2)(f) Provincial premier can call a provincial referendum

S84/ 127 – to date we have not used this mechansism in SA

<!-- Slide number: 16 -->
# Representative Democracy

Most decisions are not made by direct involvement by the citizenry
Decisions affecting the members of a political community are made by elected representatives whose power to make those decisions ultimately derives from the members = representative democracy
Citizens elect representatives to govern for a limited time

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 17 -->
# Representative Democracy
Section 42(3) :“The National Assembly is elected to represent the people and to ensure government by the people
Section 19(3)(a): Every adult citizen has the right to vote in elections
Role of political parties - our democracy is founded on a multi-party system of government (S1(d))
Link between citizens and political parties/representatives

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 18 -->
# Representative Democracy
Multi-party government:
A system where three or more political parties have the capacity to gain control of the government, either separately or through a coalition
S19 read with s1(d) = MPG Is an integral part of our democracy
It is characterised by competitive elections, proportional representation, and usually a coalition of political parties working together to form a majority in the legislation

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 19 -->
# Representative Democracy
But in New Nation Movement v President of RSA 2020 CC
CC found the Electoral Act unconstitutional as it violated citizens' political rights (Section 19) by allowing only political parties to contest national and provincial elections, invalidating the exclusion of independent candidates.
This decision necessitated fundamental electoral reform in South Africa, moving towards a system that allows for individual candidacy rather than exclusively party-based representation.
Electoral Amendment Bill – signed 20 April 2023

### Notes:
n New Nation Movement NPC and Others v President of the Republic of South Africa and Others [2020] ZACC 11, the Constitutional Court of South Africa ruled on 11 June 2020 that the Electoral Act 73 of 1998 is unconstitutional. It violated citizens' political rights (Section 19 of the Constitution) by allowing only political parties to contest national and provincial elections, invalidating the exclusion of independent candidates

<!-- Slide number: 20 -->
# Representative Democracy
Electoral Amendment Act 1 of 2023
Allows independent candidates (not afflicated to political parties) to contest elections for the National Assembly and provincial legislatures for the first time
Came into effect for 2024 elections
Independent candidates must prove support to qualify. Candidates need to have 1,000 signatures  in support of them.

### Notes:
To be nominated as a IC
Be a South African citizen, at least 18 years old, and registered to vote in the province where they intend to contest.
Submit a prescribed nomination form and pay an election deposit.
Sign a declaration to be bound by the Electoral Code of Conduct.
Not be disqualified under the Constitution (e.g., due to a prison sentence exceeding 12 months without the option of a fine)

<!-- Slide number: 21 -->
# Representative Democracy
2024 elections = No Party got Majority – GNU government
Democratic implications of the GNU
Power sharing: inclusive governance through multi-party collaboration
Checks and Balances: No single majority ensures more balanced policy-making
Challenges: tensions over ideological differences ( VAT, NHI, foreign policy)

### Notes:
Following the 29 May 2024 general elections, South Africa entered a new political era with the formation of a Government of National Unity (GNU). This became necessary after the African National Congress (ANC) failed to secure an outright majority for the first time since 1994, receiving 40.18% of the national vote.

The GNU is a multi-party coalition comprising 10 political parties that collectively represent approximately 72% of the seats in the National Assembly. The participating parties signed a Statement of Intent to cooperate in both the Executive and the Legislature.

<!-- Slide number: 22 -->
# Limitations of Representative Democracy
Representative democracy is the only workable system…
Failure to regulate political parties, elite-driven democracy
Inability to directly influence elected members in between elections
Influence of those not actively involved in political parties
Has Electoral Amendment Act fixed this?
One-party dominance
Affected democratic accountability and limited democratic participation, eroding separation between political parties and the state

### Notes:
Failure to regulate political parties – the fact that there is no requirement that political parties practise some form of internal democracy ultimately has the effect of conferring a huge amount of power on leadership who may dominate party affairs and impose their preferred representatives
The fact that the citizenry cannot really effect/influence directly their representatives outside of the election cycle – leaves the electorate in the position of onlookers as elected representatives take decisions in the name of the electorate without an opportunity to oppose independently unpopular decisoons
If not involved in a political party – next to impossible to infleucne decisions that affect them – lack of opportunities to cpntirnute their views effectively
Previously, one party dominate democracy – effects democratic accountability -

<!-- Slide number: 23 -->
# Participatory Democracy
Tries to counteract the political exclusion of citizens' opinions in decision-making
Participatory democracy = affording citizens an opportunity to have their voice heard when decisions are made that affect them
Section 1(d) “system of democratic government to ensure accountability, responsiveness and openness”
Section 59(1)(a)and 72(1)(a), and 118: NA and NCOP MUST facilitate public participation in law-making processes

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 24 -->
# Participatory Democracy
Doctors for Life v Speaker of the National Assembly para 105-117
South Africa has both representative and participatory democracy
Which are are mutually supportive
The participation by the public on a continuous basis provides vitality to the functioning of representative democracy
The court invalidated legislation in circumstances where there had not been sufficient opportunity for public participation on legislation that significancy affects the lives of people

### Notes:
The landmark case of Doctors for Life International v Speaker of the National Assembly (2006) established that public participation is a mandatory "requirement of manner and form" in South Africa's law-making process. The Constitutional Court ruled that if Parliament fails to take reasonable steps to facilitate public involvement, the resulting legislation can be declared invalid.

Facts The NGO Doctors for Life International challenged four health-related bills passed by Parliament in 2004/2005, arguing that the National Council of Provinces (NCOP) and provincial legislatures failed to properly involve the public

Representative vs. Participatory Democracy: The judgment clarified that South Africa’s system is not just representative (voting in elections) but also participatory (citizens having a say in specific decisions between elections)

<!-- Slide number: 25 -->
# Constitutional Democracy
A descriptive term, a decision affecting a political community made in terms of a Constitution, and this Constitution has certain basic features and characteristics
Notions of democracy (centrality of democracy); Constitutional supremacy, centrality of foundational values ( human dignity, equality, freedom etc), culture of human rights, democratic ideas, juridical review
A purposive concept – if we adhere to these features, we will establish the society envisaged by the Constitution

# Road to Sharpeville (1959 – March 1960)
Anti-Pass campaign
6 Dec 1959 – ANC conference – Chief Albert Luthuli announces 1960 as the “ Year of the Pass”
16 March 1960 – Robert Sobukwe and the PAC announce that on 21 March 1960 there will be a mass pass law protest
PAC had recently split from the ANC

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 34 -->
# Road to Sharpeville (1959 – March 1960)
18 March 1960:  PAC activists distribute circulars calling on black South Africans to:
Leave pass books at home
Voluntarily present themselves at police stations for arrest
The aim was to overwhelm the apartheid system and challenge pass laws directly

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 35 -->
# Sharpeville Massacre
21 March 1960:  Thousands march peacefully to the Sharpeville police station without their passbooks
Police responded by opening fire on the crowed
69 people where killed
Hundreds injured
Witnesses later testified that police fired into an unarmed crowd, and later when and placed weapons in the hands of the dead

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 36 -->
# Sharpeville: Government Response
23 March 1960: Prime Minister Verwoed tells Parliament that the protests were not about pass laws and praisesd thr police response
23 March: Robert Sobukwe and PAC leaders are arrested
Protests spread across the country in response
24 March: gatherings of 12 or more people are banned and police surveillance increases

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 37 -->
# Sharpeville: Government Response
30 March 1960: Government declares a state of emergency
 Used to suppress protests
Resulted in the mass detention of thousands of people
Resulted in the ANC and PAC being banned (Unlawful Organisations Act )
Lasted several months and marked a shift to the more violent, repressive phase of apartheid
Historical turning point and led to international criticism

# 1961 Constitution

### Notes:

# 1961 Constitution
5 October 1960: Referendum in which white-only voters approve the move to become a Republic, separate from Britain.
The British Monarch would be removed as head of state
South Africa wanted to be part of the Commonwealth but due to the recent political violence was not accepted by international community

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 40 -->
# 1961 Constitution
32 May 1961 SA became a Republic and left the commonwealth
Retained the parliamentary system from the 1910 constitution
This constitution reinforced white minority dominance, and continued to exclude black South Africans from the political process

### Notes:
Define Republic: A state in which supreme power is held by the people and their elected representatives, and which has an elected or nominated president rather than a monarch.

<!-- Slide number: 41 -->
# 1961 Constitution
Most important change was that the Monarch would no longer be the head of state, this would not vest with the President, as elected by the people.
First president was C R Swart

### Notes:
Define Republic: A state in which supreme power is held by the people and their elected representatives, and which has an elected or nominated president rather than a monarch.

<!-- Slide number: 42 -->
# Rivonia Trial
Suppression of political dissent
Suppression of Communism Act (1950),
Sabotage Act (1962),
Carried the death penalty
90-Day Detention Law (1963)
Allowed indefinite solitary confinement without charge, access to lawyers, or contact with family.

### Notes:
Named after subburn where mostwhere arrested

<!-- Slide number: 43 -->
# Rivonia Trial
Held from 1963-1964
Landmark legal proceeding that resulted n life imprisonment of Nelson Mandela and other anti-apartheid leaders
Another historical turning point, which resulted in international scrutiny on apartheid regime

### Notes:
Named after subburn where mostwhere arrested

<!-- Slide number: 44 -->
# Rivonia Trial
Trialists charged under laws specifically designed to criminalize resistance to racial oppression
Demonstrates how a legal system can be weaponised by those in power against the very people it should protect
Makes a case for why constitutions must entrench rights that constrain legislative power, not just procedural rules

### Notes:
Named after subburn where mostwhere arrested

<!-- Slide number: 45 -->
# Rivonia Trial
Rather than mount a purely criminal defence, the accused chose to put apartheid itself on trial.
Mandela's famous "I am prepared to die" statement from the dock reframed the proceedings as a question of political legitimacy:
can a government that excludes the majority from political participation claim the right to prosecute them for defying its laws?
This connects directly to social contract theory and the question of what gives law its moral authority.

### Notes:
Named after subburn where mostwhere arrested

<!-- Slide number: 46 -->
# Rivonia Trial
In short, the Rivonia Trial is a foundational case study in the difference between law and justice, the role of courts in authoritarian systems, why entrenched constitutional rights matter, and how the legacy of historical abuse shapes constitutional design.
It was a political win for the fight against apartheid, but with many of the leaders now in jail, the resistance saw setbacks and stagnation for several years following, in which time the oppression of the government continued and escalated .

### Notes:
Named after subburn where mostwhere arrested

<!-- Slide number: 47 -->
# 1983 Constitution

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 48 -->
# 1983 Constitution
Republic of South Africa Constitution Act No 110 of 1983
Key legislative reform under Apartheid Regime – to entrench apartheid  rule and response to internal protest and international pressure
Aimed to incorporate Coloured and Indian groups, to create a broader base of support for the white minority and fracture the non-racial dissent
Direct response to ever increasing urban protest and unrest, needed to ensure white control was maintained
Referendum November 2, 1983, with a 66.3% (whites only) yes vote for change

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 49 -->
# 1983 Constitution
Created the Tricameral Parliament: Parliament was restructured into three separate houses
House of Assembly: For the white population group
House of Representatives: For the Coloured population group
House of Delegates: For the Indian population group
Total exclusion of Majority of Black African population – complete exclusion from any representation in the central government
Created a hierarchy among the non-white race groups (similar to the caste system in India?)

### Notes:

<!-- Slide number: 50 -->
# 1983 Constitution
Competencies were categorised as “own” or “general” affairs
Own Affairs – handled by each separate house
General affairs – handled by full parliament
The Office of the Prime Minister was abolished
Symbolic State President replaced with executive State president, created consolidating power into an office not directly elected by the public but by the electoral college dominated by white ruling party
Executive authority rested with the cabinet

Constitutional Law 178
Separation of Powers
Dr Christiaan van Schalkwyk
christiaanvs@sun.ac.za
Chair in Urban Law and Sustainability

Structure: Separation of Powers
1. Introduction
2. Concepts & principles
3. Historical context
4. Application in South Africa
5. Counter-majoritarian dilemma & deference
6. Conclusion
7. Class activity

1. Introduction
- • Our focus is on:
- o Analysing the model of separation of powers
o Understanding the principles, concepts and historical context
o
- Applying it in the South African context
o
- Discussing the issues and consequences
- • Constitutional context + transformative constitutionalism
- o Accountability (s 1 d)
- o Constitutional supremacy (s 2)
- • Don’t get bogged down in the detail
- • Practical application exercise at the end

2. Concepts & principles
- • Constitutions as limiting public power/state coercion
- o Other functions too, of course
- ▪ Human rights to individuals and groups (Ss 9 – 35)
- ▪ Guiding judicial decision making (s 39)
▪ Administrative make-up of the state (e.g. Schedules 4 and 5)
- • Substantive and procedural ways to limit state power
- o Rights = Substantive
▪ Examples?

2. Concepts & principles
- • Procedural limits to public power
- o Ways/Manners in which government exercises public power
- • Separation of powers = Procedural
- o Divides government into 3 branches
o 1.) Executive
o 2.) Legislature
o 3.) Judiciary
o *not a hierarchy

2. Concepts & principles
- • Procedural limits to public power
- o Ways/Manners in which government exercises public power
- • Separation of powers = Procedural
- o Divides government into 3 branches

2. Concepts & principles
- • Separation of powers
- o Divides government into 3 branches → ‘Classical Model’
Executive
- Legislature Judiciary

2. Concepts & principles
• Separation of powers
o Divides government into 3 branches → But also overlaps = South Africa
o Why no overlap with the judiciary? Protect judicial independence
Executive
Legislature Judiciary

2. Concepts & principles
• Separation of powers
o Divides government into 3 branches → But also overlaps = South Africa
Chapter 9
Institutions
Executive
Legislature Judiciary

2. Concepts & principles
- • Separation of powers
- o Avoids concentration of power
- ▪ E.g. Executive takes on law-making power
- o Promotes specailisation
- ▪ E.g. Qualified and trained judges
- • Modern conceptions closely interlinked with human
rights
- o Procedural → Substantive

2. Concepts & principles
- • Four principles
- o 1.) Division of government power
- o 2.) Separation of functions
o
- 3.) Separation of personnel
o
- 4.) System of checks and balances

3. Historical background
- • Origins in 17th Century enlightenment political philosophy
- o *though perhaps an oversimplification
- o Development from Hobbes, to Locke
- o To Charles Badron de Montestuieu, to Jean Jacques
- Rosseau, and USA
o
- Specific histories of monarchical and tyrannical governments
- o Rise of liberalism and negative conceptions of freedom
- o Rise of constitutionalism
- • In principle the same, but incremental developments
o E.g. overlaps; new public institutions (*see Ch 9 institutions)

3. Historical background
- • Why is historical background important?

4. Application in South Africa
- • No express mention in Final Constitution
- o Constitutional Principle VI from Interim Constitution
- o Constitutional Court = Implicit in Final Constitution
- • South African model
- o PoD: No universal model
o
- Historical understanding and appreciation
▪ E.g. Westminster system & parliamentary sovereignty in apartheid era
- o CC in De Lange v Smuts

4. Application in South Africa
• Legislature
- o Chapter 4 of Constitution
- o National Assembly (NA) & National Council of Provinces

4. Application in South Africa
• Legislature
o Overlap with executive rationale = Policy power to legislation
- o Inherited from Westminster system
- • Executive Council of Western Cape Legislature v
- President of the Republic of South Africa
- o Delegation of law making authority
- o Permissible (to some degree)
- ▪ Limitations to nature + extent
- o But specialisation, democracy, and concentration of power?

4. Application in South Africa
• Legislature
- o Chapter 4 of Constitution
- o National Assembly (NA) & National Council of Provinces
- o Members of Parliament
- o Overlap with executive = Policy power to legislation
- • Executive Council of Western Cape Legislature v
- President of the Republic of South Africa
- o Delegation of law-making authority
- o Permissible (to some degree)
- ▪ Limitations to nature + extent
o
- But specialisation, democracy, and concentration of power?

4. Application in South Africa
• Executive
- o Ss 84 and 85 of Constitution
- o Cabinet composition of Ministers
- o Obligation to select cabinet from NA
- o Commissions of enquiry
- • NA exercises oversight
- o Can recall executive
- o Initiate votes of no confidence (impeachment, s 89)
- o Accountability to NA – s 55(2) of Constitution
- o Oversight of the executive and hold it accountable,
- particularly in the implementation of legislation

4. Application in South Africa
• Judiciary
- o Chapter 8 of Constitution
- o Hierarchy of courts
- o Appointment of judges – Judicial Services Commission
- o Manner of appointment involves all 3 branches
- o Ensures (or is supposed to) impartiality and independence

4. Application in South Africa
• Judicial review
o S 172 provides for competent courts to declare that any law
inconsistent with the Constitution is invalid to the extent of
its decision whether an Act of Parliament, a provincial Act or
- conduct of the President is constitutional (section 167(5))
o Certain principles in the Constitution to limit litigation of
- legislature and executive against one another

4. Application in South Africa
- • Judicial independence and impartiality
o CC confirmation in SA Association of Personal Injury Lawyers v
Heath
- o JSC code of conduct and removals
o Power to initiate proceedings for the removal of judges via
- the JSC (and involvement of 3 branches)
- o Only possible on limited grounds of incapacity, gross
- incompetence or gross misconduct
- o E.g. Removal of J Hlope by Pres Ramaphosa

4. Application in South Africa
- • Chapter 9 Institutions
o Unique set of institutions that do not fall within classic model
o E.g. Public Protector; South African Human Rights Commission
- o Also exercise oversight
- o But due to falling outside 3 branches, in unique position
- o Independence and introduces another layer of checks and
balances
- o Problems? Critiques?
