# S v Makwanyane — CON178 A2 S1 Case Document

**Case:** *S v Makwanyane and Another* 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC); 1995 (6) BCLR 665 (CC)
**Court:** Constitutional Court of South Africa
**Case number:** CCT 3/94
**Heard:** 15–17 February 1995
**Delivered:** 6 June 1995
**Primary judgment:** Chaskalson P
**Context:** Interim Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 200 of 1993
**Core theme for CON178 A2:** value-based constitutionalism; proportionality; limitation of rights; life; dignity; equality; cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment; constitutional interpretation; public opinion and constitutional supremacy.

---

## 1. How to use this document

This is a **derived CON178 A2 study-source document**. It is designed to replace the need to place the very large *Makwanyane* PDFs and heads of argument into the GitHub hub. It does **not** replace the official case. In essays, tutorials, or exams, cite the case itself:

> *S v Makwanyane and Another* 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC).

Use this document to understand:

- what the case was about;
- what each side argued;
- what the Constitutional Court held;
- why the case matters for section 36 limitation analysis, even though it was decided under section 33 of the Interim Constitution;
- how to use *Makwanyane* in value-based constitutionalism, constitutional supremacy, rule of law, dignity, life, democracy, and separation-of-powers style questions.

---

## 2. One-sentence case summary

*Makwanyane* held that the death penalty, as authorised by section 277 of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977, was unconstitutional because it amounted to cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and could not be justified under the Interim Constitution’s limitation clause.

---

## 3. Quick case box

- Element CON178 A2 answer
- **Facts** The accused were convicted of serious offences, including four counts of murder, and sentenced to death. Their appeal raised whether the death penalty was compatible with the 1993 Interim Constitution.
- **Issue** Whether section 277 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which allowed capital punishment, was consistent with the Interim Constitution, especially rights to life, dignity, equality, and freedom from cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment.
- **Holding** The death penalty was unconstitutional. Section 277(1)(a), (c), (d), (e) and (f), and corresponding provisions, were invalid to the extent that they authorised capital punishment.
- **Core reasoning** The death penalty destroys life, annihilates dignity, creates risks of arbitrariness and error, and cannot be justified merely by public opinion, deterrence, prevention, or retribution.
- **Exam significance** The case is the foundation of South African proportionality analysis and shows that constitutional rights must be interpreted through values, not through formal legality or majoritarian preference.

---

## 4. Facts and procedural background

The two accused, **Themba Makwanyane** and **M Mchunu**, were convicted in the Witwatersrand Local Division of the Supreme Court on:

- four counts of murder;
- one count of attempted murder; and
- one count of robbery with aggravating circumstances.

They were sentenced to death on each murder count and received long imprisonment terms on the other counts. They appealed to the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division dismissed the conviction appeals and considered the murders serious enough to attract the heaviest lawful sentence. However, because the 1993 Interim Constitution had come into force after the trial and sentence, the Appellate Division postponed the death-sentence aspect so that the Constitutional Court could decide the constitutional issues.

The key statutory provision was **section 277(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977**, which made the death penalty a competent sentence for murder.

The core constitutional provisions under the Interim Constitution were:

- **section 8** — equality before the law and equal protection of the law;
- **section 9** — right to life;
- **section 10** — dignity;
- **section 11(2)** — prohibition of torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment;
- **section 33** — limitation clause;
- **section 35** — interpretation of Chapter 3 rights;
- **section 241(8)** — transitional issue about whether Chapter 3 could apply to pending proceedings.

---

## 5. Issues before the Constitutional Court

The case raised four major issues:

1. **Constitutionality of the death penalty:** whether capital punishment was inconsistent with Chapter 3 of the Interim Constitution.
2. **Rights implicated:** whether the death penalty violated life, dignity, equality, and the prohibition of cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment.
3. **Limitation:** if those rights were limited, whether the limitation was justifiable under section 33 of the Interim Constitution.
4. **Transitional effect:** whether people sentenced before the Interim Constitution could rely on Chapter 3 to prevent execution after the Constitution came into force.

For A2, the most important issue is not the criminal-law detail. The key issue is:

> **Can the state intentionally take life as punishment in a constitutional order founded on human dignity, equality, freedom and constitutional supremacy?**

---

## 6. Applicants’ argument

The applicants argued that the death penalty was unconstitutional because it violated several fundamental rights:

- the **right to life**;
- the **right to dignity**;
- the prohibition of **physical, mental and emotional torture**;
- the prohibition of **cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment or punishment**.

They argued that these violations could not be justified under section 33 because the death penalty:

1. **negated the essential content** of the rights to life and dignity;
2. was **not necessary**;
3. was **not reasonable and justifiable** in an open and democratic society based on freedom and equality;
4. was **arbitrary**, because the decision between life and death could depend on chance factors in investigation, prosecution, defence quality, or judicial attitude;
5. was **unequal**, because race, poverty, and social inequality shaped who was most vulnerable in capital cases;
6. was **fallible**, because a wrongful execution cannot be corrected;
7. did **not use the least drastic means**, because life imprisonment could serve the legitimate aims of punishment without killing the offender;
8. had a **disproportionately severe effect** because it permanently destroyed all rights of the person executed.

They also relied on the international trend away from the death penalty and on the growing constitutional emphasis on life, dignity, and protection against cruel punishment.

### Applicant-side exam formulation

> The applicants’ strongest point was that death is different. Ordinary punishment may limit rights, but capital punishment extinguishes the rights-holder permanently. Because execution is final and irreversible, ordinary safeguards cannot make it constitutionally acceptable.

---

## 7. Respondent’s argument

The respondent, represented by the Attorney-General, defended the constitutionality of the death penalty.

The respondent argued that:

1. the death penalty had developed from a mandatory punishment into a discretionary sentence;
2. post-1990 reforms created safeguards, including consideration of mitigating and aggravating factors and automatic appeal or review mechanisms;
3. the death penalty served legitimate aims of punishment, especially **deterrence**, **prevention**, and **retribution**;
4. South African society, given high violent crime levels, still regarded the death penalty as necessary in extreme cases;
5. the Constitution did not expressly abolish the death penalty, so the issue should not be treated as automatically resolved against retention;
6. public confidence in the criminal justice system required serious punishment for serious crimes;
7. the rights of victims and society should not be ignored merely because the condemned prisoner also had constitutional rights.

A central respondent theme was that the question was not merely whether death was abhorrent, but whether South African society could afford to do without it in extreme cases. The respondent’s heads also argued that if the Court invalidated capital punishment against prevailing social values, society might lose faith in the criminal justice system and resort to private vengeance.

### Respondent-side exam formulation

> The respondent’s strongest point was that constitutional rights do not exist in a vacuum: society also has an interest in protection from serious violent crime, and the criminal justice system must retain legitimacy by responding adequately to the gravest offences.

---

## 8. Court’s approach to constitutional interpretation

The Court treated the case as an early test of the new constitutional order. The Interim Constitution created a break from parliamentary sovereignty and established a supreme Constitution with justiciable rights.

Key interpretive principles:

1. **The Constitution is not ordinary legislation.** It is the source of public power and the standard against which law and conduct are measured.
2. **Rights must be interpreted generously and purposively.** The Court followed *S v Zuma* in adopting a rights-protective approach aimed at giving individuals the full benefit of constitutional protection.
3. **Rights must be read contextually.** Section 11(2) could not be interpreted in isolation. It had to be understood in the context of the rights to life, dignity, equality and the Constitution’s historical purpose.
4. **International and foreign law may assist but does not control.** The Court considered comparative law because section 35 allowed reference to public international law and comparable foreign case law, but emphasised that the South African Constitution must be interpreted according to South Africa’s own text, structure, history and values.

### Why this matters for A2

*Makwanyane* is not just a death-penalty case. It is a case about **how courts reason under a value-based Constitution**. Courts do not merely ask whether Parliament authorised something. They ask whether the law is consistent with constitutional values and rights.

---

## 9. The rights analysis

### 9.1 Cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment

The Court found that death is the most extreme punishment. It is final and irrevocable. It ends the right to life and all other personal rights. It is cruel because the condemned prisoner waits under uncertainty on death row. It is inhuman because it denies the humanity of the person executed. It is degrading because the state treats the person as an object to be eliminated.

The Court did not simply rely on ordinary dictionary meaning. It asked whether capital punishment was cruel, inhuman or degrading **in the constitutional sense**, interpreted through the rights and values of the Interim Constitution.

### 9.2 Life

The right to life was central. The Interim Constitution protected life in unqualified terms. The Court treated life as one of the most important rights because it is the source of all other personal rights.

### 9.3 Dignity

Dignity was equally central. Capital punishment strips the condemned person of dignity by reducing them to an object of state punishment. The state cannot model respect for life and dignity by deliberately destroying life and dignity.

### 9.4 Equality and arbitrariness

The Court recognised that capital cases are vulnerable to inequality and arbitrariness. Factors such as poverty, race, legal representation, prosecutorial approach, judicial attitude and investigative quality can affect who receives the death penalty. Imperfections exist in all criminal justice systems, but the Court emphasised that death is qualitatively different because errors cannot be corrected after execution.

---

## 10. Public opinion and constitutional supremacy

The Attorney-General relied heavily on public support for capital punishment. Chaskalson P was prepared to assume, for purposes of argument, that the majority of South Africans favoured the death penalty in extreme murder cases. But the Court held that this did not resolve the constitutional question.

The constitutional issue was not:

> What does the majority want?

The constitutional issue was:

> What does the Constitution permit?

This is one of the most examinable parts of the case.

### Rule

Public opinion may be relevant, but it is not a substitute for constitutional adjudication. If public opinion were decisive, rights protection could be left to Parliament or a referendum. That would return South Africa to parliamentary sovereignty and undermine the purpose of constitutional supremacy.

### Exam use

Use this point whenever a question asks about:

- constitutional supremacy vs parliamentary sovereignty;
- courts and democracy;
- counter-majoritarian difficulty;
- judicial review;
- rights protection for marginalised persons;
- whether courts should follow majority sentiment.

### Strong exam sentence

> *Makwanyane* shows that constitutional democracy is not simple majoritarianism: courts must uphold entrenched rights even when doing so may conflict with popular opinion.

---

## 11. The limitation analysis: section 33 and section 36

*Makwanyane* was decided under **section 33 of the Interim Constitution**, not section 36 of the 1996 Constitution. However, it remains central to section 36 because the First Certification judgment later explained that section 36 substantially reflects the limitation approach developed in *Makwanyane*.

### 11.1 The proportionality test

Chaskalson P held that limiting constitutional rights involves:

- weighing competing values;
- assessing proportionality;
- considering the nature and importance of the right;
- considering the purpose and importance of the limitation;
- considering the nature and extent of the limitation;
- considering the relation between the limitation and its purpose;
- considering whether less restrictive means could achieve the same purpose.

This became the backbone of modern South African limitation analysis.

### 11.2 Section 36 link

Under the 1996 Constitution, section 36 asks whether a limitation is reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom, taking into account relevant factors such as:

1. the nature of the right;
2. the importance of the purpose of the limitation;
3. the nature and extent of the limitation;
4. the relation between the limitation and its purpose;
5. less restrictive means to achieve the purpose.

### 11.3 Application in Makwanyane

- Limitation factor Application to the death penalty
- **Nature of the right** Life and dignity are among the most important rights. Life is the source of all personal rights. Dignity is central to the new constitutional order.
- **Purpose of limitation** The state relied on deterrence, prevention, retribution, and public safety. These are legitimate and important aims.
- **Nature and extent of limitation** The limitation is total and irreversible: execution destroys life and all remaining rights.
- **Relation between means and purpose** The connection between death and deterrence was not proven to be materially stronger than life imprisonment.
- **Less restrictive means** Life imprisonment can protect society and punish severely without extinguishing life.
- **Overall proportionality** The state failed to make the clear and convincing case required to justify the death penalty.

---

## 12. The purposes of punishment

The Court considered the traditional purposes of punishment:

1. **Deterrence**
2. **Prevention**
3. **Retribution**
4. **Reformation**

### 12.1 Deterrence

The state argued that the death penalty deterred murder. The Court was not persuaded that death was materially more effective than life imprisonment as a deterrent. Because the right at stake was life itself, speculative deterrence could not justify the irreversible destruction of life.

### 12.2 Prevention

The state argued that execution prevents the offender from killing again. The Court accepted that prevention is important, but held that life imprisonment can also protect society by removing the offender from the community.

### 12.3 Retribution

The Court accepted that retribution is a recognised purpose of punishment. However, it gave retribution less constitutional weight than life and dignity. Constitutional punishment may express moral outrage, but it may not collapse into vengeance.

### 12.4 Reformation

Execution makes reformation impossible. A constitutional order committed to dignity must remain aware that punishment is not only about destruction or retaliation.

---

## 13. Why the death penalty failed the limitation test

The death penalty failed because the Court weighed the state’s aims against the constitutional cost of execution.

### Factors against constitutionality

- Death permanently destroys life.
- Death annihilates dignity.
- Death is final and irreversible.
- Error cannot be corrected after execution.
- Capital sentencing contains risks of arbitrariness.
- Race, poverty and inequality affect criminal justice outcomes.
- Life imprisonment is a severe alternative punishment.
- Deterrence was not proven to be materially stronger than life imprisonment.
- Retribution cannot outweigh life and dignity.
- Public opinion cannot override constitutional rights.

### Core conclusion

The state did not make a clear and convincing case that the death penalty was a reasonable and necessary limitation of rights.

---

## 14. The order

The Court declared invalid:

- section 277(1)(a), (c), (d), (e) and (f) of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977; and
- corresponding provisions in force elsewhere in the national territory,

because they authorised capital punishment and were inconsistent with the Constitution.

The Court also ordered that:

- the State and all its organs were forbidden from executing anyone already sentenced to death under the invalid provisions; and
- those persons would remain in custody until their sentences were lawfully set aside and replaced with lawful punishments.

The Court did **not** decide the proper substituted sentence for Makwanyane and Mchunu. That was for the Appellate Division.

---

## 15. Concurring judgments: what to know for A2

The case contains many concurring judgments. For CON178 A2, you do not need to memorise every separate judgment in detail, but you should understand the most examinable themes.

### 15.1 Chaskalson P

The main judgment provides the core legal framework:

- generous and purposive interpretation;
- life, dignity and equality as giving meaning to cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment;
- public opinion is not decisive;
- proportionality under the limitation clause;
- death penalty unjustifiable.

### 15.2 Langa J and ubuntu

Langa J linked ubuntu to life, dignity, communality, mutual respect and co-responsibility. Ubuntu does not justify vengeance. It emphasises that every person has dignity and value, including those who commit serious crimes.

Use Langa J for:

- ubuntu;
- dignity;
- value-based constitutionalism;
- transformation;
- rejection of vengeance.

### 15.3 Mahomed J and the transformative Constitution

Mahomed J emphasised that the South African Constitution is not merely a technical legal instrument. It represents a break from a painful past and commits the country to a different moral and legal future. This connects strongly to transformative constitutionalism.

Use Mahomed J for:

- constitutionalism as a new ethos;
- transition from past injustice;
- values disciplining state power;
- the Constitution as a moral and legal break from apartheid.

### 15.4 Mokgoro J and human dignity

Mokgoro J emphasised human dignity and ubuntu as constitutional values. Her reasoning helps connect *Makwanyane* to the broader idea that the Constitution must be interpreted through values rooted in South Africa’s own context.

### 15.5 Sachs J and constitutional history

Sachs J placed the case in historical context. His judgment shows why the new constitutional order rejected practices that brutalised society and diminished respect for life.

Use Sachs J for:

- history and constitutional values;
- rejection of state brutality;
- life and dignity after apartheid;
- constitutionalism as a response to abuse of power.

---

## 17. How to use Makwanyane in A2 answers

### 17.1 If the question asks about limitation of rights

Use *Makwanyane* as the foundational case for proportionality.

**Answer structure:**

1. Identify the right limited.
2. Identify the purpose of the limitation.
3. Explain that limitations require proportionality.
4. Apply the *Makwanyane* factors:
   - nature and importance of the right;
   - purpose and importance of the limitation;
   - extent of the limitation;
   - relation between limitation and purpose;
   - less restrictive means.
5. Conclude whether the state has justified the limitation.

**Ready sentence:**

> In *Makwanyane*, Chaskalson P held that limitation analysis involves a proportionality inquiry in which courts weigh the nature and importance of the right against the purpose, extent and efficacy of the limitation, including whether less restrictive means are available.

---

### 17.2 If the question asks about constitutional supremacy

Use *Makwanyane* to show that courts must enforce the Constitution even against legislation and public opinion.

**Ready sentence:**

> *Makwanyane* illustrates the move from parliamentary sovereignty to constitutional supremacy: even if Parliament had authorised the death penalty and even if public opinion supported it, the Court had to test the law against the Constitution.

---

### 17.3 If the question asks about democracy

Use the public opinion section.

**Ready sentence:**

> The case shows that South Africa is a constitutional democracy, not a system of unlimited majority rule; entrenched rights protect even unpopular or marginalised persons.

---

### 17.4 If the question asks about dignity

Use the Court’s view that execution objectifies the offender and strips them of humanity.

**Ready sentence:**

> The Court treated dignity as central to the constitutional order and held that the state cannot affirm human dignity by deliberately annihilating the dignity and life of even the worst offender.

---

### 17.5 If the question asks about transformative constitutionalism

Use Mahomed J, Langa J, Sachs J, and the postamble.

**Ready sentence:**

> *Makwanyane* is transformative because it rejects a punitive, authority-based legal culture and insists that punishment must be justified through constitutional values such as life, dignity, equality, ubuntu and freedom.

---

### 17.6 If the question asks about separation of powers

Use the Court’s distinction between policy and constitutional validity.

**Ready sentence:**

> Although punishment policy usually belongs to the legislature, *Makwanyane* shows that courts must intervene when legislation conflicts with entrenched constitutional rights; this is not judicial overreach but the function of constitutional review.

---

## 18. Common mistakes to avoid

### Mistake 1: Saying Makwanyane was decided under section 36

Incorrect. It was decided under **section 33 of the Interim Constitution**. But it remains central to section 36 because section 36 substantially reflects the proportionality approach developed in the case.

### Mistake 2: Saying the Court ignored victims

Incorrect. The Court recognised deterrence, prevention, retribution and public safety as legitimate aims. It held that those aims did not justify the irreversible destruction of life and dignity.

### Mistake 3: Saying public opinion is irrelevant

Too broad. Public opinion may be relevant, but it is **not decisive**. Courts must enforce the Constitution.

### Mistake 4: Treating the case as only about death penalty

Too narrow. The case is also about constitutional interpretation, limitation, dignity, life, public opinion, democracy, constitutional supremacy and transformation.

### Mistake 5: Forgetting the alternative of life imprisonment

The availability of life imprisonment was central to the proportionality analysis because it showed that the state had a severe but less rights-destructive alternative.

### Mistake 6: Ignoring arbitrariness and error

The Court did not only say death is harsh. It also focused on the risk that capital punishment may operate unequally or mistakenly in a society shaped by poverty, race and unequal access to legal resources.

---

## 19. Exam answer templates

### 19.1 Five-mark answer: limitation analysis

*Makwanyane* is the leading case on proportionality in South African limitation analysis. Although decided under section 33 of the Interim Constitution, it informs section 36 of the 1996 Constitution. Chaskalson P held that limiting rights requires weighing competing values and assessing proportionality. Relevant factors include the nature and importance of the right, the purpose and importance of the limitation, the extent of the limitation, the relation between the limitation and its purpose, and whether less restrictive means are available. Applied to the death penalty, the Court held that deterrence, prevention and retribution could not justify the destruction of life and dignity, especially because life imprisonment was available as a severe alternative.

### 19.2 Ten-mark answer: death penalty and constitutional values

In *S v Makwanyane*, the Constitutional Court considered whether section 277 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which allowed capital punishment, was consistent with the Interim Constitution. The accused had been sentenced to death after being convicted of murder, and the Appellate Division referred the constitutional issue to the Constitutional Court. The Court held that the death penalty implicated the rights to life, dignity, equality and freedom from cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment. Chaskalson P reasoned that death is final and irreversible, destroys all personal rights, strips the offender of dignity, and carries risks of arbitrariness and error. Although the state relied on deterrence, prevention, retribution and public opinion, the Court held that public opinion cannot replace constitutional adjudication and that retribution cannot carry the same weight as life and dignity. Applying proportionality, the Court found that the state had not shown that the death penalty was materially more effective than life imprisonment. The death penalty was therefore unconstitutional. The case is significant because it established proportionality as the core of limitation analysis and confirmed South Africa’s break from parliamentary sovereignty to value-based constitutional supremacy.

### 19.3 Critical engagement answer: public opinion and democracy

*Makwanyane* is especially important for understanding the relationship between democracy and rights. The Attorney-General argued that many South Africans supported the death penalty, especially in serious murder cases. The Court accepted that public opinion may be relevant but held that it cannot be decisive. If rights depended only on majority preference, constitutional adjudication would be unnecessary and South Africa would return to parliamentary sovereignty. The purpose of a supreme Constitution and a justiciable Bill of Rights is to protect all people, including unpopular and marginalised persons. This does not make the Court anti-democratic. It reflects constitutional democracy: majority rule operates within limits set by dignity, equality, freedom and the rule of law.

---

## 20. Mini hub version

### S v Makwanyane and Another 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC)

**Facts:** The accused were convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The Appellate Division postponed the death-sentence appeal so the Constitutional Court could decide whether section 277 of the Criminal Procedure Act was constitutional under the Interim Constitution.

**Issue:** Was the death penalty consistent with the rights to life, dignity, equality and freedom from cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment?

**Reasoning:** The Court held that the death penalty destroys life, annihilates dignity, creates risks of arbitrariness and error, and cannot be justified merely by deterrence, prevention, retribution or public opinion. Chaskalson P developed a proportionality test for limitation analysis, requiring the Court to balance the nature and importance of the right, the purpose and importance of the limitation, the extent of the limitation, the relation between the limitation and its purpose, and less restrictive means.

**Judgment:** The death penalty was unconstitutional. Section 277(1)(a), (c), (d), (e) and (f), and corresponding provisions, were declared invalid to the extent that they authorised capital punishment.

**Constitutional significance:** The case is foundational for value-based constitutionalism and limitation analysis. It confirms that public opinion cannot override constitutional rights and that South African constitutional democracy is built on life, dignity, equality, freedom and constitutional supremacy.

**INTRODUCTION TO CONSTITUTIONAL LAW 178**

**THEME 4 CASE + LEGISLATION DOCKET**

*The Constitution of 1996: Basic Principles, Concepts and Doctrines*

- ---
- **What this document does**  Collects the cases, Acts, constitutional sections and legislation mentioned or strongly linked in Theme 4 materials.  Gives each case in the required exam format: facts, issue, reasoning, judgment, constitutional significance and exam use.  Flags which sources are prescribed and whether more textbook pages are probably needed for complete coverage.

# 1. Scope check: what Theme 4 actually requires

- ---
- **Prescribed Theme 4 materials from the Study Guide**  Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996: sections 1, 2, 8, 9, 10, 36, 39 and 172.  De Vos and Freedman, South African Constitutional Law in Context 2nd ed 2021: sections 2.1, 2.2, 2.3.1-2.3.2, 2.4, 2.5 and 10.3.3.3.  S v Makwanyane 1995 3 SA 391 (CC), as discussed in De Vos and Freedman table 11.1 / para 11.6.  Additional but outdated helpful reading: Currie & De Waal pages 40-57 and 72-89.

- ---
- **Do you need more textbook pages?**  Yes - for a complete, lecturer-aligned Theme 4 case document, you should ideally have the De Vos and Freedman pages/sections listed above. The uploaded lectures give the exam map, examples and lecturer emphasis, but the prescribed textbook sections will give fuller doctrinal explanation and additional case context.  Minimum for passing: lecture slides + Constitution sections + S v Makwanyane. Distinction-level: add De Vos sections 2.1, 2.2, 2.3.1-2.3.2, 2.4, 2.5, 10.3.3.3 and the De Vos discussion of Makwanyane.  Because Currie & De Waal is expressly described as outdated, use it only to clarify older concepts - do not let it override newer lecture developments.

# 3. Detailed case bank

## ⚖️ S v Makwanyane 1995 (3) SA 391 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this for any answer on foundational values, limitation of rights, dignity, judicial review, constitutional supremacy, or value-based interpretation.

- **Legal theme** Value-based constitutionalism; limitation of rights; human dignity, equality and freedom; judicial review of legislation.
- **Facts** Makwanyane and Mchunu were convicted of murder and sentenced to death under s 277(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977. They challenged the constitutionality of the death penalty under the 1993 Interim Constitution. The case became the first major constitutional review of legislation by the new Constitutional Court.
- **Issue** Whether the death penalty was compatible with the rights to life, dignity and freedom from cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment, and whether it could be justified under the limitation clause.
- **Court reasoning** The Court treated the Constitution as a value-based document. It did not only ask what the statute allowed; it asked whether the death penalty could survive a constitutional system founded on dignity, equality and freedom. The State relied on deterrence, prevention, retribution and public opinion. The Court held that public opinion cannot decide constitutional rights. Rights must be interpreted through constitutional values. The death penalty objectifies the condemned person and places the person outside the protection of humanity.
- **Judgment / outcome** The death penalty was declared unconstitutional and invalid. Section 277(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Act was invalid to the extent that it authorised capital punishment.
- **Constitutional significance** Foundational case for value-based constitutionalism. It shows that courts can invalidate legislation inconsistent with the Constitution; rights are not absolute but limitations must be reasonable and justifiable; human dignity is central to constitutional interpretation.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Interim Constitution ss 9, 10, 11(2), 33; Constitution 1996 ss 10, 11, 12, 36, 39; Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977 s 277(1)(a).
- **How to write it in the exam** “In S v Makwanyane, the Constitutional Court used the values of human dignity, equality and freedom to hold that the death penalty could not be justified in a constitutional democracy, even if public opinion supported it.”

## ⚖️ S v Walters

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this when asked “explain the limitation clause” or “how do courts decide if a limitation is reasonable and justifiable?”.

- **Legal theme** Limitation clause; two-stage enquiry; interpretation of rights and impugned law.
- **Facts** The Court considered whether a statutory provision limiting constitutional rights could survive constitutional scrutiny. The case is used in the lecture for the mechanics of the limitation enquiry.
- **Issue** How must a court determine whether a right has been limited and, if so, whether that limitation is constitutionally justifiable?
- **Court reasoning** The Court explained a two-stage process. First, identify the content and scope of the right and the meaning/effect of the impugned law to see whether there is a limitation. If there is no limitation, the challenge fails. If there is a limitation, the second stage is the limitations exercise: weigh the nature and importance of the right and the extent of limitation against the purpose and importance of the limiting law.
- **Judgment / outcome** The case provides the analytical structure for s 36 limitation analysis rather than merely stating an outcome for Theme 4 purposes.
- **Constitutional significance** High-yield because it gives the exam method for limitation questions: right infringed first, justification second.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 36 and 39.
- **How to write it in the exam** “Following S v Walters, the limitation analysis is a two-stage enquiry: first determine whether the right is limited; then determine whether the limitation is reasonable and justifiable under s 36.”

## ⚖️ Daniels v Campbell 2004 (5) SA 331 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this for value-based constitutionalism, statutory interpretation, diversity, equality and religious/cultural inclusion.

- **Legal theme** Value-based interpretation of legislation; s 39(2); equality, tolerance and diversity.
- **Facts** The case concerned whether the word “spouse” in the Intestate Succession Act and the Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act included a surviving spouse from a Muslim marriage.
- **Issue** Whether statutes should be interpreted broadly and inclusively to recognise a surviving spouse in a Muslim marriage.
- **Court reasoning** Justice Sachs reasoned that constitutional values of equality, tolerance and respect for diversity supported a broad and inclusive interpretation of “spouse”. The Court used constitutional values to interpret ordinary legislation in a way that promoted the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights.
- **Judgment / outcome** The Court held that “spouse” included a surviving spouse to a Muslim marriage for the purposes of the relevant Acts.
- **Constitutional significance** Shows s 39(2) in action: courts interpret legislation through constitutional values instead of reading statutes narrowly in a way that excludes vulnerable groups.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 s 39(2); Intestate Succession Act 81 of 1987; Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act 27 of 1990.
- **How to write it in the exam** “Daniels v Campbell illustrates that s 39(2) requires courts to interpret legislation in a way that promotes equality, tolerance and diversity.”

## ⚖️ Port Elizabeth Municipality v Various Occupiers 2005 (1) SA 217 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this for values, limitation/balancing, housing, property, evictions, and the class task about municipal land.

- **Legal theme** Balancing competing rights through constitutional values; property vs housing; eviction justice.
- **Facts** A municipality sought the eviction of unlawful occupiers. The dispute required the Court to consider the interests of landowners/municipality and the occupiers’ vulnerability and potential homelessness.
- **Issue** How should courts balance property rights and housing/dignity interests when deciding whether eviction is just and equitable?
- **Court reasoning** Justice Sachs emphasised that eviction law must be interpreted in light of South Africa’s history of forced removals and homelessness. Fairness requires attention to both the owners’ rights and the occupiers’ dignity. The Constitution does not allow mechanical eviction; it requires a humane, context-sensitive balancing exercise.
- **Judgment / outcome** Eviction must only occur where it is just and equitable after considering all relevant circumstances.
- **Constitutional significance** Excellent case for showing that constitutional values operate when rights conflict. It connects dignity, housing, property, transformative constitutionalism and historical context.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 25 and 26; especially s 26(3) on evictions.
- **How to write it in the exam** “Port Elizabeth Municipality shows that courts balance competing rights by asking which outcome best reflects dignity, equality, freedom and South Africa’s history of dispossession.”

## ⚖️ Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie 2006 (1) SA 524 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this for transformative constitutionalism, value-based interpretation, equality, dignity and the role of courts in protecting minorities.

- **Legal theme** Transformative constitutionalism; equality and dignity; social inclusion; values against majoritarian exclusion.
- **Facts** Same-sex couples were excluded from the institution of civil marriage. The applicants argued that this exclusion violated their rights to equality and dignity.
- **Issue** Whether excluding same-sex couples from marriage was constitutionally permissible.
- **Court reasoning** The Court held that exclusion from marriage rendered same-sex couples outsiders to a central social institution of love and commitment. Constitutional democracy requires equal concern and respect. Religious objections could not justify state exclusion because South Africa requires coexistence between sacred and secular spheres.
- **Judgment / outcome** The exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage was unconstitutional. Parliament was given time to correct the defect, leading to the Civil Union Act.
- **Constitutional significance** Shows values driving social transformation. It links equality, dignity, freedom, minority protection and the counter-majoritarian role of courts.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 9, 10, 15, 36, 39; Civil Union Act 17 of 2006 as legislative response.
- **How to write it in the exam** “Fourie shows that the Constitution aims not merely to regulate society but to transform social institutions so that previously excluded groups enjoy equal dignity and belonging.”

## ⚖️ Carmichele v Minister of Safety and Security 2001 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this for direct vs indirect application and s 39(2) common-law development.

- **Legal theme** Indirect application of Bill of Rights; development of common law; state duties to protect rights.
- **Facts** Ms Carmichele was attacked by a man who had been released despite prior charges and warning signs. She claimed that police and prosecutors had failed to protect her. The question was whether the common law of delict should recognise liability in such circumstances.
- **Issue** Whether courts must develop the common law of delict to reflect constitutional rights and values.
- **Court reasoning** The Court held that courts have a duty under s 39(2) to develop the common law where it is deficient and inconsistent with the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights. The Constitution influences private/common-law rules indirectly by requiring their development in light of rights.
- **Judgment / outcome** The matter was sent back for reconsideration in light of the constitutional duty to develop the common law.
- **Constitutional significance** Core case for indirect application. It shows that constitutional rights transform ordinary law without necessarily invalidating a statute.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 7(2), 8, 12, 39(2).
- **How to write it in the exam** “Carmichele is the key example of indirect application: instead of invalidating law, the Court required the common law to be developed to promote the Bill of Rights.”

## ⚖️ Government of the Republic of South Africa v Grootboom 2000 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this for vertical application, socio-economic rights, housing, reasonableness and transformative constitutionalism.

- **Legal theme** Vertical application of socio-economic rights; housing; reasonableness review.
- **Facts** A group of people living in desperate conditions sought emergency shelter and access to housing. They challenged the government’s housing programme.
- **Issue** Whether the state had complied with its constitutional obligation to take reasonable measures to progressively realise the right of access to adequate housing.
- **Court reasoning** The Court held that socio-economic rights are justiciable. The state does not have to provide a house immediately to everyone, but its programme must be reasonable and must make provision for people in crisis or desperate need.
- **Judgment / outcome** The government’s housing programme was constitutionally defective because it failed to provide for those in desperate need.
- **Constitutional significance** Core vertical application example. It shows courts reviewing state policy against the Bill of Rights and demanding reasonableness while respecting institutional limits.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 26 and 7(2).
- **How to write it in the exam** “Grootboom shows that socio-economic rights are enforceable and that government programmes must be reasonable, especially for those in desperate need.”

## ⚖️ Soobramoney v Minister of Health, KwaZulu-Natal 1997 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use this for transformative constitutionalism and the socio-economic context of the Constitution.

- **Legal theme** Transformative constitutionalism; socio-economic context; scarce resources; dignity, freedom and equality.
- **Facts** Mr Soobramoney suffered from chronic renal failure and sought access to dialysis at a public hospital. The hospital had limited resources and criteria for treatment.
- **Issue** Whether refusal to provide dialysis violated the rights to emergency medical treatment and access to health care.
- **Court reasoning** The Court recognised the severe inequality and poverty existing at the birth of the Constitution. It held that transformation lies at the heart of the constitutional order, but courts must consider resource constraints and institutional competence when assessing socio-economic rights.
- **Judgment / outcome** The claim failed because the treatment did not fall within emergency medical treatment and the hospital’s resource-based policy was not shown to be unconstitutional.
- **Constitutional significance** Often used for the famous statement that the Constitution is committed to transforming society into one based on human dignity, freedom and equality. It shows the promise and limits of socio-economic rights litigation.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 27 and 36; also linked to values in s 1.
- **How to write it in the exam** “Soobramoney shows that the transformative Constitution is both backward-looking and forward-looking: it responds to existing poverty while aiming toward dignity, freedom and equality.”

## ⚖️ Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly 2016 (CC) [Nkandla / EFF 1]

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use for rule of law, accountability, constitutional supremacy, legality, Chapter 9 institutions and separation of powers/accountability.

- **Legal theme** Rule of law; constitutional supremacy; accountability; Public Protector remedial action.
- **Facts** The Public Protector investigated spending on upgrades at President Zuma’s Nkandla residence and directed remedial action. The President and National Assembly did not comply and attempted to replace or second-guess the remedial action.
- **Issue** Whether the Public Protector’s remedial action was binding and whether the President and National Assembly acted inconsistently with the Constitution.
- **Court reasoning** The Court linked the rule of law, constitutional supremacy and accountability. It held that no decision grounded in the Constitution or law may be ignored merely because a person disagrees with it; recourse must be had to a court. Ignoring binding remedial action would amount to self-help, which is inconsistent with the rule of law.
- **Judgment / outcome** The remedial action was binding. The President’s non-compliance and the National Assembly resolution absolving him were unconstitutional and invalid.
- **Constitutional significance** Major Theme 4 rule of law case. Shows that even the President must obey the Constitution and lawful constitutional decisions.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 1(c), 2, 42(3), 55(2), 83(b), 181, 182.
- **How to write it in the exam** “EFF v Speaker confirms that constitutionalism, accountability and the rule of law prevent public officials from treating constitutional obligations as optional.”

## ⚖️ Fedsure Life Assurance Ltd v Greater Johannesburg Transitional Metropolitan Council 1998 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use for rule of law and legality definition.

- **Legal theme** Rule of law; legality; authorised public power.
- **Facts** A local government body exercised public powers affecting rates/levies. The case became an early authority on the principle that all public power must be sourced in law.
- **Issue** Whether organs of state may exercise powers beyond those conferred by law.
- **Court reasoning** The Court held that the rule of law includes the principle of legality: the legislature and executive in every sphere may exercise no power and perform no function beyond that conferred by law.
- **Judgment / outcome** The legality principle was affirmed as a constitutional control on public power.
- **Constitutional significance** Foundational legality case. It gives the basic exam formula: public power must be authorised by law.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 1(c) and 2.
- **How to write it in the exam** “Fedsure establishes that legality is part of the rule of law: every exercise of public power must be authorised by law.”

## ⚖️ Affordable Medicines Trust v Minister of Health 2005 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use when explaining that legality is not just administrative-law language; it is constitutional law.

- **Legal theme** Legality; control of public power; rationality.
- **Facts** Regulations and licensing powers in the medicines/health context were challenged. The case is used in Theme 4 for the general rule that public power must comply with the Constitution and legality.
- **Issue** What constitutional controls apply to the exercise of public power?
- **Court reasoning** The Court held that the exercise of public power must comply with the Constitution and the doctrine of legality. Legality is an incident of the rule of law and one of the constitutional mechanisms for controlling public power.
- **Judgment / outcome** The Court affirmed legality as a foundation for the control of public power.
- **Constitutional significance** Use with Fedsure and Albutt to build the rule of law/legality line of authority.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 1(c), 2 and 172.
- **How to write it in the exam** “Affordable Medicines confirms that legality is an incident of the rule of law and forms part of the constitutional control of public power.”

## ⚖️ Albutt v Centre for the Study of Violence and Reconciliation 2010 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use for legality, rationality, procedural fairness and public power.

- **Legal theme** Legality and rationality; procedural rationality; presidential pardons.
- **Facts** The President created a special process for pardons of offenders convicted of politically motivated crimes who had not received amnesty through the TRC process. Victims and families wanted to make representations before pardons were granted, but were excluded.
- **Issue** Whether victims had to be afforded an opportunity to be heard before the President could grant pardons under the special dispensation.
- **Court reasoning** The Court held that all public power must comply with legality and rationality. Because the purpose of the special dispensation was linked to national reconciliation, excluding victims from the process was irrational. Rationality can require a fair procedure where the process chosen must be rationally connected to the purpose.
- **Judgment / outcome** Victims had to be given an opportunity to make representations before pardons were granted.
- **Constitutional significance** Key rule of law case for rationality. It shows that legality is not only “is there authorisation?” but also whether the means chosen rationally connect to a legitimate governmental purpose.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 1(c), 2 and 84(2)(j).
- **How to write it in the exam** “Albutt shows that the exercise of public power must be rationally connected to its purpose; if reconciliation is the aim, excluding victims from the pardon process is irrational.”

## ⚖️ S v Dodo 2001 (3) SA 382 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use for separation of powers, judicial function and comparative law.

- **Legal theme** Separation of powers; sentencing; judicial independence; foreign law under s 39.
- **Facts** The case concerned mandatory minimum sentences prescribed by legislation and whether such sentencing laws impermissibly interfered with judicial sentencing discretion.
- **Issue** Whether mandatory minimum sentences violate the separation of powers by limiting the judiciary’s sentencing function.
- **Court reasoning** The Court considered comparative foreign law and observed that many constitutional democracies permit the legislature to set sentencing frameworks. Mere legislative involvement in sentencing does not automatically violate separation of powers. The key question is whether judicial power is undermined to an unconstitutional degree.
- **Judgment / outcome** Mandatory minimum sentencing does not, merely by existing, violate separation of powers.
- **Constitutional significance** Useful for separation of powers and s 39(1) foreign law. It shows that separation of powers does not require absolute separation; some overlap is constitutionally permissible.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 ss 12, 36, 39; Criminal Law Amendment Act minimum sentencing framework as background.
- **How to write it in the exam** “S v Dodo shows that separation of powers is not absolute: legislative regulation of sentencing is permissible if it does not destroy the judiciary’s constitutional role.”

## ⚖️ H v Fetal Assessment Centre 2015 (2) SA 193 (CC)

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use only if a question mentions international/foreign law or comparative interpretation.

- **Legal theme** Use of foreign law; development of common law; s 39.
- **Facts** The case concerned whether South African law should recognise a child’s claim relating to negligent failure to detect serious foetal abnormalities. It is used in the textbook extract for principles on using foreign law.
- **Issue** How should foreign law be used in constitutional interpretation and common-law development?
- **Court reasoning** The Court explained that foreign law can be useful when approaching constitutional problems, but it must be used carefully and contextually. South African courts must not transplant foreign rules without considering local constitutional values and conditions.
- **Judgment / outcome** The case developed the law cautiously while clarifying principles for comparative legal reasoning.
- **Constitutional significance** Not a core lecture case, but useful if a question asks about s 39(1)(c) and the role of foreign law.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Constitution 1996 s 39(1)(c) and s 39(2).
- **How to write it in the exam** “H v Fetal Assessment Centre reminds us that foreign law may assist constitutional reasoning, but South African courts must adapt it to local constitutional values.”

## ⚖️ Ex Parte Chairperson of the Constitutional Assembly: Certification judgments

- ---
- **High-yield exam use**  Use when linking Theme 3 to Theme 4: the doctrines in Theme 4 were not accidental; they were constitutional commitments certified by the Court.

- **Legal theme** Background link to 1996 Constitution; constitutional supremacy; separation of powers; legitimacy.
- **Facts** The Constitutional Court had to certify whether the constitutional text complied with the Constitutional Principles agreed during the transition. The Theme 4 lectures refer back to certification as part of understanding how the 1996 Constitution came into force.
- **Issue** Whether the Final Constitution complied with the binding Constitutional Principles.
- **Court reasoning** The Court treated certification as a legal/judicial task rather than a political preference exercise. The text had to comply with agreed principles such as constitutional supremacy, justiciable rights, democracy and separation of powers.
- **Judgment / outcome** The first text was not fully certified; after amendment, the constitutional text was certified and the Constitution came into force on 4 February 1997.
- **Constitutional significance** Useful background case for why the 1996 Constitution has legal legitimacy and why its doctrines are binding.
- **Legislation / sections linked** Interim Constitution Schedule 4 Constitutional Principles; Constitution 1996 generally.
- **How to write it in the exam** “The Certification judgments show that the 1996 Constitution’s core principles were legally tested against agreed Constitutional Principles before the Constitution came into force.”

# 4. Legislation, constitutional sections and legal instruments bank

## 📜 Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Central legal source for Theme 4. Prescribed sections: 1, 2, 8, 9, 10, 36, 39, 172. Lecture examples also use ss 7, 12, 16, 25, 26, 27, 32, 35, 74, 83, 84, 181 and 182.
- **What it says / does** Supreme law of the Republic; creates values, rights, institutions, limitations, interpretation duties and remedies for invalid law/conduct.
- **Why it matters** Theme 4 is essentially about how the 1996 Constitution structures, constrains and transforms public and private power.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, Daniels, PE Municipality, Fourie, Carmichele, Grootboom, Soobramoney, EFF, Fedsure, Affordable Medicines, Albutt, Dodo.
- **Exam sentence** “The Constitution is both a founding-value document and a binding supreme law: s 1 states the values, while s 2 gives them enforceable supremacy.”

## 📜 Section 1 - Founding values

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Value-based constitutionalism and rule of law sections.
- **What it says / does** South Africa is founded on dignity, equality, human rights, non-racialism, non-sexism, supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, universal adult suffrage, regular elections, multi-party democracy, accountability, responsiveness and openness.
- **Why it matters** These values permeate interpretation, limitation, democracy, rule of law and separation of powers.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, Soobramoney, Fourie, EFF, Fedsure.
- **Exam sentence** “Section 1 makes constitutional values foundational, meaning courts must interpret law consistently with dignity, equality, freedom, accountability and the rule of law.”

## 📜 Section 2 - Supremacy of the Constitution

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Constitutional supremacy.
- **What it says / does** The Constitution is the supreme law; law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid; obligations imposed by it must be fulfilled.
- **Why it matters** Makes judicial review possible and separates South Africa from parliamentary sovereignty.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, EFF, Fedsure, Affordable Medicines, Albutt.
- **Exam sentence** “Section 2 converts constitutional supremacy into a binding rule: inconsistent law or conduct is invalid.”

## 📜 Section 7 - Rights

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Bill of Rights framework.
- **What it says / does** Bill of Rights is a cornerstone of democracy; the state must respect, protect, promote and fulfil rights; rights are subject to limitations.
- **Why it matters** Links transformative constitutionalism and the state’s positive obligations.
- **Cases linked** Grootboom, Carmichele, Soobramoney.
- **Exam sentence** “Section 7(2) means the state must not only avoid violating rights but must actively protect, promote and fulfil them.”

## 📜 Section 8 - Application of the Bill of Rights

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Direct/indirect and vertical/horizontal application.
- **What it says / does** The Bill of Rights applies to all law and binds the legislature, executive, judiciary and organs of state. It may bind natural and juristic persons depending on the nature of the right and duty.
- **Why it matters** Core section for explaining vertical and horizontal application.
- **Cases linked** Carmichele; equality examples; private discrimination examples.
- **Exam sentence** “Section 8 is the gateway provision for deciding whether the Bill of Rights applies vertically, horizontally, directly or indirectly.”

## 📜 Section 9 - Equality

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Value-based constitutionalism; horizontal application examples.
- **What it says / does** Everyone is equal before the law; unfair discrimination by the state and by private persons is prohibited; national legislation must prevent/prohibit unfair discrimination.
- **Why it matters** Shows substantive equality and direct horizontal application.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, Fourie, Daniels; linked to PEPUDA.
- **Exam sentence** “Section 9 is especially important because it expressly applies to private persons through s 9(4), supporting horizontal application.”

## 📜 Section 10 - Human dignity

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Foundational value/right; Makwanyane; Fourie; PE Municipality.
- **What it says / does** Everyone has inherent dignity and the right to have dignity respected and protected.
- **Why it matters** Often treated as a core value in South African constitutionalism.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, Fourie, PE Municipality, Soobramoney.
- **Exam sentence** “Dignity is both a right and an organising value that shapes interpretation, limitation and remedies.”

## 📜 Section 36 - Limitation of rights

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Limitations clause.
- **What it says / does** Rights may be limited only by law of general application to the extent reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society based on dignity, equality and freedom. Factors include nature of right, purpose, extent, relationship between limitation and purpose, and less restrictive means.
- **Why it matters** Core exam structure for limitation questions.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, Walters, Fourie, Dodo.
- **Exam sentence** “A s 36 answer must first identify the infringement, then weigh whether the limitation is reasonable and justifiable.”

## 📜 Section 39 - Interpretation of the Bill of Rights / legislation / common law / customary law

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Value-based interpretation; indirect application.
- **What it says / does** When interpreting the Bill of Rights, courts must promote dignity, equality and freedom; must consider international law; may consider foreign law. When interpreting legislation or developing common/customary law, courts must promote the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights.
- **Why it matters** Central to value-based constitutionalism and indirect application.
- **Cases linked** Daniels, Carmichele, H v Fetal Assessment Centre, S v Walters.
- **Exam sentence** “Section 39(2) is the bridge between constitutional values and ordinary law.”

## 📜 Section 172 - Constitutional invalidity and remedies

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Constitutional supremacy and judicial review.
- **What it says / does** When deciding a constitutional matter, a court must declare inconsistent law/conduct invalid to the extent of inconsistency and may make a just and equitable order.
- **Why it matters** This is the remedial consequence of constitutional supremacy.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, EFF, Affordable Medicines.
- **Exam sentence** “Section 172 gives courts the remedial power that makes constitutional supremacy practical.”

## 📜 Interim Constitution of 1993

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Makwanyane and s 33 limitation comparison.
- **What it says / does** The transitional constitution containing an interim Bill of Rights and limitation clause.
- **Why it matters** Several early Constitutional Court cases, including Makwanyane, were decided under the Interim Constitution, but the principles remain foundational.
- **Cases linked** Makwanyane, Certification judgments.
- **Exam sentence** “The Interim Constitution introduced justiciable rights and began the shift from parliamentary sovereignty to constitutional supremacy.”

## 📜 Criminal Procedure Act 51 of 1977 - s 277(1)(a)

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** S v Makwanyane.
- **What it says / does** Authorised the death penalty for certain crimes before constitutional invalidation.
- **Why it matters** Shows how old-order legislation was tested against the new constitutional order.
- **Cases linked** S v Makwanyane.
- **Exam sentence** “Makwanyane invalidated the death penalty provision in the Criminal Procedure Act because it was inconsistent with constitutional rights and values.”

## 📜 Intestate Succession Act 81 of 1987

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Daniels v Campbell.
- **What it says / does** Regulates inheritance where a person dies without a will. The term “spouse” was interpreted to include a surviving spouse in a Muslim marriage.
- **Why it matters** Shows values-based statutory interpretation and inclusion.
- **Cases linked** Daniels v Campbell.
- **Exam sentence** “Daniels shows that ordinary statutory words must be interpreted through constitutional values where possible.”

## 📜 Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act 27 of 1990

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Daniels v Campbell.
- **What it says / does** Allows claims for maintenance by surviving spouses. “Spouse” was interpreted inclusively.
- **Why it matters** Works with Intestate Succession Act in Daniels.
- **Cases linked** Daniels v Campbell.
- **Exam sentence** “The Acts were read inclusively to avoid exclusion inconsistent with equality, tolerance and diversity.”

## 📜 Disaster Management Act 57 of 2002 - s 27

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Rule of law lecture example on lockdown regulations.
- **What it says / does** Allows the responsible Minister, after a national state of disaster, to make regulations or issue directions on matters such as movement, resources, evacuation, traffic, premises, alcohol, communication, procurement and other steps necessary to prevent escalation.
- **Why it matters** Used to explain legality and rationality: is there authority, and is there a rational relationship between the regulation and legitimate government purpose?
- **Cases linked** Rule-of-law example; linked conceptually to Fedsure, Affordable Medicines and Albutt.
- **Exam sentence** “The Disaster Management Act example shows that lawful public power requires both authorisation and rational connection to a legitimate purpose.”

## 📜 Promotion of Access to Information Act 2 of 2000 (PAIA)

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Vertical application example for s 32 access to information.
- **What it says / does** Legislation giving effect to the right of access to information.
- **Why it matters** Shows how a constitutional right is implemented through national legislation and enforced against public bodies.
- **Cases linked** Not a core Theme 4 case; used in examples.
- **Exam sentence** “PAIA is the statutory mechanism used to give effect to s 32 access-to-information rights.”

## 📜 Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000 (PEPUDA)

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Horizontal equality and s 9(4).
- **What it says / does** National legislation enacted to prevent or prohibit unfair discrimination.
- **Why it matters** Shows how the Constitution requires legislation to regulate private discrimination.
- **Cases linked** Linked to equality and horizontal application examples.
- **Exam sentence** “PEPUDA operationalises s 9(4), which prohibits unfair discrimination by private persons.”

## 📜 Common law and customary law under s 39(2)

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Indirect application and Carmichele.
- **What it says / does** Courts must develop common law and customary law to promote the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights.
- **Why it matters** This is how the Bill of Rights transforms ordinary legal rules without always invalidating legislation.
- **Cases linked** Carmichele; H v Fetal Assessment Centre.
- **Exam sentence** “Indirect application occurs when courts develop common law or customary law under s 39(2) to align it with constitutional values.”

## 📜 Civil Union Act 17 of 2006

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Consequence of Fourie.
- **What it says / does** Legislation enacted after Fourie to provide legal recognition for same-sex unions.
- **Why it matters** Shows how a Constitutional Court decision can require Parliament to correct unconstitutional exclusion.
- **Cases linked** Minister of Home Affairs v Fourie.
- **Exam sentence** “Fourie resulted in legislative reform, showing the Constitution’s transformative effect on social institutions.”

## 📜 Promotion of Administrative Justice Act 3 of 2000 (PAJA)

- **Where it appears in Theme 4** Background to administrative justice; not central in your Theme 4 slide extracts but useful if s 33/legality is raised.
- **What it says / does** National legislation giving effect to the constitutional right to just administrative action.
- **Why it matters** Do not confuse PAJA review with legality review: legality is used where no specific review route applies or where broad public power is assessed.
- **Cases linked** Albutt, Affordable Medicines and Fedsure are legality/rule-of-law cases rather than ordinary PAJA case examples in your lecture.
- **Exam sentence** “If a question is about rule of law/legality rather than administrative action, focus on authorisation and rationality rather than defaulting to PAJA.”

# 5. Exam-ready comparison tables

- **Concept** **Key question** **Main authority/examples** **Exam trigger**
- Constitutional supremacy Is law/conduct inconsistent with the Constitution? Constitution ss 1(c), 2, 172; Makwanyane; EFF “supreme law”, “invalid”, “judicial review”
- Rule of law / legality Was the power authorised by law and exercised rationally? Fedsure; Affordable Medicines; Albutt; EFF “public power”, “authorised”, “rational connection”
- Value-based constitutionalism What outcome best reflects dignity, equality and freedom? Makwanyane; Daniels; PE Municipality; Fourie “values”, “interpretation”, “dignity”
- Limitation clause Has a right been limited and is it justified? s 36; Walters; Makwanyane “reasonable and justifiable”, “less restrictive means”
- Direct application Does the Bill of Rights directly invalidate conduct/law? s 8; Makwanyane “violates a constitutional right directly”
- Indirect application Must ordinary law be interpreted/developed to align with rights? s 39(2); Daniels; Carmichele “develop common law”, “interpret legislation”
- Vertical application State vs individual relationship? s 8(1); Grootboom; PAIA examples “government department”, “police”, “state policy”
- Horizontal application Private person/company vs private person? s 8(2); s 9(4); equality examples “private employer”, “private restaurant”, “company”
- Separation of powers Are branches properly checking and respecting each other? Dodo; EFF; Certification background “judicial review”, “elected legislature”, “court power”

# 6. What to memorise before a Theme 4 test

- ---
- **Memory list**  Constitutionalism = government authority is derived from and limited by a constitution; it must structure and constrain state power.  Constitutional supremacy = Constitution is supreme; inconsistent law/conduct is invalid; courts can review law/conduct.  Rule of law / legality = public power must be authorised by law and exercised rationally.  Values = dignity, equality, freedom, non-racialism, non-sexism, accountability, responsiveness, openness and rule of law permeate interpretation and limitation.  s 36 method = right limited? If yes, is limitation reasonable and justifiable? Apply nature of right, purpose, extent, relation and less restrictive means.  s 39 method = interpret rights and ordinary law to promote dignity, equality and freedom and the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights.  Application = direct/indirect + vertical/horizontal. Always identify both in a rights problem.  Use Makwanyane for values and limitation; Daniels for s 39 interpretation; Carmichele for common-law development; EFF/Fedsure/Affordable Medicines/Albutt for rule of law; PE Municipality/Fourie for balancing and transformation.

# 7. Mini model answer templates

- ---
- **5-mark: Explain constitutional supremacy**  Constitutional supremacy means the Constitution is the highest law. Section 2 provides that law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid and that constitutional obligations must be fulfilled. This makes the Constitution justiciable: courts may test laws and conduct against it. It also rejects parliamentary sovereignty because Parliament is bound by the Constitution. Cases such as S v Makwanyane and EFF v Speaker show that courts may invalidate old legislation or unlawful conduct when inconsistent with constitutional rights, values and obligations.

- ---
- **5-mark: Explain rule of law and legality**  The rule of law is a founding value in s 1(c). At minimum, it requires that public power must be authorised by law and exercised rationally. Fedsure states that the legislature and executive may exercise no power beyond that conferred by law. Affordable Medicines confirms that legality is part of the constitutional control of public power. Albutt shows that rationality may require a fair process where the process must be connected to the purpose. EFF v Speaker shows that no constitutional decision may simply be ignored without court challenge.

- ---
- **10/15-mark: Application of the Bill of Rights structure**  1. Identify the right and section involved.  2. State whether the Bill of Rights applies directly or indirectly.  3. State whether it applies vertically or horizontally.  4. If direct: explain that the right itself is relied upon and inconsistent law/conduct may be invalid.  5. If indirect: use s 39(2) to interpret legislation or develop common/customary law.  6. If vertical: state actor/state organ is bound by s 8(1).  7. If horizontal: private actor may be bound under s 8(2), considering nature of right and duty.  8. Add example/case: Makwanyane for direct invalidity; Carmichele for indirect development; Grootboom for vertical socio-economic rights; equality examples/PEPUDA for horizontal discrimination.

S v Bhulwana; S v Gwadiso (1995) was a landmark Constitutional Court of South Africa case that established key principles regarding the presumption of innocence in the post-apartheid legal system.

> [Image/base64 placeholder removed during cleaning: no readable legal text preserved in placeholder.]

Core Facts and Legal Issue

* The Law: Section 21(1)(a)(i) of the Drugs and Drug Trafficking Act, 1992, created a "reverse onus" provision. If a person was found in possession of more than 115 grams of dagga, they were presumed guilty of dealing in dagga, and had to prove their innocence in court.
* The Cases: Mr. Bhulwana and Mr. Gwadiso were convicted of drug dealing based on this presumption, rather than direct evidence of selling.
* Constitutional Issue: The High Court referred the matter to the Constitutional Court to decide if this "reverse onus" violated the right to a fair trial, specifically the presumption of innocence under the Interim Constitution.


Judgment and Reasoning (29 November 1995)

* Unanimous Decision: The court, with the judgment delivered by Justice Kate O'Regan, held that the provision was unconstitutional.
* Violation of Rights: The court found that forcing an accused to prove their innocence (reverse onus) violated the presumption of innocence.
* No Justification: The state failed to prove that the presumption was necessary or that it effectively helped to combat drug trafficking.
* Result: Section 21(1)(a)(i) was declared invalid, and the cases were sent back to the High Court.

Impact
This case affirmed that the state must prove all elements of a crime beyond a reasonable doubt, and strengthened the protection of accused individuals against unfair burdens of proof

Th9is is from <https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZACC/1995/11media.pdf>: S v Bhulwana Case CCT 12/95 Explanatory Note

The following explanation is provided to assist the media in reporting this case and is not binding on the Constitutional Court or any member of the Court.

Legal Issue: Section 21 (1)(a)(i) of the Drugs and Drug Trafficking Act 140 of 1992 provides that if an accused has been found in possession of more than 115 grams of dagga, he or she will be presumed to have been dealing in dagga and will be convicted of the offence of dealing (as opposed to the lesser offence of possession) unless that person proves that he or she has not been dealing in dagga.

Application In This Case: Considering a reference to the issue of the validity of the section from the Supreme Court, the Constitutional Court held the section to be unconstitutional with effect from the date of the judgment. The Court considered the section to be an infringement of the right of an accused person to be presumed innocent in s 25(3)(c) of the Constitution. The Court found that the section was not justifiable in terms of s 33(1) of the Constitution, holding that the State had failed to prove that the presumption substantially furthered the aim of combating the trafficking of illegal drugs. The Court ordered that the declaration of invalidity should invalidate the use of the presumption in any criminal trial in which the verdict was given after the Constitution came into operation and in which, at the time of the judgment, either an appeal or review is pending or the time for noting an appeal has not yet expired. The judgment of the Court was delivered by O'Regan J and was concurred in by all the other members of the Court.
